title: Megan Moroney cancels show mid-performance, leaves stage in tears
summary: Megan Moroney called canceling her Denver concert at Ball Arena "the hardest decision" she's ever made. The show is rescheduled for Aug. 27.
story: Country music star Megan Moroney told Fox News Digital she is not ‘emotionally available’ for a romantic relationship, putting all her energy into her music career.
Country star Megan Moroney cut her Denver concert short Tuesday night after becoming too sick to continue performing, later telling fans it was "the hardest decision" she has ever had to make.
The singer took the stage at Ball Arena but struggled through just three songs before stopping the show. Moroney returned to address the audience herself, apologizing as she fought back tears.
"I am obviously extremely sick, and I thought I did everything to make myself better, and obviously, two songs in, I just can't play this show tonight," she told the crowd in a fan-recorded video.
JON BON JOVI ABRUPTLY ENDS MADISON SQUARE GARDEN SHOW AFTER HEALTH SETBACK
Fan-recorded video captures Megan Moroney fighting back tears as she stops her Denver Ball Arena show after just three songs due to illness. (Photo by Rick Kern/Getty Images for CMT)
MEGAN MORONEY STUNS IN ORANGE BIKINI DURING FRIEND'S BAHAMAS BACHELORETTE
Despite ending the performance early, Moroney assured concertgoers she planned to make up for the disappointing night.
"I want to give you guys the show you deserve. ... I'm sorry," she said.
Fans inside the arena responded with encouragement, with one audience member shouting, "That's OK Meg, I love you," as the visibly emotional singer exited the stage.
Ball Arena later confirmed the concert had been canceled because Moroney was feeling under the weather.
The "Am I Okay?" singer shared an emotional Instagram message after ending her concert early, promising Denver fans a rescheduled date. (NDZ/Star Max/GC Images)
"Megan is unable to continue her performance this evening due to illness, and we must end the show at this time," the venue said in a statement.
"Please allow event staff to direct you to the nearest exit, and we will follow up with more information as soon as we're able."
COUNTRY SINGER MEGAN MORONEY SWEARS OFF DATING AFTER MEN 'RUINED' HER BIGGEST MOMENTS
Moroney apologized to fans for canceling her Denver show, saying she was unable to perform at 100% and announcing the concert has been rescheduled. (Megan Moroney/Instagram)
The venue added that updates would be posted on its website and apologized "for the inconvenience" while thanking fans for their understanding and cooperation.
Shortly after, Moroney shared an emotional message with fans on Instagram, explaining that continuing the concert would have meant delivering a performance below her own standards.
"That was the hardest decision I've ever had to make & I'm so sorry to cancel the show tonight," she wrote.
LIKE WHAT YOU'RE READING? CLICK HERE FOR MORE ENTERTAINMENT NEWS
"I never ever will give you guys a show that is not 100% and by song 3 I knew that I was not capable of giving that to you tonight."
The "Am I Okay?" singer said she was devastated by the decision, adding, "I'm typing this as I'm quite literally bawling my eyes out in my dressing room & it hurts me so much to disappoint you all."

Moroney also announced that the Denver concert has been rescheduled for Aug. 27. Tickets purchased for Tuesday night's performance will be honored for the new date, and fans unable to attend can request refunds through their original point of purchase.
"I've never had to do this & I'm truly so sorry," she wrote before closing her message with, "i love u guys."
Fox News Digital reached out to Moroney for comment.
CLICK HERE TO SIGN UP FOR THE ENTERTAINMENT NEWSLETTER
After leaving college, she moved to Nashville. Moroney's "Tennessee Orange" breakthrough helped transform her into an award-winning country sensation. (John Shearer/Getty Images for CMT)
The abrupt cancellation comes as Moroney continues touring following the success of her third album and a string of sold-out performances across the country.
Her emotional apology and promise to return were met with widespread support from fans online, many of whom encouraged the singer to focus on recovering before getting back on stage.
Despite the canceled show, Moroney's music career continues to soar.
After attending the University of Georgia, she moved to Nashville to pursue music full time.
CLICK HERE TO DOWNLOAD THE FOX NEWS APP
Her 2022 breakout hit, "Tennessee Orange," launched her into the country music spotlight, and she has released three albums since: "Lucky" (2023), "Am I Okay?" (2024) and "Cloud 9" (2026).
Moroney also earned ACM and CMA honors as the country's top new female artist before releasing her latest project, "Cloud 9," in February and launching her current tour in May.

story: ‘The Five’ co-hosts analyze Halle Berry accusing Gov. Gavin Newsom of 'devaluing' women 'in midlife.'

Berry showed off her fit figure with a picture of her in a black one-piece swimsuit with a plunging neckline. (Halle Berry Instagram)
GISELE BÜNDCHEN CELEBRATES BIRTHDAY IN LEOPARD-PRINT BIKINI AS SHE REFLECTS ON GRATITUDE

title: Willie Nelson urges Americans to fight 'water thieving' AI data centers devouring rural Texas farmland

story: Fox News Flash top entertainment and celebrity headlines are here.
Willie Nelson urged Americans to think again when it comes to building the future.
Nelson, 93, encouraged followers to "fight against data centers invading our land" in a social media plea shared Tuesday.
The country music legend reflected on being able to see "stars at night" in his Texas hometown, but that light pollution and "water thieving" were imminent in a looming industrial climate.
KACEY MUSGRAVES ABRUPTLY CANCELS CONCERT DATES FROM 'MIDDLE OF NOWHERE' TOUR
Willie Nelson pleaded with his followers Tuesday to focus on the environmental impacts of data farming centers. (Peter Pakvis)

SINGER ZACH TOP SLAMS MODERN COUNTRY MUSIC, SAYS IT LACKS 'SOUL'
"The last thing we need is a loud, water thieving, light polluting, data center anywhere near our town (or any others for that matter)."
The "On the Road Again" singer noted how "the strength of rural America has never come from big industrial footprints."
A post shared by Willie Nelson (@willienelsonofficial)

"It comes from generations of people, open spaces, local businesses, and a connection to the land," Nelson wrote. title: Jared Leto responds to sexual misconduct allegations made by multiple women in explosive documentary
summary: Jared Leto denies sexual assault allegations from four women who claim offenses occurred when they were teenagers, calling the claims "categorically false."
story: Fox News Flash top entertainment and celebrity headlines are here.
Jared Leto is denying allegations of criminal sexual conduct after four women accused the Oscar-winning actor and musician of offenses they claim occurred when they were teenagers.
"I have never sexually assaulted anyone in my entire life," Leto said in a statement provided to Fox News Digital. "These claims are absolutely and categorically false."

The allegations are detailed in the new BBC documentary, "Jared Leto: Hollywood's Dark Secret," which premiered Wednesday. The film features interviews with 10 participants, nine of whom shared their stories publicly for the first time.
According to the documentary, four women allege Leto engaged in criminal sexual conduct between 2002 and 2016, when the actor and Thirty Seconds to Mars frontman — now 54 — was in his 30s and 40s.
JASON ALEXANDER APOLOGIZES AFTER COURTNEY STODDEN SAYS 2012 COMEDY SKETCH OBJECTIFIED HER AS A MINOR
Jared Leto has denied allegations of sexual misconduct, telling Fox News Digital the claims are "categorically false." (Christopher Polk/Variety via Getty Images)

In a BBC story published Wednesday, one woman alleged she had sex with Leto at his California home when she was 17 years old. According to the outlet, the woman said Leto, who was 34 at the time, dismissed concerns after they discussed California's age of consent being 18.
"It wasn't a huge concern for him," she alleged. "He told me, 'I would like you to call me daddy.' And it was either pretend to be a little girl or 'my little girl.'"
The woman said that because she was "so naive and vulnerable" at the time, she didn't understand that this behavior wasn't "normal" in an adult relationship.
"It was only as time went on that I realized more and more how scary that really was," she said.
OSCAR WINNER JARED LETO ADMITS DEPTHS OF DRUG ADDICTION: 'IT TOOK ME FOR A RIDE'
A second woman alleged Leto sexually assaulted her in what she described as a "dingy gross motel" in Las Vegas in 2002, saying he invited her there after meeting her at the store where she worked.
According to the documentary, the woman said Leto called her into the bathroom while he was showering.
Multiple women have alleged sexual misconduct against Leto, four of whom were teens at the time.  (Mike Marsland/WireImage)
"I don't think there was many words exchanged, and he opened the shower curtain and started kissing me," she alleged.
She claimed Leto then grabbed her hand and forced her to masturbate him.
"Most of my life I had viewed this event as, I was a stupid girl … and so this bad thing happened," she said.
A third woman alleged Leto threatened her with sexual assault after inviting her to a hotel room in London after a Thirty Seconds to Mars concert in 2013.

The former model said she was 19 at the time but told Leto she was 17 because she "felt the need" to pretend to be younger to protect herself. After telling Leto she was 17, the woman claimed he said, "Age is just a number, and, anyway, we're in Europe."
JARED LETO RECALLS ‘NEARLY DYING’ WHILE ROCK CLIMBING
The woman claimed one of Leto's assistants encouraged her to join in on another party at a nearby hotel room. However, when she arrived, she realized there was no party.
Ten participants spoke about their experiences with Leto in a new BBC documentary.  (Jason Kempin/Getty Images for MTV)
"I get into the hotel room, it's really dark and then I see that it's just him," she said. "Weren't there supposed to be other people?"
The woman claimed she asked Leto for a phone charger or some cash to get home, but he dismissed her requests.

After asking if she could sleep on a chaise lounge because she had no way home, the woman claimed Leto repeatedly told her she would wake up "with a d--- in her ass."
After realizing she "was not safe," the woman left the room.
A fourth woman said Leto began grooming her when she was 16, made repeated sexually explicit phone calls to her and on at least one occasion suggested the two have sex.

According to the BBC, the woman was later presented with a nondisclosure agreement intended to prevent her from discussing her alleged relationship with Leto. She declined to sign the document, which BBC said it had reviewed.
Leto reportedly did not respond to requests for comment during the making of the documentary. (Axelle/Bauer-Griffin/FilmMagic)
Additional women also accused the actor of making what they described as "strange" and sexually explicit phone calls while they were underage or teenagers.

The documentary also featured interviews with two former employees connected to Thirty Seconds to Mars, who claim staff members were uncomfortable with Leto's interactions with teenage girls.
One former employee alleged Leto would invite teenage girls backstage to his dressing room or to a house where the band was recording.
"I think everyone thought the age gap was way too big," the former employee said.
The allegations are the latest in a series of claims against the Academy Award winner.

In June 2025, Air Mail published interviews with nine women who alleged Leto engaged in inappropriate sexual behavior over the years, including accusations involving minors. Those allegations included claims that Leto asked sexually explicit questions to a 16-year-old, exposed himself to a 17-year-old and placed an 18-year-old's hand "on him."
The Thirty Seconds to Mars frontman was in his 30s and 40s at the time of the alleged allegations.  (Lia Toby/Getty Images)
The Air Mail report followed allegations by Los Angeles DJ Allie Teilz, who publicly claimed she was assaulted by Leto when she was 17.
At the time, representatives for Leto "expressly" denied the Air Mail allegations, calling Teilz's claims "demonstrably false."

title: Oscar-winning singer Glen Hansard dead at 56
summary: Glen Hansard, the Oscar-winning Irish singer-songwriter behind "Falling Slowly" and star of "Once," died at 56 in a motorcycle crash in Dublin.
story: Fox News Flash top entertainment and celebrity headlines are here.

Irish singer-songwriter Glen Hansard, the Academy Award-winning musician behind the beloved song "Falling Slowly" and star of the acclaimed film "Once," has died after a motorcycle crash in Dublin. He was 56.
Hansard's management confirmed his death Wednesday, telling Irish broadcaster RTÉ that his family was "deeply shocked and heartbroken."

According to Irish police, a man in his 50s was killed in a single-vehicle motorcycle crash in Lucan, on the outskirts of Dublin, before 4:30 a.m. Wednesday. First responders treated the rider at the scene, but he was pronounced dead shortly after.
'IT TAKES TWO' RAPPER ROB BASE DEAD AT 59 AFTER CANCER FIGHT HE KEPT HIDDEN FROM FRIENDS
Glen Hansard died after a motorcycle crash on July 29. (Luciano Viti/Getty Images)
Hansard's legacy was tied to "Once," the 2007 Irish musical drama that transformed him from a respected hometown musician into an international star.
Starring opposite Markéta Irglová, Hansard played a struggling street musician whose connection with a fellow artist unfolds through music on the streets of Dublin.
The film became a global success, earning roughly $23 million at the worldwide box office and producing one of the decade's most memorable original songs, according to Rolling Stone.
GEORGE MICHAEL DIED WORTH $128M, BUT FRIENDS SAY HE SECRETLY GAVE AWAY MILLIONS FOR DECADES: AUTHOR
Hansard was best known for starring in "Once," which contained the Oscar-winning song "Falling Slowly." (Luciano Viti/Getty Images)
Hansard and Irglová won the Academy Award for best original song in 2008 for "Falling Slowly," a quiet acoustic ballad that became synonymous with the film.
Long before Hollywood recognition, Hansard had already established himself as one of Ireland's most respected performers.
Born in Ballymun, Dublin, in 1970, he began playing music as a teenager while busking throughout the city.

In 1990, he founded The Frames, a band that developed a devoted following over several decades. Around the same time, Hansard expanded into acting, appearing as guitarist Outspan Foster in Alan Parker's 1991 film "The Commitments."
His career continued to evolve after "Once." Alongside Irglová, he formed The Swell Season while also maintaining an active solo career.

Markéta Irglová and Glen Hansard of The Swell Season are seen performing during the 2025 Newport Folk Festival. (Douglas Mason/Getty Images)
His 2015 album "Didn't He Ramble" earned a Grammy nomination for Best Folk Album.
Hansard was equally recognized for the way he remained connected to Dublin's music community despite his international success.

Each Christmas Eve, he gathered fellow musicians outside Dublin's Gaiety Theatre for a charity busking tradition benefiting the Dublin Simon Community, an annual event that became a holiday fixture for locals.
He also played a prominent role during one of Ireland's most emotional public farewells.

At the funeral of Pogues frontman Shane MacGowan in December 2023, Hansard and Irish singer Lisa O'Neill performed "Fairytale of New York," inspiring mourners throughout the church to sing and dance in celebration of MacGowan's life.
Hansard's reputation reached well beyond Ireland.
Hansard is seen performing at Michael Dorf Presents: The Music Of Van Morrison at Carnegie Hall on March 21, 2019, in New York City. (Bobby Bank/Getty Images)
The Irish musician joined Bruce Springsteen onstage at Kilkenny's Nowlan Park in 2013 for a performance of "Drive All Night."
Tributes from across Ireland began pouring in within hours of news of his death.
Irish Prime Minister Micheál Martin wrote on X that he was "deeply saddened to learn of the passing of Glen Hansard."
"A talented musician and actor who made a significant contribution to Ireland's cultural landscape over many years," Martin posted.

Waterboys frontman Mike Scott also reflected on Hansard's legacy, writing on X, "Just heard that Glen Hansard has died. Travel on well, Buddy. You made your dreams come true. I'm so sorry that he leaves his wife and 3-year-old child."

Hansard is survived by his partner, Finnish poet Maire Saaritsa, and their son, Christy, who was born in 2022.
His career leaves behind a catalog that stretched from Dublin sidewalks to the Oscar stage, making him one of Ireland's most enduring musical voices.
The Associated Press contributed to this report.
Stephanie Giang-Paunon is an entertainment reporter for Fox News Digital.

title: King Charles sends 'defiance' message to Prince William with Buckingham Palace room offer to Harry: expert
summary: Royal experts say Prince William demands hard boundaries with Prince Harry while King Charles seeks healing, creating a rift over the monarchy's future.
story: Dan Wakeford, founder of Celebrity Intelligence, discusses Prince Harry's expected UK return, his relationship with King Charles, and why a meeting with Prince William remains unlikely.
King Charles and his heir are said to be at odds over how to handle Prince Harry.

Multiple royal experts echoed the sentiment to Fox News Digital after royal author Robert Jobson told Page Six that Prince William and his estranged brother have "different agendas" and maintain very different relationships with their father.
Fox News Digital reached out to Buckingham Palace and Kensington Palace for comment.
KING CHARLES KEPT PRINCE WILLIAM, KATE MIDDLETON IN THE DARK ABOUT SECRET HARRY AND MEGHAN REUNION: REPORT

The Sun reported that Prince Harry is expected to visit the U.K. in September and his father, King Charles (center), will offer his son a room at Buckingham Palace in London. (Aaron Chown - WPA Pool/Getty Images)

"When it comes to Harry, William drew a line in the sand after the publication of Harry's memoir, 'Spare,' and he is disappointed that his father is not standing up for him," Christopher Andersen, author of "The King," told Fox News Digital.

"William loves his father and appreciates better than anyone how underestimated Charles has been over the years. He wants the king to leave his mark on history. But deep down, he knows he and his family — particularly his wife, Kate — are the future of the monarchy."
WATCH: PRINCE WILLIAM UNLIKELY TO RECONCILE WITH PRINCE HARRY SOON: EXPERT
While Charles and William are described as being "perfectly civil to each other," sources told Page Six there are ongoing disagreements about how the monarchy should be led.
"The problem with William is that he thinks he knows best," royal biographer Hugo Vickers told the outlet.
Prince William, Prince of Wales, meets young people and volunteers in the Common Room at Eagle House on July 9, 2026, in Hastings, England. (WPA Pool/Getty Images)

"King Charles is tired," Andersen stressed to Fox News Digital. "He would like to have everything as it was before Megxit. But he knows how willful William is. Queen Elizabeth's cousin Margaret Rhodes told me more than once that the relationship between Charles and his late mother wasn't cozy. But what people don't know is that the royal family isn't set up to be 'cozy.' Well, it still isn't. It's 'The Firm,' remember?"

Prince William, Prince of Wales and King Charles III walk behind Queen Elizabeth II's coffin as it is transported on a gun carriage from Buckingham Palace to Westminster Hall ahead of her lying in state on Sept. 14, 2022, in London. William is heir to the British throne. (Max Mumby/Indigo/Getty Images)

People magazine reported Harry is expected to visit his home country again in September. The Sun also reported that the king plans to offer him a room at Buckingham Palace in London for his stay. Buckingham Palace and Harry's representatives had no comment on the report when reached by People magazine.

Royal broadcaster Ian Pelham Turner told Fox News Digital that Charles' reported offer to accommodate Harry in September is "a potential lifeline" that also sends a message of "defiance" to William, who reportedly wants "no further contact with his estranged brother."

Prince Harry, Duke of Sussex departs from The Invictus Games Foundation Conversation: From Policy to Practice at Chatham House on July 7, 2026, in London. Multiple royal experts told Fox News Digital that there's no doubt King Charles' younger son misses his life in the U.K. (Eamonn M. McCormack/Getty Images)
British broadcaster and photographer Helena Chard told Fox News Digital that William is known for being stubborn behind palace doors and is not one to forgive easily.
CLICK HERE TO SIGN UP FOR THE ENTERTAINMENT NEWSLETTER

Prince William (pictured here) did not meet with his estranged younger brother, Prince Harry, who spent time with their father, King Charles III, at Highgrove House, the monarch's private residence, on July 10, 2026. (Chris Jackson/Getty Images)
"Megxit forced William to grow up fast as the future king," she said.

"Prince Harry’s potential lifeline return to the United Kingdom in September and being offered accommodation at Buckingham Palace by King Charles is, to me, a major sign of defiance to William’s wishes of no future contact with his erstwhile brother," royal broadcaster Ian Pelham Turner told Fox News Digital. (Samir Hussein/WireImage)

"He had to protect the institution while his brother walked away. William believes the monarchy must be seen to do the right thing, even when it's painful. From what I understand, he felt his father didn't handle that firmly enough. He also believes in protecting it by drawing hard lines. But he's not the king yet."

Prince William, Prince of Wales, known as the Duke of Rothesay and Catherine, Princess of Wales, known as the Duchess of Rothesay when in Scotland, smile to well-wishers as they arrive for a visit to Aros Hall, a local community hub on April 29, 2025, in Tobermory, Scotland. (Chris Jackson/Getty Images)

"Where Charles may want to smooth things over, to play peacemaker with Harry, William and Catherine are determined to set boundaries. Charles is reigning, but William and Catherine are planning. And that planning is starting to look a lot like leading. Charles wants healing. William and Catherine want survival and stability. William is not doing this to be difficult. He’s doing it because he believes it’s right."

Since marrying in 2018 and making their royal exit in 2020, the Duke and Duchess of Sussex have been attempting to carve out their own independent roles outside the monarchy. (Joshua Sammer/Getty Images)

Royal experts told Fox News Digital that William and Harry have remained estranged since the Duke and Duchess of Sussex stepped back as senior working royals in 2020 and relocated to California. Harry and Meghan have maintained that relentless tabloid scrutiny and what they describe as a lack of support from the palace drove their decision to leave royal life.

Prince William, Prince of Wales and Prince Harry, Duke of Sussex attend the Committal Service for Queen Elizabeth II at St. George's Chapel, Windsor Castle on Sept. 19, 2022, in Windsor, England. (Getty Images)

Since stepping away from royal life, Harry and Meghan have publicly aired their grievances in high-profile interviews and documentaries. Harry's 2023 memoir, "Spare," further deepened the fallout within the royal family.
Prince Harry's book "Spare" is displayed in a bookstore on Dec. 16, 2023, in Bath, England. (Matt Cardy/Getty Images)

On July 10, the king hosted his younger son and his family for the first time in years in what royal observers viewed as an effort to repair the longstanding rift. The Sussexes secretly met with the king and Queen Camilla at Highgrove House, a country estate west of London, Buckingham Palace confirmed.
LIKE WHAT YOU’RE READING? CLICK HERE FOR MORE ENTERTAINMENT NEWS
Prince Harry and Meghan Markle, the Duke and Duchess of Sussex, relocated to California in 2020. (Chris Jackson/Getty Images)

Vanity Fair royal correspondent Katie Nicholl reported that, according to sources, "not even the Prince and Princess of Wales were made aware that the meeting was taking place." A source close to Charles also told Nicholl the hour-long meeting was "completely cloak-and-dagger, orchestrated by the king."
Meanwhile, William and Kate attended the DMI Royal Charity Polo Cup 2026 at Guards Polo Club in Windsor. The brothers did not see each other.
Kate Middleton kisses Prince William as she presents the prizes after the DMI Royal Charity Polo Cup 2026. (Max Mumby/Indigo/Getty Images)

"Obviously, King Charles and Prince William are very different characters, sometimes with conflicting temperaments," royal expert Richard Fitzwilliams told Fox News Digital. "What no one can alter is that William, Kate, and their family are the future of the monarchy. And it is natural for the king, who is battling cancer, to want to see his grandchildren."
British royals expert Hilary Fordwich told Fox News Digital there's no feud between Prince William and his father, King Charles. (Max Mumby/Indigo/Getty Images)
Fitzwilliams argued that William made his disapproval clear on the day the king and queen saw the Sussexes by being absent from the reunion.
"William is making it clear that he has his own set of principles, his own set of rules about what is right and wrong," Andersen said.
A general view of Buckingham Palace in London, England, on July 6, 2026. (Dan Kitwood/Getty Images)

"He feels Harry has violated those rules one too many times. It's not entirely personal. William has a strong sense of duty when it comes not only to his family but also to his country and his family's place in history. He feels Harry has shot the royal family's reputation full of holes. And for what? To become a SoCal influencer?"
CLICK HERE TO GET THE FOX NEWS APP

Prince Harry (left) and Prince William (right) attend the unveiling of a statue of their mother, Princess Diana, at The Sunken Garden in Kensington Palace, London on July 1, 2021, which would have been her 60th birthday. Royal experts told Fox News Digital the last time the brothers spoke was in 2022 during Queen Elizabeth II's funeral. (Dominic Lipinski/POOL/AFP via Getty Images)
"William feels Harry has betrayed not only the current generation of royals but also past generations, including their grandmother, Queen Elizabeth II, and future generations," Andersen added.

British royal expert Hilary Fordwich told Fox News Digital that while reports of a fracture between Charles and William are overstated, the two are far from aligned on how to deal with Harry. Whether father and son can find common ground on Harry remains to be seen.

From left: Prince William, Prince of Wales, King Charles III and Queen Camilla attend the Thistle Service at St. Giles' Cathedral in Edinburgh, Scotland on July 1, 2026. (Aaron Chown/POOL/AFP via Getty Images)
"Prince William is no fool," Fordwich said. "Every time his zero-tolerance approach is proven correct, his influence increases."
Prince Harry attends the Time100 Sports Gala at Pier Sixty on July 16, 2026, in New York City. (WWD via Getty Images)
In May 2025, Harry told the BBC he would like to reconcile with his family.
"There's no point in continuing to fight anymore."
Stephanie Nolasco is an Entertainment Reporter for Fox News Digital.

title: Anthony Fauci's Hollywood supporters: Julia Roberts, Katy Perry and Orlando Bloom among celebrity backers
summary: From Julia Roberts' "personal hero" to Katy Perry and Orlando Bloom's "Fauci Gang," Hollywood's biggest stars rallied behind Dr. Anthony Fauci during COVID-19.
story: Laura Ingraham and Raymond Arroyo examine newly released diary entries from Dr. Anthony Fauci, highlighting his fascination with Hollywood and celebrity culture. The entries detail Fauci's interactions with celebrities like Julia Roberts and Barbra Streisand.
Julia Roberts, Katy Perry and Orlando Bloom were among Dr. Anthony Fauci's biggest celebrity supporters during the height of the COVID-19 pandemic.

As the 85-year-old infectious disease expert became the face of America's COVID-19 response after the pandemic became a global crisis in March 2020, he also attracted an unlikely fan club in Hollywood – including Brad Pitt portraying him on "Saturday Night Live at Home."

While chronicling his management of the spiraling health emergency, Fauci also wrote frequently of his rapidly rising fame in his private 2020 journals, which were released by Senate Homeland Security Committee Chairman Rand Paul, R-Ky, earlier this week.
FAUCI'S NEWLY RELEASED COVID DIARIES REVEAL BIZARRE FIXATION ON FAME AS PANDEMIC DEATHS MOUNTED
"The situation with my national and international fame is explosive and really unimaginable," Fauci wrote in a May 21, 2020, entry in his diary.

Julia Roberts, Katy Perry and Orlando Bloom were among the stars who lined up behind Dr. Anthony Fauci during the COVID-19 pandemic. (William B. Plowman/NBC via Getty Images; Kevin Mazur/Getty Images; Taylor Hill/FilmMagic)
"It is not hyoperbole [sic] to say that today I am the most famous and talked about person in the country and one of the most recognizable peson [sic] in the world," he added.
Fauci also dedicated significant space across numerous entries to logging his personal interactions with Hollywood A-listers, including Julia Roberts, Barbra Streisand and Sean Penn among others.
Fauci's personal journals were released ahead of his scheduled testimony before the Senate Homeland Security and Governmental Affairs Committee. (Chip Somodevilla/Getty Images)
INSIDE FAUCI'S PRIVATE DIARY: WHAT HE WROTE ABOUT TRUMP, TV PERSONALITIES AND CELEBRITIES

As Fauci comes under increasing scrutiny ahead of his scheduled testimony before the Senate Homeland Security Committee as part of its investigation into the origins of the pandemic, here's a look at the celebrities who publicly championed the longtime public health official during the pandemic.
Julia Roberts
Julia Roberts gushed that Fauci was her "personal hero." (Amy Sussman/Getty Images)
Julia Roberts raved over Fauci while conducting an Instagram Live interview with him as part of ONE Campaign’s new #PassTheMic series.
"How rad that we have maybe the coolest man on the planet right now," the Oscar winner told viewers before Fauci joined her on the video call. "Wow, this is intense."
Roberts then gasped and beamed when Fauci appeared on the screen, saying, "Oh, this is such a thrill."

"This is a thrill for me because there are very few experts of anything in the world, and you truly have emerged as a personal hero for me," she added. "Just to have this little corner of your time for us is such a joy."

In a May 2020 diary entry, Fauci wrote about his "wonderful discussion" with Roberts, who he described as "absolutely fabulous" and "totally down to earth." He also shared that he was "embarrassed" when she told him that he was her personal hero.

On Feb. 10, 2021, Fauci detailed how Roberts presented him with amfAR's Award of Courage virtually from her home in California. "When my image came up on the screen she gasped and said that every time she sees me her throat gets dry and she gets nervous and excused herself to go into the kitchen and get a glass of water," he wrote.
Kim Kardashian
Kim Kardashian organized a Zoom call with Fauci and 36 other celebrities. (Taylor Hill/Getty Images)

In April 2020, Kim Kardashian organized a private Zoom call with Fauci which included 36 other celebrities, athletes and influencers. Katy Perry, Orlando Bloom, Gwyneth Paltrow, Ashton Kutcher, Mila Kunis, Brad Falchuk, Tiffany Haddish, 2 Chainz and Dennis Quaid were among the notable attendees.

"It was a whole bunch of movie stars and some sports figures, and they wanted to know about what they could do to stay safe, about wearing masks and avoiding crowds," Fauci said of the hourlong call in a November 2020 interview with CNN. "I was impressed by the questions they asked, by their level of sophistication."
EXPOSED FAUCI DIARY SHOWS HE ESTIMATED COVID-19 DEATH RATE TO BE MUCH LOWER THAN WHAT HE TOLD CONGRESS
Fauci explained that he agreed to the call due to the group's enormous reach, noting that they had "megaphones" and "could get the word out about staying safe."

"Each of them has enormous numbers of followers on their social media accounts," he told CNN. "I could say to them, for example, it's important to wear a mask, and they get on their accounts and say 'wear a mask' and it goes out to an additional couple of million people."
Katy Perry and Orlando Bloom
Katy Perry and Orlando Bloom wore "Fauci Gang" hoodies. (Stefanie Keenan/Getty Images for Academy Museum of Motion Pictures)

Katy Perry and Orlando Bloom, who were engaged at the time, actively demonstrated their support for Fauci as the crisis was unfolding. Along with participating in the Zoom call, the former couple donned matching black hoodies emblazoned with the wording "Fauci Gang" for an Instagram post that Bloom shared in May 2020.
"Double tap if you’re in the #drfauci gang," Bloom wrote in the caption.

The hoodies were created as part of a Jerry Media x PizzaSlime collaboration and priced at $69. According to Bustle, the first batch of hoodies quickly sold out after their release. A portion of the proceeds from each sale benefited the CDC Foundation's Coronavirus Emergency Response Fund.
Jennifer Garner
Jennifer Garner said she loved Fauci ahead of interviewing him. (Chris Haston/WBTV via Getty Images)
Jennifer Garner publicly praised Fauci before hosting the infectious disease expert for a lengthy Instagram Live in September 2020 in which they discussed parents' concerns during the pandemic.

Garner later shared the interview in an Instagram post, writing in the caption, "Conversation with Dr. Fauci Back-to-School/vaccine/sports/and more questions answered here. I love Dr. Fauci—and you will, too."
The actress and Fauci's conversation spanned a wide range of topics, including schools reopening, youth sports, vaccines, vitamins, flu shots and when Americans could safely return to movie theaters.
During the interview, Garner expressed her gratitude to Fauci, telling him, "I just wanted to start by just saying thank you for never lying to us. Thank you for always giving it to us straight."
"I know that you have saved, I mean, countless lives," she added.
TOM HANKS JOKES ABOUT THE NAME HE WOULD GIVE CORONAVIRUS VACCINE
Leonardo DiCaprio
Leonardo DiCaprio paid tribute to Fauci at a virtual gala. (Jason Armond)

Leonardo DiCaprio honored Fauci during the National Italian American Foundation's 2020 virtual gala, where the infectious disease expert received the Leonardo da Vinci Award for Leadership in Health and Science.

"While COVID is keeping most of us at home, people like Dr. Fauci go to work each morning with one goal: to see our nation through the most devastating pandemic in a century," DiCaprio said via the Washingtonian.
"I am delighted that NIAF is honoring his lifelong commitment to serving the public good, we are fortunate to have Dr Fauci's leadership and guidance in these difficult times," he added.

Other celebrities who shared tributes to Fauci at the gala included Al Pacino, Robert De Niro, Martin Scorsese, Francis Ford Coppola, Michael Douglas, Patti LuPone, Bono, Marisa Tomei, Alan Alda, Dionne Warwick and Angelica Huston.
Matthew McConaughey
Matthew McConaughey discussed myths and vaccines with Fauci during a 40-minute conversation in August 2020. (Getty Images)
Matthew McConaughey gave Fauci one of his biggest celebrity platforms during the pandemic when he interviewed the infectious disease expert on Instagram in August 2020.

During their 40-minute conversation, McConaughey and Fauci discussed COVID-19 myths and vaccines. The Oscar winner expressed his anger and disappointment over how he felt the virus had become "politicized."
"Like a lot of people, I've been more than disillusioned — actually quite full of rage — at how COVID has been politicized," McConaughey said.

The actor closed their conversation by embracing Fauci's call for Americans to "pull together" as the former Chief Medical Advisor to the President noted they had done in the aftermath of World War II and 9/11.
"This is equivalent to that, Matthew. We've got to pull together, absolutely," Fauci said.
"That's it," McConaughey said. "We can have our freedom and our party later. Right now, let's pull together."
Alyssa Milano
Alyssa Milano vocally defended Fauci during the pandemic. (Gerardo Mora/Getty Images)

Alyssa Milano was among Hollywood's most vocal defenders of Fauci during the pandemic. The actress frequently shared his interviews on social media, encouraged followers to trust the nation's top infectious disease expert and repeatedly criticized political attacks against him as debates over masks, shutdowns and vaccines intensified.

However, Milano, who is a longtime critic of President Donald Trump, publicly expressed frustration with Fauci as she shared her opinion that he hadn't been outspoken enough in challenging the administration's response to the pandemic.

"Dr. Fauci might be great and a national treasure, but please let us not forget that he just sat there as Trump made ridiculous uneducated public health claims," she wrote on X in July 2020. "He has also allowed the White House to silence him as things continued to spiral out of control."
LIKE WHAT YOU'RE READING? CLICK HERE FOR MORE ENTERTAINMENT NEWS
Mark Ruffalo
Mark Ruffalo praised Fauci for "speaking truth to power." (Lia Toby/Getty Images)
Mark Ruffalo repeatedly praised Fauci and amplified the infectious disease expert on social media. In an April 2020 post on X, Ruffalo wrote, "Thank you Dr. Fauci for speaking truth to power."

Throughout the pandemic, Ruffalo shared the doctor's public health guidance with his followers, including posting Fauci's interviews along with vaccine information and messages encouraging Americans to follow scientific recommendations.

As criticism of Fauci intensified in mid-2020, Ruffalo often defended the infectious disease expert on social media. He amplified stories defending Fauci and called attention to what he viewed as attacks on public health experts.
CLICK HERE TO SIGN UP FOR THE ENTERTAINMENT NEWSLETTER
George Takei
George Takei consistently supported Fauci. (Tommaso Boddi/Getty Images for AMC)

George Takei was one of Fauci's most consistent celebrity supporters on social media. The "Star Trek" actor celebrated former President Joe Biden's decision to keep Fauci as chief medical adviser when he took office in January 2021.
In an X post he shared in December 2020, Takei shared a clip about Fauci continuing his role in Biden's administration, writing, "Wonderful news, indeed."
Throughout 2020 and beyond, Takei used his large social media following to defend Fauci, praise his work and criticize attacks on him.

title: Trace Adkins survived ex-wife's 'kill shot' after bullet passed through heart and lungs
summary: Trace Adkins revealed on Theo Von's podcast how ex-wife Julie Curtis shot him through the heart and both lungs in 1994 in what he called a "kill shot."
story: Grammy-winning country star Trace Adkins talks to Fox News Digital about his new single ‘American Made’ and why now is the perfect time for a song reminding Americans of American greatness. (Credit: Nicholas Ballasy for Fox News Digital)
Trace Adkins is going into detail about how he survived a "kill shot" from one of his ex-wives.

During a recent appearance on the "This Past Weekend with Theo Von" podcast, the 64-year-old country singer discussed his four marriages and how one of his exes "took it a little far" when asking him to leave, and shot him.
"She was mad. Wanted me to leave, and I wasn't going to leave, so that's how it went down," he said. "She put it under my left arm and the bullet came out under my right arm."
He went on to share that as she was holding the gun and preparing to fire it, he approached her with his hand out, asking her to give him the gun when she fired the shot.
Adkins discussed the circumstances surrounding one of his ex-wives shooting him during a recent podcast appearance. (Jason Kempin/Getty Images)
COUNTRY SINGER RAELYNN FILES FOR DIVORCE FROM ARMY VETERAN HUSBAND AFTER DECADE-LONG MARRIAGE

When asked what it felt like to be shot, Adkins explained that in his opinion, when the situation "is that serious, your body protects you," and "you just go into shock," adding that he doesn't remember feeling anything.

"I just remember getting up off the floor and then taking a few steps and then going back down and that's all I remember," he said. It went under this arm, came out this arm. So it went straight through. It went straight through my heart and both my lungs. It was a kill shot."

The "Ladies Love Country Boys" singer added: "The doctor said the only reason I survived was cause the bullet went through at point-blank velocity at muzzle velocity. So it didn't have time to mushroom. It was just muzzle velocity, so it just went straight through."
He went on to say that the pain from his injury came during the recovery process, saying that in order to repair his heart and lungs, "they just cut you and just crack you open."

title: Kelsey Grammer suspects he 'may have' lost Hollywood roles due to conservative views
summary: Kelsey Grammer suspects being a conservative in Hollywood for 40 years may have kept him off casting lists and out of awards conversations entirely.
story: Kelsey Grammer told Fox News Digital that the key to success in America is hard work and hurting as few people in the process.
Kelsey Grammer suggested his decades-long embrace of conservative politics may have come at a professional cost.
The "Frasier" star said he couldn't say for certain whether his politics had cost him work, but he believed his conservative views may have kept him off Hollywood's radar altogether.

"I have no idea," he said when asked whether he'd ever lost a role because of his political views during an appearance on "The Katie Miller Podcast." "I suspect I may have, but I suspect I may be, you know, in that category where they just don't even think about me, so it’s okay."
"'Oh, we wouldn't work with him, he's a conservative,'" he mused. "I hope that's not the case because I'm actually pretty good at what I do."

Grammer said the same political dynamics extended beyond casting decisions and into Hollywood's biggest honors. The 71-year-old actor argued political leanings had possibly become part of the equation when performances alone should decide who gets recognized.

"You know, there's always been sort of a popularity contest with awards anyway," Grammer explained. "And you surprise them a little bit, you do something good once in a while that might get attention. But there's so many overlays of what people will vote for and not vote for."

"I mean, politically, I'm kind of, you know, on the fringe of Hollywood. It's okay, I don’t mind, because I've been a, I'm a conservative. I've been a conservative in Hollywood for 40 years. I declared early. So, it’s been okay. They're kind of used to it with me," he added. "But there are other concerns that actually probably shouldn't enter into it. It shouldn't be politics. It should be performance, you know."
Kelsey Grammer's portrayal of psychiatrist Dr. Frasier Crane on "Cheers" paved the way for the Emmy-winning sitcom "Frasier," cementing his TV legacy. (NBCUniversal via Getty Images)
Grammer said he had privately found support from others in the entertainment industry who shared his political views but had chosen not to express them publicly.
"There's several of us in the closet," he admitted. "There's never those who aren't in the closet. Some of us who left the acting profession entirely."

Kelsey Grammer won multiple Emmy Awards for his portrayal of Dr. Frasier Crane, turning the psychiatrist into one of television's most beloved sitcom characters. (Bob Riha, Jr./Getty Images)
Grammer also weighed in on the state of television comedy, arguing modern sitcoms had lost the qualities that once made them resonate with audiences.

"...as a format, it's struggling again for the right writers and for trust in the human experience. They don't trust their audience anymore," the actor explained on the podcast. "And the key, the key to ‘Frasier's' success, was that it trusted the audience."

"It thought it was smart enough, and we thought they were intelligent enough to enjoy discovering that we had a family and lives and things we cared about, as well as being funny," Grammer added. "And they've lost that again."
When asked whether Hollywood writers had become too disconnected from audiences by embracing political correctness and an insular industry mindset, Grammer said one factor stood out.

"But, so, I think it may have maybe made a big wrong turn in terms of what people think is funny. It's mostly slapstick, and you have to earn slapstick to make it believable," Grammer noted. "If it's not believable, it's just a terrible joke. And I think that's where they've gone mostly."

Kelsey Grammer's portrayal of Dr. Frasier Crane helped make "Frasier" one of the most acclaimed sitcoms in TV history, with the series earning dozens of Emmy Awards during its run. (NBCUniversal via Getty Images)

title: Older adults taking 5 or more prescription drugs face higher risk of death, study finds
summary: Each additional prescription medication was linked to a 7% increase in death risk among older adults, raising urgent questions about deprescribing.
story: Older adults who walked at a significantly faster speed than their peers were about half as likely to develop cognitive impairment, according to Dr. Joe Verghese, MD, neurologist at Stony Brook Medicine.

Older adults who take five or more prescription medications face a significantly higher risk of death compared to those taking fewer drugs, according to a study published in the Journal of the American Geriatrics Society.
The research highlights the growing concern over polypharmacy, the medical term for taking five or more daily prescriptions, and its long-term effects on aging populations.
Led by Dr. Alexander Chaitoff of the University of Michigan School of Medicine, researchers analyzed national survey data collected from 7,828 adults aged 65 and older between 1999 and 2016.
LONGER LIVES, WORSE HEALTH? SCIENTISTS UNCOVER TROUBLING TREND ACROSS GENERATIONS
Trained staff directly inspected participants' pill bottles to verify medication use over the previous 30 days, then followed them for an average of 8.5 years, according to a press release.
More than half of participants (54.3%) fell into at least one high-risk medication category. The largest group consisted of older adults taking five or more prescription drugs (polypharmacy).
Over 40% of older adults studied were taking five or more prescription medications, a situation known as polypharmacy. (iStock)
Another group, 37.6% of those studied, used medications deemed risky for older individuals, such as drugs that can increase the risk of confusion or falls, the study revealed.
Additionally, 11.4% took combinations of medications that are known to cause major drug-to-drug interactions.
DOCTORS REVEAL HIDDEN DANGER FOR SOME OZEMPIC, WEGOVY USERS WITH BRAIN DISORDERS

"People taking more medications often have more underlying health conditions, which may also contribute to their higher mortality risk," Katy Dubinsky, New York-based pharmacist and founder of PostGigs, who was not involved in the study, told Fox News Digital.

After accounting for overall health and underlying conditions, taking five or more prescriptions was associated with a 38% increase in overall mortality risk. Each additional prescription medication added to a patient’s routine was linked to a 7% increase in death risk.
CLICK HERE FOR MORE HEALTH STORIES

Taking multiple medications has been shown to increase the likelihood of side effects, adverse drug reactions and accidental overdose, particularly as the liver and kidneys age and process drugs less efficiently, according to medical experts at Cleveland Clinic.
Researchers emphasized that these findings can help doctors identify patients who would benefit from safely stopping or reducing unnecessary medications. (iStock)

The total number of medications participants took was the strongest independent predictor of mortality, even after accounting for drug-to-drug interactions and potentially inappropriate prescriptions.
TEST YOURSELF WITH OUR LATEST LIFESTYLE QUIZ
These findings could help doctors determine which patients are the best candidates for "deprescribing," or carefully reducing or stopping unnecessary medications, the researchers stated.
CLICK HERE TO DOWNLOAD THE FOX NEWS APP
The authors noted several limitations, including that the study focused strictly on community-dwelling older adults, excluding those living in nursing homes or assisted care facilities.

Additionally, medication use was documented during a single 30-day snapshot at the start of the study, meaning researchers could not track subsequent changes in prescriptions or evolving health conditions over time.
Because the study relied on a single 30-day snapshot of medication use, it shows an association rather than direct proof that the prescriptions caused the higher death risk. (iStock)
Experts emphasized that observational studies show association rather than direct causation.
"I would not recommend that anyone stop a medication because of this study," said Dubinsky.

Instead, she recommends that people taking multiple medications should periodically review everything they take with their physician or pharmacist, including prescriptions, over-the-counter medications, vitamins and supplements.
"Ask why each medication is being taken, whether it is still needed and whether the dose remains appropriate," Dubinsky advised.

title: Daily eating habit linked to better brain health in older adults, new research suggests
summary: A six-month trial found that older women who ate within eight to nine hours daily showed cognitive improvements beyond what weight loss alone provided.
story: Dr. Mary Claire Haver breaks down how the menopause shift rewires metabolism, raising abdominal fat and inflammation, and reveals why tracking strength and fat distribution beats relying on the number on the scale.
Eating within a shorter daily window could help support brain health as people age, according to new research.

Preliminary findings presented at NUTRITION 2026 — the American Society for Nutrition’s annual meeting in Maryland — suggests that older women who ate within eight to nine hours per day saw slight cognitive improvement compared to those who spread their meals over about 12 hours each day.
The small six-month trial included 47 postmenopausal obese or overweight women aged 50 to 79. They were each advised to reduce their daily food intake by about 500 calories.
INTERMITTENT FASTING'S REAL BENEFIT MAY COME AFTER YOU START EATING AGAIN
Study findings

The participants were divided into two groups. One ate in a time-restricted window within an average of 8.2 hours, usually from 10 a.m. to 6 p.m. The other group ate across a 12.3-hour window, according to a news release.
Both groups saw weight-loss results, but the shorter-window group scored higher on cognitive tests. (iStock)
Both groups lost about 15 pounds over six months, but those in the shorter eating-window group performed better on cognitive tests measuring spatial planning and problem-solving.
The shorter-window group also showed fewer errors on memory and learning tests, but no meaningful differences in reaction time or multi-tasking ability.
PEOPLE LOST WEIGHT WHILE EATING SIGNIFICANTLY MORE FOOD — HERE'S THE SECRET

"These outcomes suggest a better ability to remember information during everyday tasks and reduce mistakes related to memory, attention and problem-solving," lead researcher Sue Shapses, Ph.D., a professor at Rutgers University and Rutgers-RWJ Medical Center, said in a press release. "Reductions in the eating window predicted greater improvements."

Although the pilot study included only a small number of participants, the researchers believe that time-restricted eating may support brain health by regulating circadian rhythm, reducing inflammation and improving metabolic health.
"Think of meal timing as one potential piece of the puzzle rather than a magic bullet."
Losing weight alone can help "ward off some of the aging-related cognitive decline," according to Shapses.

"And these data suggest there may be additional benefits if you stop eating four hours prior to going to sleep and reduce food intake to eight to nine hours per day, compared to the usual eating window of 12 hours per day."
People who are overweight or obese tend to face a higher likelihood of developing dementia as they age, the researchers said. (iStock)
Women, as well as adults who are overweight or obese, tend to face a higher likelihood of developing Alzheimer’s disease and other forms of dementia as they age, according to the researchers.
How might meal timing help the brain?

Lauri Wright, Ph.D., director of nutrition programs and associate professor at the USF College of Public Health, who was not involved in this research, reflected on these findings in an interview with Fox News Digital.
TEST YOURSELF WITH OUR LATEST LIFESTYLE QUIZ

"This is an interesting study because it suggests that when we eat may matter in addition to what and how much we eat," she said. "That suggests meal timing itself may have played a role, not just weight loss."
"The results are promising, but we need larger, longer studies before recommending time-restricted eating specifically to improve brain health."
Brain imaging should be performed within the first several hours after seeking medical attention for a stroke, a doctor advised. (iStock)
Experts are still learning about how intermittent fasting affects the brain, although "several biological mechanisms are being considered," Wright noted.

"Giving the body a longer overnight break from eating may improve insulin sensitivity, reduce chronic inflammation, support healthy circadian rhythms and allow cells more time for repair and maintenance," she said. "Those processes are all linked to healthy brain aging."
CLICK HERE FOR MORE HEALTH STORIES

From a practical standpoint, eating within a shorter daily window often leads people to consume fewer calories, which can promote weight loss, according to New York-based certified holistic nutritionist Robin DeCicco.
"We know that maintaining a healthy weight helps with virtually everything," she told Fox News Digital. "Eating within a restricted window helps people cut calories."
"When you fast or... have periods of time where you're not just eating throughout the whole day, it does help to lower markers of inflammation and certain sources of oxidative stress."
CLICK HERE TO SIGN UP FOR OUR HEALTH NEWSLETTER
Many people have reported "feeling better" when fasting, DeCicco noted — especially those who have inflammatory conditions, which can include neurological disorders like Alzheimer’s and dementia.
"When you're fasting, you're giving your organs a chance to rest, you're giving the digestive system a chance to ‘rest and digest,’" she added.
Fasting gives the organs a chance to "rest and digest," an expert said. (iStock)
Intermittent fasting isn’t the only way to support cognitive health, Wright countered.

"Regular physical activity, adequate sleep, controlling blood pressure and blood sugar, avoiding smoking, maintaining social connections and following an overall healthy dietary pattern, such as the Mediterranean diet, have much stronger evidence for protecting cognitive function over time," she said. "Think of meal timing as one potential piece of the puzzle rather than a magic bullet."
CLICK HERE TO DOWNLOAD THE FOX NEWS APP

Intermittent fasting "isn’t appropriate for everyone," Wright warned, adding that she would advise against it for children and teens, pregnant or breastfeeding women, anyone with a history of an eating disorder, and people with diabetes who are taking insulin.
DeCicco agreed that fasting should be recommended and monitored by a medical professional, especially for those who take certain medications or have certain conditions.
Angelica Stabile is a lifestyle reporter for Fox News Digital.

title: Weight-loss joke turns serious as 'cyclospora skinny' trend fuels health warnings
summary: A dangerous social media trend jokes about getting "Cyclospora skinny," but doctors warn the intestinal parasite causes deadly dehydration and illness.
story: Dr. Marc Siegel discusses the alarming cyclosporiasis outbreak, with over 4,000 cases in 41 states linked to contaminated produce. He emphasizes the need for caution as the parasitic infection isn't fully controlled, despite FDA tracing efforts. Siegel also critiques the FDA panel's recommendation to ease peptide restrictions, highlighting insufficient human studies on their long-term health impacts.
A social media trend dubbed "cyclospora skinny" is prompting warnings from medical professionals as Arizona health officials investigate 36 locally acquired cases of the intestinal illness.
Videos and jokes referencing the outbreak have spread across social platforms, with some users suggesting the parasite could be used as a rapid weight-loss method.
Medical experts emphasize that infection from Cyclospora cayetanensis, a foodborne intestinal parasite, is a painful illness.
MORE THAN 12,000 POUNDS OF BACON RECALLED AFTER USDA ISSUES HIGHEST-RISK ALERT

"Getting any kind of illness to purposely cause something like that is just a bad idea," Dr. Andrew Carroll, president of IntraCare and a physician in Chandler, Arizona, told Fox 10. "Plus, cyclosporiasis can be deadly. There are folks ending up in the hospital for long periods of time."
An outbreak of 36 Cyclospora cases in Arizona has sparked a dangerous social media trend promoting "Cyclospora skinny" for rapid weight loss. (iStock)
Cyclospora cayetanensis is a microscopic foodborne parasite that causes the intestinal illness cyclosporiasis, according to Mayo Clinic.
The parasite spreads through food or water contaminated with fecal matter, often linked to fresh produce such as berries, basil, cilantro and bagged salad mixes.
CYCLOSPORA OUTBREAK: IS IT STILL SAFE TO EAT AT RESTAURANTS? HERE'S WHAT TO KNOW
The parasite infects the small intestine, causing prolonged, watery and sometimes explosive diarrhea, loss of appetite, abdominal cramping and severe fatigue.
Infectious disease specialists emphasize that while weight loss can occur with cyclosporiasis, it results from fluid loss, muscle wasting and nutrient malabsorption — not healthy fat reduction.
Left untreated, a Cyclospora infection can persist for weeks or even months, cycling through periods of apparent improvement followed by relapses. (iStock)
Intentionally exposing yourself to Cyclospora — or ignoring symptoms of infection — can carry serious health risks, according to Cleveland Clinic.
Left untreated, a Cyclospora infection can persist for weeks or even months, cycling through periods of apparent improvement followed by relapses.
DOCTORS WARN YOUR 'STOMACH BUG' MAY ACTUALLY BE A PARASITE THAT'S HARDER TO DETECT
Cyclospora cannot be detected through standard bacterial stool cultures and requires a specific laboratory test ordered by a physician.

Unlike many common stomach bugs that resolve on their own, severe or persistent Cyclospora infections typically require a prescription antibiotic, most often trimethoprim-sulfamethoxazole, to fully eliminate the parasite.
Weight lost during a Cyclospora infection stems from severe fluid loss and nutrient malabsorption rather than healthy fat reduction. (iStock)

Severe diarrhea and vomiting can also lead to dehydration, electrolyte imbalances and complications that are especially dangerous for children, older adults and people with weakened immune systems, experts warn.

"With diarrhea, if you’re not able to control that part of it, you’re going to lose a lot of electrolytes, so you’re going to have problems with muscle cramps and headaches and all those sorts of things," Carroll said.
CLICK HERE TO SIGN UP FOR OUR HEALTH NEWSLETTER
"We’re really aware of dehydration in this state; you don’t want to get to the state where your heart just can’t pump enough blood because there is no water in there."

Medical professionals urge the public not to view parasitic infections as a weight-loss shortcut. Instead, experts from Mayo Clinic and Cleveland Clinic recommend practicing safe food handling and seeking medical attention for persistent gastrointestinal symptoms.
An untreated Cyclospora infection can cause persistent gastrointestinal illness that lasts for weeks or months with recurring relapses. (Andrew Harrer/Bloomberg via Getty Images)

"People who are influencers on social media, a lot of people listen to them," Carroll said. "There’s millions of followers for these people and even the most off-colored comment, or meant to be funny, could be considered something serious."
TEST YOURSELF WITH OUR LATEST LIFESTYLE QUIZ
"Especially to someone who might be dealing and struggling with their weight; they might think, ‘Hey, it might be a good idea,’ and it’s never a good idea."

title: Shark Week puts shark bite survival in focus with ER doc's expert tips
summary: An emergency physician reveals the tourniquet and pressure dressing steps that determine survival in the first five minutes after a shark attack.
story: Jesse Watters hosts Chris Fischer, founder of OCEARCH, to discuss the early surge in shark attacks this summer. Recent incidents include a New York beach closure due to bull sharks, a swimmer bitten in Queens and a child attacked in knee-deep water in Florida.
While shark encounters are exceedingly rare, an unexpected bite can pose an immediate, life-threatening emergency.
In the critical first five minutes following an attack, swift action is the single biggest factor in survival.

Dr. Kenneth J. Perry, an emergency medicine physician based in South Carolina, broke down the vital steps bystanders and victims should take to manage the situation before professional medical care arrives.
SHARK WEEK SHOCKER AS GREAT WHITE BREACHES JUST YARDS FROM OBLIVIOUS BOOGIE BOARDER
No. 1: Exit the water and prioritize bleeding control
The first step is to get the victim onto land or a boat to prevent further bites and avoid drowning. Once out of the water, the focus can shift to bleeding control.
The first step after a bite is to get out of the water to prevent further attacks and eliminate the risk of drowning. (iStock)
"Shark bites vary in intensity and severity, but the main issue that all of them share is the need to stop the bleeding," Perry told Fox News Digital.
Because shark teeth can easily tear through major arteries, veins and tendons, uncontrolled blood loss is the biggest immediate threat.
10-FOOT GREAT WHITE SHARK SPOTTED SWIMMING DANGEROUSLY CLOSE TO YOUNG PEOPLE
No. 2: Apply a tourniquet

For severe limb injuries, it's essential to apply a tourniquet, but many people fail to apply sufficient pressure. The tourniquet must be placed above the wound and tightened to the point where a pulse can no longer be felt, according to Perry.
For example, if a victim is bitten near the elbow, the tourniquet must be placed around the upper bicep and tightened until the pulse at the wrist disappears completely.
"It may be painful, but it is necessary."
"It may be painful, but it is necessary," Perry noted.

This aligns with national trauma protocols from the American College of Surgeons' Stop the Bleed initiative, which emphasizes that effective tourniquet placement requires firm, tight compression to fully stop arterial blood flow.
CLICK HERE TO SIGN UP FOR OUR HEALTH NEWSLETTER
No. 3: Adapt for delayed medical care

Tourniquets are temporary tools and should be used for as short a duration as possible, Perry cautioned. There is a maximum window of about two hours before tissue damage occurs from lack of oxygenated blood flow.
A tourniquet is a tight band or device applied around a bleeding limb to compress blood vessels and temporarily stop the flow of blood during a life-threatening hemorrhage. (iStock)
If someone is stranded in a remote area and immediate emergency transport is unavailable, Perry recommends using a pressure dressing.
CLICK HERE FOR MORE HEALTH STORIES

This involves folding gauze multiple times, placing it directly over the specific point of bleeding, and wrapping it tightly. While a pressure dressing does not eliminate blood loss as completely as a tourniquet, it carries a much lower risk of tissue necrosis (death) during prolonged waits.
No. 4: Calm the victim and monitor consciousness
Tourniquets should only remain applied for a maximum of two hours to prevent irreversible tissue damage from lack of blood flow, the doctor advised. (iStock)

Bystanders play a crucial role beyond physical first aid by helping the victim stay motionless and quiet. Panic increases heart rate and blood pressure, which accelerates blood loss, the doctor noted.
CLICK HERE TO DOWNLOAD THE FOX NEWS APP
Loss of consciousness after a shark attack can have more than one cause, Perry said.

A sudden drop in blood pressure and the body's stress response may trigger fainting. If the victim was deep underwater and surfaced too quickly during the attack, unconsciousness could signal a pressure-related diving injury, such as arterial gas embolism or barotrauma, which requires emergency treatment.
No. 5: Prepare for secondary risks
Bystanders should actively help the victim relax, as elevated heart rates and higher blood pressure accelerate the rate of blood loss. (iStock)
While controlling blood loss is crucial in the first five minutes, long-term recovery involves fighting off severe marine bacteria.
Aquatic bites are notorious sources of aggressive skin and soft-tissue infections like cellulitis, Perry warned.
TEST YOURSELF WITH OUR LATEST LIFESTYLE QUIZ
Once a patient is resuscitated with fluids and blood products at a medical facility, aggressive antibiotic treatment usually follows.
Khloe Quill is a lifestyle writer with Fox News Digital. She and the lifestyle team cover a range of story topics including food and drink, travel, and health.

title: Carly Simon reveals the common condition that masked her Parkinson's diagnosis
summary: Carly Simon revealed her Parkinson's disease was initially mistaken for arthritis after joint replacements, raising questions about overlapping symptoms.
story: Dr. Guy Schwartz, a neurologist with Stony Brook Medicine in New York, describes how symptoms can overlap across the two conditions.
Singer Carly Simon has revealed that her Parkinson's disease was initially mistaken for arthritis, highlighting how the two conditions can share similar symptoms, particularly in the early stages.

"My health issues began with arthritis in both knees and one hip. I had all three joints replaced, and at first, I thought the difficulty I was having walking was simply part of the long recovery process," Simon said in a statement shared with multiple media outlets on July 27.

"Eventually, there were periods when I could not walk without considerable help. My family and I knew that something more was going on. After an extensive evaluation at Mayo Clinic, I was diagnosed with Parkinson's."
'YOU'RE SO VAIN' SINGER CARLY SIMON SAYS PARKINSON'S AND CANCER DIAGNOSES KEPT HER FROM PUBLIC EYE

Arthritis is far more common than Parkinson's disease, affecting nearly 60 million U.S. adults compared with about 1.1 million Americans living with Parkinson's, according to the Centers for Disease Control and Prevention.
Even so, about 90,000 Americans are diagnosed with Parkinson's disease each year, making it a relatively common neurological disorder despite being far less prevalent than arthritis.

Singer Carly Simon (pictured in 2019) has revealed that her Parkinson's disease was initially mistaken for arthritis, highlighting how the two conditions can share similar symptoms, particularly in the early stages. (Getty Images)

Arthritis primarily affects the joints and connective tissues, causing pain, inflammation, stiffness and structural damage, per the CDC. The most common types are osteoarthritis (wear-and-tear of cartilage) and rheumatoid arthritis (an autoimmune disease).

Parkinson's disease is a progressive neurological disorder that mainly affects the brain and nervous system, according to the National Institute on Aging (NIA). Dopamine-producing nerve cells in the brain gradually die or become impaired, affecting movement.
HOW EATING HABITS COULD INFLUENCE PARKINSON’S DISEASE RISK, ACCORDING TO EXPERTS

Although the conditions can share mobility problems, arthritis is typically driven by painful joint inflammation, while Parkinson's primarily affects movement through changes in the brain, according to Dr. Guy Schwartz, a neurologist with Stony Brook Medicine in New York.
Overlapping symptoms

"Parkinson's disease can sometimes be misdiagnosed as arthritis, and vice versa," Schwartz, who specializes in Parkinson's disease, told Fox News Digital. "The one main symptom that they share is difficulty with walking — some kind of impediment, limitation or disability."

Arthritis is far more common than Parkinson's disease, affecting nearly 60 million U.S. adults compared with about 1.1 million Americans living with Parkinson's, according to the Centers for Disease Control and Prevention. (iStock)
While arthritis and Parkinson's are fundamentally different diseases, health experts say they can share the following symptoms that can make diagnosis difficult.

The two conditions can also occur in the same person, Schwartz noted, since both become more common with age. "I've definitely been challenged by individuals who come to me with these symptoms," he said. "Sometimes the examination is confounded by significant arthritis."
The two conditions can be especially difficult to distinguish because both are largely diagnosed based on a patient's symptoms and physical examination rather than one definitive test. (iStock)
While many people may connect Parkinson’s with tremors, early signs of the disease usually include stiffness, slowness and changes in gait.
In older adults who have been diagnosed with arthritis or have had joint replacements, those same symptoms can easily be attributed to joint disease or surgical recovery.
Parkinson’s-specific symptoms
Some Parkinson’s symptoms are not typically seen in arthritis cases. People who experience the following signs should consult a neurologist, according to the Parkinson's Foundation.

"It's not unusual for there to be misdiagnoses."

While tremor is often considered a hallmark symptom, Schwartz cautioned that it isn't always present. "About a third of individuals with Parkinson's disease do not have a tremor," he said. "That's when the diagnosis becomes more challenging."

"In Parkinson's disease, dexterity becomes compromised because of slowness and stiffness," the expert added. "In arthritis, it's more of a mechanical issue, where the joints don't allow full range of motion."
How is Parkinson’s diagnosed?

The two conditions can be especially difficult to distinguish because both are largely diagnosed based on a patient's symptoms and physical examination rather than one definitive test, according to Schwartz.

There is no single blood test or imaging scan that can definitively confirm Parkinson’s, as "very few things in medicine are 100%," he said.
However, newer diagnostic tools have emerged, including specialized imaging and skin biopsy testing. "We're still learning," the neurologist said, adding that a blood test may be on the horizon.
While many people may connect Parkinson’s with tremors, early signs of the disease usually include stiffness, slowness and changes in gait. (iStock)
For now, diagnoses are made based on the following factors, per the National Institute of Neurological Disorders and Stroke (NINDS).

Schwartz emphasized that early diagnostic uncertainty is not uncommon. "It's not unusual for there to be misdiagnoses," he said. "Sometimes seeing a patient over time helps — eventually the disease declares itself, and then it's easier to make the diagnosis."

Anyone experiencing persistent walking difficulties, stiffness or other symptoms that don't seem fully explained by arthritis should discuss them with a healthcare provider, who can determine whether a neurological evaluation is appropriate.

title: Drink-spiking defense: New bracelet aims to expose drugs with a drop of your cocktail
summary: A student's electromagnetic sensor detects benzodiazepines in drinks and sends an alert through an app, sharing your live location with a safety network.
story: Fox News senior medical analyst Dr. Marc Siegel explains ACTXA's Core Smart Ring, an AI-powered wearable offering non-invasive glucose monitoring. This new technology senses blood flow and pulse, using machine learning to detect elevated blood sugar. Siegel notes its importance given the nearly quadrupled global diabetes cases since 2000, emphasizing lifestyle changes alongside technological advancements for better care.
A University of South Florida (USF) graduate student is developing a high-tech new way to stay safe in style.

Addison Bounds, a 22-year-old former USF beach volleyball player, co-founded Elora Armor, a brand that creates jewelry with a sensor designed to warn its wearer when dangerous substances have been slipped into their drinks.
The company plans to offer bracelets, pendants, keychains and potentially phone cases that can alert if a drink has been drugged, Bounds told Fox 13 Tampa Bay.
COULD A PAINT-ON ELECTRONIC TATTOO SPOT HEART ATTACKS?
Bounds co-founded the brand with Kira Robichaud, a friend with a science background who is helping lead a small team of women developing the technology.

"You just drop – whatever's on your finger is plenty – onto the surface of the product," Bounds said.

"You’ll receive a notification to your phone telling you if that drink is safe to consume or not, and if your drink has been spiked, your live location is immediately sent to your safety network that you've connected to the app."
Bounds shared that a friend of hers was drugged in high school and later found unconscious in a closet, where she had been assaulted.

"It's like a really rude awakening ... there are people who really intend to do harm, and there isn't really anyone looking out for us except for ourselves," she said.
Elora Armor co-founders Addison Bounds and Kira Robichaud are pictured in the lab. (Elora Armor)
Bounds said she hopes to launch the bracelets in January 2028, ahead of the L.A. Olympics, with the goal to "stop drink spiking from happening in the first place."
Statistics on drink spiking in America remain limited, as it's difficult to measure and a national tracking system does not exist.

However, a 2017 study of more than 6,000 college students at three universities found that 7.8% reported having been drugged without their knowledge or consent. The group included about 10% of the female students and 4% of the males.

Common drink-spiking drugs are often hard to detect and their effect can worsen when mixed with alcohol, according to the Center for Violence Prevention and Self Defense Training. Drink spiking happens most commonly in busy social settings, making it more difficult to detect.

CVPSD shares strategies for preventing drink spiking, including never leaving your drink unattended, only accepting drinks from trusted people, using drink covers, avoiding communal containers, sticking with friends who have your back, and being aware of your surroundings. (iStock)

CVPSD warned to watch out for cues and symptoms that a drink may have been spiked and consumed. Those include rapid or unexpected intoxication, sudden behavioral changes, memory lapses, hallucinations, paranoia, and an unusual appearance or taste of a drink.
Physical symptoms can also include loss of balance, blurred vision, slurred speech, nausea, vomiting and trouble breathing.

title: More than 12,000 pounds of bacon recalled after USDA issues highest-risk alert
summary: Federal food safety officials have recalled more than 12,000 pounds of imported bacon after discovering the products entered the country without undergoing a mandatory inspection.
story: April 30, 2026 - Do you even know where the bacon you’re eating comes from?
More than 12,000 pounds of imported smoked bacon have been recalled, according to an alert from the USDA's Food Safety and Inspection Service (FSIS).

The not-ready-to-eat bacon, which is sold in three states, is produced by Maple Leaf Foods, Inc., located in Lisle, Illinois. It was distributed to grocery distributors and retailers in Idaho, Oregon and Washington.
Fox News Digital reached out to Maple Leaf Foods requesting comment.

The bacon was recalled because it was imported from Canada without undergoing a required U.S. import inspection, the USDA stated in its July 24 alert.
The issue was discovered during routine inspection activities.
More than 12,000 pounds of imported smoked bacon have been recalled, according to an alert from the USDA's Food Safety and Inspection Service. (iStock)
The USDA classified this as a Class I recall, its most serious category of recalls.
The FSIS defines a Class I recall as a "health hazard situation where there is a reasonable probability that the use of the product will cause serious, adverse health consequences or death."

The recall includes a 12-oz. vacuum package of "Royale Natural Applewood Smoked ALL NATURAL Uncured Bacon Product of Canada" with sell-by dates of "SEP 01 2026" and "SEP 07 2026" printed on the side of the package. (U.S. Department of Agriculture's Food Safety and Inspection Service)
