"Those are some simple activities that you can do that will make huge changes in the future," the interim surgeon general added.
Khloe Quill is a lifestyle writer with Fox News Digital. She and the lifestyle team cover a range of story topics including food and drink, travel, and health.

title: Man who beat rare cancer celebrates by canoeing 2,000 miles with his dog
summary: Frank Carter, 67, and his dog Amos completed a 2,000-mile canoe trip down the Missouri River four years after CAR T-cell therapy cleared his lymphoma.
story: Patient Laurie Adami credits the cancer treatment Car-T with saving her life on ‘Fox News @ Night.’

A 67-year-old cancer survivor from Orange County, Florida, completed a more than 2,000-mile journey down the Missouri River alongside his dog, Amos, after undergoing a groundbreaking immunotherapy treatment.
Frank Carter spent 64 days navigating the longest U.S. river in a cedar-strip canoe he built by hand, according to reports from the Moffitt Cancer Center and FOX 13 News.
The expedition began in Montana and concluded near St. Louis, Missouri, requiring the pair to camp along the riverbank while enduring severe storms, high winds and hail, FOX 13 News reported.
'FIT MOM' DID 'EVERYTHING RIGHT' — THEN A COLON CANCER DIAGNOSIS CHANGED HER LIFE

Before his diagnosis, Carter was a long-distance adventurer. According to the Moffitt Cancer Center, he spent five months hiking the Appalachian Trail in 2019 and completed an eight-week cross-country bicycle ride from San Diego to New Smyrna Beach, Florida, in 2020.
However, his physical limits were tested in a new way in 2021 after a routine 5K race.
Frank Carter, a 67-year-old cancer survivor from Orange County, Fla., paddled 2,341 miles down the Missouri River over 64 days with his golden retriever, Amos. (UCG/Universal Images Group via G)
"I was wiped out. I just wasn't recovering," Carter told FOX 13 News. "I went to my doctor, had blood tests. Long story short, in two weeks I was getting chemo."
CLICK HERE TO DOWNLOAD THE FOX NEWS APP

Doctors diagnosed Carter with mantle cell lymphoma, a rare form of blood cancer that originates in white blood cells known as lymphocytes. He underwent 15 rounds of chemotherapy in Orlando, according to Moffitt Cancer Center.
Carter hand-built the cedar-strip canoe (not pictured) for the journey, and is now sharing his story to encourage other patients to remain active and hopeful. (iStock)
Although the treatment significantly reduced the cancer, follow-up exams showed lingering traces of the disease.
CLICK HERE TO SIGN UP FOR OUR HEALTH NEWSLETTER

Carter then sought care at the Moffitt Cancer Center in Tampa to undergo chimeric antigen receptor (CAR) T-cell therapy, which involves extracting the patient's own immune cells, genetically altering them in a laboratory to identify cancer cells, and adding them back into the body.
Doctors treated Carter with CAR T-cell therapy, a groundbreaking immunotherapy that genetically alters a patient's own T-cells to attack cancer, leaving him cancer-free for four years. (iStock)

"We take those T-cells and genetically engineer them by putting something called a CAR into them," Dr. Michael Jain, an oncologist at Moffitt Cancer Center, told FOX 13 News. "Now these T-cells can see the tumor and get rid of it, where before the tumor was able to hide from it."
TEST YOURSELF WITH OUR LATEST LIFESTYLE QUIZ

Carter has remained cancer-free for four years after the single infusion. Throughout his recovery, he has found constant support in his dog, Amos, whom he brought home right before beginning chemotherapy.
CLICK HERE FOR MORE HEALTH STORIES

"After my cancer diagnosis, I told myself I was going to beat this, and I really wanted a dog during the process," Carter told Moffitt's Endeavor publication. "I got Amos right before my first treatment."
Khloe Quill is a lifestyle writer with Fox News Digital. She and the lifestyle team cover a range of story topics including food and drink, travel, and health.

title: Longer lives, worse health? Scientists uncover troubling trend across generations
summary: The morbidity gap between life expectancy and healthy life expectancy is widest in America, where people spend about 14 years in poor health.
story: Rates of chronic disease, obesity and stress continue to rise across America. Experts warn that some of the healthiest habits from the nation's earlier centuries may have fallen by the wayside.
People across the world are living longer, but they’re also spending more years coping with ill health, a recent study observed.

The "morbidity gap" — the number of years people spend in poor health, typically struggling with chronic challenges such as low back pain, hearing loss and depression — widened across 203 of 204 countries analyzed and was the most pronounced in America, the researchers found.

"Globally in 2023, an average of 14.5% of life was spent in poor health, compared to 13.6% in 1990," the researchers at the Institute for Health Metrics and Evaluation at the University of Washington reported.
JANE SEYMOUR, 75, SHARES HOW SHE APPROACHES AGING WITH VITALITY: 'BEST I CAN BE'
In the United States, the morbidity gap is about 14 years, or 17.8% of the expected lifespan.

"Between 1990 and 2023, global life expectancy at birth increased from 64.6 years to 73.8 years, while healthy life expectancy rose from 55.9 years to 63.1 years," the researchers reported in a news release.
CLICK HERE FOR MORE LIFESTYLE NEWS
"Because gains in survival consistently outpaced gains in healthy years of life, people are spending more years living with chronic disease and disability."
A recent study found that the number of years people spend in poor health is widening, especially in America. (iStock)

The gap widened the most in the wealthiest countries where populations have access to life-extending resources, the researchers reported. Women are also living longer than men but are also spending more years in poor health, they found.

"To me, the most important message of this study is not that people are living longer. It is that we have become far better at delaying death than delaying functional decline," Dr. Antony Chu, clinical assistant professor at Brown University’s Warren Alpert School of Medicine, told Fox News Digital.

"Modern medicine has achieved remarkable success in reducing mortality from cardiovascular disease, cancer, trauma and infectious illness," he added. "Yet many of those additional years are now lived with chronic pain, disability, sensory loss, depression or reduced independence."
TEST YOURSELF WITH OUR LATEST LIFESTYLE QUIZ

Researchers analyzed Global Burden of Disease data covering 204 countries and territories from 1990 through 2023. In their report, published by The Lancet Public Health, scientists observed that a small number of chronic, largely non-fatal causes were the primary contributors to the morbidity gap.

Musculoskeletal disorders, especially low back pain; mental disorders, such as depression and anxiety; hearing loss, falls and other non-communicable accounted for about 57% of all years lived in poor health worldwide. High fasting plasma glucose, obesity and aging populations were also important contributors.
The researchers noted that the study points to broad health trends but doesn’t prove exactly what's causing people to spend more years in poor health.
Researchers recently found people are spending more years living with chronic diseases and disabilities. (iStock)

"Our findings suggest that future gains in population health will come not only from helping people live longer, but from helping them live healthier," said Dr. Christopher Murray, director of the Institute for Health Metrics and Evaluation (IHME) at the University of Washington School of Medicine and senior author of the study.

"Progress in healthy aging should be measured not only by lifespan, but by healthspan [the number of years spent in good health], with greater investment in prevention, long-term disease management and chronic care to reduce years lived in poor health."

The goal should no longer be simply extending lifespan, but compressing morbidity and maximizing the number of years people remain physically, cognitively and socially well, Chu told Fox News Digital.
CLICK HERE TO SIGN UP FOR OUR LIFESTYLE NEWSLETTER

"Ultimately, I believe the next frontier of medicine is not simply adding years to life, but adding life to years," he said. "First, we need to focus on preserving function rather than simply reacting to disease."

The approach involves routinely assessing mobility, muscle strength, balance, hearing, cognition and overall physical resilience. Chu said this may prove just as important as monitoring blood pressure, cholesterol and glucose.
"Functional decline often begins years before disability becomes obvious, providing an opportunity for earlier intervention," he said.
Many older Americans are socially isolated, though research shows relationships are important to longevity, an expert said. (iStock)
Musculoskeletal health also deserves much greater emphasis, Chu said.

"Progressive resistance training, fall prevention, maintenance of muscle mass and early treatment of chronic back pain should become core components of preventive medicine rather than afterthoughts," he said. "Preserving mobility may ultimately have as much impact on healthy aging as preventing heart disease."
Mental health and social connection are another vital component to healthspan, Chu said.
CLICK HERE TO DOWNLOAD THE FOX NEWS APP

"Hearing loss, depression, anxiety and loneliness frequently reinforce one another, accelerating physical decline while diminishing quality of life," he said. "Addressing these conditions early may improve both longevity and independence."
Chu, who is the child of immigrants, said it’s his belief that Americans often overlook an important cultural dimension of healthy aging.

"In many societies outside the United States, older adults continue to play an active and respected role within multigenerational families," he said. "They remain mentors, caregivers, historians and sources of wisdom. This continued sense of purpose and belonging may provide meaningful protection against loneliness, depression and loss of identity.
A continued sense of purpose and belonging may lead people to live longer and healthier lives, according to an expert. (iStock)

"By contrast, many older Americans experience increasing social isolation precisely when maintaining meaningful relationships may be most important," Chu added. "Healthy aging is not determined solely by biology; it is also shaped by community, purpose and human connection."
Teresa Mull is a freelance writer with the Lifestyle team at Fox News Digital.

title: 'Fit Mom' did 'everything right' — then a colon cancer diagnosis changed her life
summary: Maria Kang, the viral "No Excuses Mom" fitness influencer, reveals how Stage 4 colon cancer blindsided her despite years of healthy living.
story: Maria Kang told Fox News Digital she thought healthy eating and regular exercise would protect her until a Stage 4 colon cancer diagnosis revealed a different reality.

Maria Kang built her career around fitness, healthy eating and helping other moms prioritize wellness. Despite believing she had done "everything right," the California mother of three was blindsided by colon cancer.
Kang, now 46, said the diagnosis reshaped her understanding of what it means to be healthy.
She became an internet sensation in 2013 after a photo of her sculpted physique alongside her three young sons sparked a global conversation about fitness and motherhood.
LEADING ONCOLOGIST REVEALS 6 HABITS THAT COULD PROMOTE LONGEVITY AND REDUCE YOUR RISK OF CHRONIC ILLNESS
The viral image — captioned "What’s your excuse?" — led to her being dubbed the "No Excuse Mom" and inspired the launch of hundreds of wellness communities around the world.
More than a decade later, Kang’s world was turned upside down when she learned that she had Stage 4 colon cancer in November 2023.
Maria Kang built her career around fitness, healthy eating and helping other moms prioritize wellness but then was blindsided by colon cancer. (Beth Baugher, Maria Kang)

"It was definitely a complete shock because I was the healthiest person I knew," she shared with Fox News Digital. "I wanted to blame the food, but I didn't eat bad food. I filtered my water. There was no excuse why I had this cancer."
Looking back, Kang said she had experienced persistent digestive problems since adolescence, including chronic constipation and bloating that worsened with stress.
PANCREATIC CANCER VACCINE SHOWS PROMISE IN FIRST HUMAN TRIAL, PREVENTING DISEASE IN HIGH-RISK PATIENTS
"It didn't matter how many fiber pills or laxatives, it just took a long time to go," she said. "So, that's been an ongoing journey throughout my life."
Over the years, Kang said, she convinced herself that her digestive problems were just something she had to live with.
Kang became an internet sensation in 2013 after a photo of her sculpted physique alongside her three young sons sparked a global conversation about fitness and motherhood. (Mike Byerly)

"One thing that I realized is that we normalize problems, and we think it's OK, but it’s not OK," she said. "Digestion should be like breathing. It should be like inhaling and exhaling. It should be simple. But it wasn't simple."

After a tumor was detected through a biopsy after a colonoscopy, Kang said she initially pursued holistic approaches for 12 weeks, but the tumor did not shrink and may have grown slightly. She then began FOLFOX, a combination of chemotherapy drugs used to treat some gastrointestinal cancers, in 2024.
MELINDA FRENCH GATES SAYS IT TOOK 3 DOCTORS TO DIAGNOSE THE CONDITION SHE WAS SUFFERING FROM

After one treatment, Kang went to the emergency room when her colostomy stoma retracted, and a scan reportedly showed that the tumor had shrunk substantially. She then asked to stop chemotherapy and proceed with surgery.

Kang later underwent extensive surgery to remove the tumor and about a foot of her colon, along with multiple reproductive organs and her appendix. She temporarily required a colostomy and later an ileostomy.
"It was definitely a complete shock because I was the healthiest person I knew."
Today, Kang says her MRIs have shown "no suspicious mass detected." She gets regular blood screenings and scans every six months.

"Much of what remains appears related to postoperative healing and inflammation," she shared. "Because of my history, my doctors continue surveillance, but I have not been formally declared NED (no evidence of disease)."
Alarming trends
An estimated 158,850 Americans will be diagnosed with colorectal cancer in 2026, and around 55,230 people will die from the disease this year, according to the American Cancer Society.

Although colorectal cancer incidence has declined overall — largely among older adults, a trend linked in part to increased screening and changes in certain risk factors — rates are rising in younger age groups.
Kang said her fitness and nutrition regimens also look drastically different from her pre-cancer routines. (Maria Kang)
Among adults younger than 50, colorectal cancer incidence increased by 2.9% per year from 2013 to 2022.

The American Cancer Society and U.S. Preventive Services Task Force recommend that people at average risk begin regular colorectal cancer screening at age 45, although those with certain risk factors may need to start earlier.
Anyone experiencing persistent or concerning symptoms should consult a doctor, regardless of age.
‘I look healthy’
"It was a really big, humbling look in the mirror when you say to yourself, 'I look healthy, but I'm not healthy,’" Kang told Fox News Digital.
"When someone is at a normal range in their weight, they could have cancer. They could have autoimmune issues.
DOCTORS PUSH NEW BLOOD TESTS FOR COLON CANCER AS CASES SURGE IN YOUNGER ADULTS
"We don't know what's going on inside of a person. We always just want to look the part versus be the part."
Wellness redefined
Kang said her cancer journey has changed her perception of health and what’s important in life.

"Cancer makes everything extremely clear — what's important, what is not important, what you should eat, what you shouldn't eat," she said. "If you really listen to yourself, it becomes crystal clear when you have no energy."
Kang’s world was turned upside down when she learned that she had Stage 4 colon cancer in November 2023. (Maria Kang)
Kang said her fitness and nutrition regimens also look drastically different from her pre-cancer routines.

"I used to train five or six days a week, but now I only move when I want to," she said. "Walking is my best friend. I love to dance. I still love to strength-train because it's fun for me and it makes me strong."
CLICK HERE TO DOWNLOAD THE FOX NEWS APP
Perhaps the biggest shift is that Kang no longer does anything that feels forced.
"If there's anything that I feel forced to do, I don't do it," she said. "If I feel awful, my body's going to express awful."
Her approach to food has also shifted, she shared.
CLICK HERE TO SIGN UP FOR OUR HEALTH NEWSLETTER
"In the past, there were bad foods and good foods and cheat days … what I understand now is balance," Kang said.
While she does naturally veer toward fruits and vegetables — "things that have water and life and light in them" — Kang said she is still open to eating any other foods, including pizza.
Kang underwent extensive surgery to remove the tumor and about a foot of her colon, along with multiple reproductive organs and her appendix. (Maria Kang)
Overall, Kang wants people to know that maintaining healthy habits does not eliminate the possibility of developing cancer.
"It could happen to anybody. That was the most humbling realization," she said.
CLICK HERE FOR MORE HEALTH STORIES
"You may think you're young and healthy and this won't happen to you, but this world is so unpredictable right now. Anything can happen to anybody.
"Health is not what you think it is," she said. "It's not just how you look. It's how you feel."
TEST YOURSELF WITH OUR LATEST LIFESTYLE QUIZ

The American Cancer Society recommends seeing a healthcare provider about persistent changes in bowel habits, blood in the stool, abdominal pain, unexplained weight loss or other concerning gastrointestinal symptoms.
While such symptoms can have many causes other than cancer, they should be evaluated regardless of a person’s age.
Melissa Rudy is senior health editor and a member of the lifestyle team at Fox News Digital. Story tips can be sent to melissa.rudy@fox.com.

title: Measles surge hits new milestone as US cases surpass last year's total
summary: U.S. measles cases in 2026 have officially surpassed 2025 totals, with 93% of patients unvaccinated or unknown for MMR as outbreaks persist.
story: Dr. Nicole Saphier discusses the significant measles outbreak in Spartanburg County, South Carolina, with declining vaccination rates across the U.S.
Measles has reemerged as a persistent public health challenge in the U.S. over the past two years — and the spread isn't slowing down.
According to a Johns Hopkins University tracker that compiles local and state health data, there were 2,295 confirmed measles cases in the U.S. as of July 22.
This figure has officially surpassed the 2025 numbers, which totaled 2,286 measles cases nationwide.
MEASLES-INFECTED TRAVELER MAY HAVE EXPOSED PASSENGERS AT LAX AND NEARBY HOTEL, HEALTH OFFICIALS WARN
Cases have been reported across the country, but concentrated outbreaks have worsened in some areas of Pennsylvania, South Carolina, Florida, Virginia, Utah, Texas and Arizona.
In 2025, Texas had the largest outbreak — totaling 803 cases throughout the state.
Measles cases have officially surpassed 2025 numbers, which totaled 2,286 cases. The U.S. has reported 2,295 measles cases so far in 2026. (iStock)

In the latest CDC measles update on July 17, there were 34 new outbreaks reported in 2026, compared to 48 outbreaks in 2025. Most cases were associated with local outbreaks, while some were linked to international visitors.
TEST YOURSELF WITH OUR LATEST LIFESTYLE QUIZ
Both this year and last year, 93% of all measles patients were either unvaccinated for measles, mumps and rubella (MMR), or had an unknown vaccination status, data shows.
Most cases have occurred in children and young adults between the ages of 5 and 19.
There have been no deaths reported in 2026, according to the CDC, but there were three deaths in 2025.

Most cases have occurred in children and young adults between the ages of 5 and 19. There have been no deaths reported in 2026, according to the CDC, but there were three deaths in 2025. (Brandon Bell/Getty Images)
The rise in cases comes more than two decades after health agencies reported that the disease was eliminated in 2000.

Measles can be spread through direct contact with infectious droplets, or can be airborne when an infected person breathes, coughs or sneezes, according to health officials. The virus can remain infectious in the air for up to two hours after an infected person leaves an area.
CLICK HERE TO SIGN UP FOR OUR HEALTH NEWSLETTER
Symptoms usually appear within a week or two, and may include a high fever, cough, runny nose and red, watery eyes.
A few days later, flat, red spots appear on the face and then spread down the neck to the rest of the body. People are most contagious in the four days before and four days after the rash appears.
Community protection
Dr. Marc Siegel, Fox News senior medical analyst, emphasized the highly contagious nature of measles.

"Measles is so contagious that up to 90% of susceptible people who are exposed to an infected person will become infected," he told Fox News Digital, noting the importance of community protection. "We need a 95% vaccine coverage rate to ensure herd immunity," he said.
A paramedic administers a dose of the measles vaccine at a health center in Lubbock, Texas, on Feb. 27, 2025. (RONALDO SCHEMIDT/AFP via Getty Images)
The herd immunity threshold is a mathematical estimate based on how contagious a disease is and how effectively immunity from vaccination or prior infection prevents its spread, according to Siegel.

"In this case, two-dose vaccination is almost 100% effective, and natural immunity after a measles infection is generally lifelong," the doctor said. "This isn’t about personal choice, it’s about community protection. We need to protect those who can’t have a live virus vaccine because they are immunocompromised or pregnant."
CLICK HERE FOR MORE HEALTH STORIES

The doctor also cautioned that the U.S. could be at risk of losing its measles elimination status, as the number and duration of outbreaks suggest sustained local transmission within the U.S., rather than isolated cases linked only to international travel.
CLICK HERE TO DOWNLOAD THE FOX NEWS APP
The CDC recommends that everyone receive two doses of the MMR vaccine, calling vaccination the best protection against measles.
Anyone who is showing measles symptoms or thinks they’ve been exposed should self-isolate and contact their doctor before showing up to a medical center and infecting others.
Angelica Stabile is a lifestyle reporter for Fox News Digital.

title: Sharon Stone's terrifying weed withdrawal sparks warning about today's potent marijuana
summary: Sharon Stone's marijuana withdrawal symptoms were so severe that she saw a neurologist, highlighting the dangers of quitting high-potency THC without a plan.
story: Fox News senior medical analyst Dr. Marc Siegel discusses new research that casts doubt on cannabis benefits and highlights increased mental health risks, especially for teenagers. Modern marijuana, with 70-90% THC potency, is linked to higher rates of PTSD, anxiety, depression, ADHD, and bipolar disorder. Usage among Americans aged 12 and older has skyrocketed by 180% since the early 2000s, leading to concerns about addiction and health issues.
Hollywood icon Sharon Stone recently opened up about a health scare after quitting marijuana, revealing her symptoms were so intense that she turned to a neurologist.
During an interview with Variety, the actress said her decision to quit was driven by a desire for a drug-free life.
"And because I think they put so much stuff in it now — they really do — when I stopped smoking pot, I also got sick," she said.
CANNABIS COMPOUNDS COULD REVERSE DISEASE AFFECTING ONE-THIRD OF ADULTS
"I got pretty sick for a month. I went to my neurologist, and he said, ‘Sharon, I’ve had people dying in the emergency room from marijuana.'"
Stone attributed her ordeal to the potency of modern weed, saying, "It’s not like you’re pulling it out of the ground anymore ... It’s not like when we were kids."
American actress Sharon Stone quit "smoking pot" and got so sick that she consulted a neurologist, she revealed in a recent interview. (Getty Images, iStock)

Experts note that cannabis withdrawal itself is generally not considered life-threatening, although severe symptoms, underlying medical conditions or interactions with other substances can complicate recovery.
FLYING WITH CANNABIS? TSA'S NEW GUIDANCE COMES WITH A MAJOR HEALTH WARNING
Dr. Chris Tuell, clinical director of addiction services at the Lindner Center in Cincinnati, confirmed that today's cannabis products are vastly different from the strains of decades past.
THC levels in marijuana have surged from about 3% to 5% in the 1980s to as high as 30% in today's cannabis products, while concentrates can exceed 90% THC, he told Fox News Digital.
"I do believe cannabis is addicting, especially with the high levels of THC."

Higher THC concentrations have been linked to greater risks of dependence, cannabis use disorder (CUD), psychosis in some users and more severe withdrawal symptoms, according to the National Institute on Drug Abuse.

As today's cannabis products become increasingly potent, experts say there are several risks and warning signs that daily users should know before deciding whether to continue — or quit — using marijuana.
No. 1: High-potency THC changes the brain's reward system
According to Cleveland Clinic, CUD occurs when marijuana takes over the brain's reward pathways, amplifying compulsive behavior.
"I do believe cannabis is addicting, especially with the high levels of THC," Tuell told Fox News Digital.
No. 2: Addiction isn't always obvious

The American Psychiatric Association’s DSM-5 (Diagnostic and Statistical Manual of Mental Disorders, Fifth Edition) outlines the following diagnostic criteria signaling that casual use may have crossed into dependency.
CLICK HERE TO DOWNLOAD THE FOX NEWS APP

Taking larger amounts over longer periods than intendedExperiencing unsuccessful attempts to cut down or control usageFailing to fulfill work, school or home responsibilitiesContinuing use despite clear relationship problems
Taking larger amounts over longer periods than intended
Experiencing unsuccessful attempts to cut down or control usage
Failing to fulfill work, school or home responsibilities
Continuing use despite clear relationship problems
Today’s cannabis flower and concentrates contain up to 90% THC, making modern products exponentially stronger than those from decades past, experts say. (iStock)
No. 3: Withdrawal can be intense
Quitting heavy, long-term cannabis use can trigger withdrawal symptoms within 24 to 48 hours, Cleveland Clinic notes.
CLICK HERE FOR MORE HEALTH STORIES

Users frequently experience severe insomnia, intense irritability, anxiety, appetite loss, sweating, headaches and stomach upset. While acute physical symptoms typically resolve within a month, mood swings and sleep issues can linger much longer, according to Tuell.
CLICK HERE TO SIGN UP FOR OUR HEALTH NEWSLETTER
4. Medical guidance may be needed

While cannabis withdrawal alone rarely requires hospitalization, Cleveland Clinic notes that people with significant medical or mental health conditions — or those stopping cannabis while also withdrawing from alcohol, opioids or certain other medications — may benefit from medical supervision.
Addiction experts strongly advise stepping down THC intake slowly to cushion the impact on the nervous system and avoid severe rebound symptoms. (iStock)
No. 5: Underlying issues may fuel dependence

Mental health conditions often occur alongside cannabis use disorder, and treating those underlying issues may help reduce problematic marijuana use, according to the National Institute on Drug Abuse and the Cleveland Clinic.
TEST YOURSELF WITH OUR LATEST LIFESTYLE QUIZ
"I strongly believe that CUD and mental health issues co-exist, and that mental health counseling can address the issues driving the addictive behaviors," Tuell said.
Fox News Digital reached out to Stone's representatives requesting comment.
Khloe Quill is a lifestyle writer with Fox News Digital. She and the lifestyle team cover a range of story topics including food and drink, travel, and health.

title: 'The irony': Ketanji Brown Jackson roasted after stressing impartiality on Michelle Obama's podcast
summary: Ketanji Brown Jackson told Michelle Obama's "IMO" podcast she is "very, very mindful" of impartiality, sparking swift mockery over the perceived irony.
story: Supreme Court Justice Ketanji Brown Jackson agreed with former first lady Michelle Obama’s criticism of elite schools isolating students of color and recalled finding

Supreme Court Justice Ketanji Brown Jackson is being mocked online over the "irony" of saying she is "very, very mindful and scrupulous" about being impartial during a guest appearance on former first lady Michelle Obama’s podcast, "IMO."
During an appearance of more than an hour on the podcast, Jackson, a Biden appointee to the Supreme Court, stressed the importance of being unbiased, saying, "You really have to be focused on that."

"There are lots of limits on what judges can do, and I try to be very, very mindful and scrupulous with respect to that because, as you say, our obligation is to be unbiased in our approach," said Jackson.
MICHELLE OBAMA ACCUSES MEDIA OF WEAPONIZING FASHION TO 'DIMINISH' HER AS A CAMPAIGN THREAT
"And, so, you have to then navigate all the sources that could make for an appearance of partiality, which you want to avoid."
She added that "there are lots of things that I end up not accepting for that reason."

Supreme Court Justice Ketanji Brown Jackson, left, recently appeared on a podcast episode hosted by former first lady Michelle Obama, right. (Emma McIntyre/Getty Images for The Recording Academy; Kent Nishimura/AFP via Getty Images)
The former first lady asked Jackson about the practices she follows to remain unbiased.

"You also have to watch your exposure to things, so that there isn’t a bias," said Obama. "What does that mean for you in terms of reading the paper and listening to the news? And how do get your information and what do you have to be careful about? And how are you dealing with the potential conflicts so that you do stay above board?"
SIGN UP TO GET THE POLITICS NEWSLETTER
Jackson said there are employees in the court whose job is to be "assisting us in that way."

"When I get invitations to do things, I always have them screened by the legal office, the public information office, just to make sure that there are no ethical conflicts, that this is not a fundraiser, you know," she told Obama.
ALITO RIPS JACKSON’S ‘UTTERLY IRRESPONSIBLE’ SOLO DISSENT AS SUPREME COURT FIGHT SHAKES UP 2026 MAP

Michelle Obama speaks at "IMO Live: Michelle Obama, Craig Robinson & Dr. Laurie Santos" during the SXSW Conference and Festivals at the Austin Convention Center in Austin, Texas, March 13, 2025. (Andy Wenstrand/SXSW Conference & Festivals)
Reactions poured in quickly.
"Supreme Court Justice Ketanji Brown discusses the importance of being neutral while she is sitting on Michelle Obama’s podcast set!" Turning Point USA contributor John Amanchukwu wrote.
"She doesn’t really expect anyone to believe that, does she?" conservative influencer Patricia Foster wrote.
"Make it make sense," commentator DeVory Darkins wrote.

"Justice Ketanji Brown Jackson can't be real. She says it is important to be neutral as a Supreme Court justice........while she is literally on MAJOR leftist Michelle Obama's podcast," Darkins wrote. "We ALL know how impartial she is."
'WOKE' SMITHSONIAN EXHIBIT LIONIZES EMBATTLED FAUCI AMID CONSERVATIVE SCRUTINY OF MUSEUM'S MESSAGING
Justice Ketanji Brown Jackson on the cover of Essence Magazine. (Essence Magazine)
CLICK HERE TO DOWNLOAD THE FOX NEWS APP
Harris Rigby, a columnist for the Babylon Bee's non-satirical site "Not the Bee," wrote, "There isn't a strong enough word for the irony in this video clip."
He ripped Jackson as "the most public, loud-mouthed, self-assured judge in the history of the United States," adding that she now "wants to lecture us about the dignity of the courts."
Fox News Digital reached out to Obama and the Supreme Court for comment.
Peter Pinedo is a politics writer for Fox News Digital.

title: Trump promotes Freedom Haulers Initiative to fast-track military veterans into trucking jobs
summary: President Trump's Freedom Haulers Initiative streamlines CDL licensing for military veterans while removing over 24,000 non-English-speaking commercial drivers.
story: Program streamlines CDL licensing for veterans with military driving experience as administration touts crackdown on illegal immigrant commercial drivers.

President Donald Trump on Thursday formally kicked off an administration initiative designed to fast-track military veterans into trucking jobs while removing illegal immigrant commercial drivers from America's roadways, arguing the effort will improve highway safety and create new employment opportunities for former service members.

Speaking at the White House alongside Transportation Secretary Sean Duffy, Veterans Affairs Secretary Doug Collins and trucking industry leaders, Trump promoted the "Freedom Haulers Initiative," which streamlines the commercial driver's license (CDL) process for veterans with heavy vehicle experience gained during military service.
"Today, we're taking action to get illegal alien truck drivers off the American roadways and replace them with proud American veterans," Trump said. "It's about time."
TRUMP TAPS VETERANS TO FIX ILLEGAL ALIEN TRUCKING PROBLEM PLAGUING US ROADWAYS

President Donald Trump speaks during an event promoting the Freedom Haulers Initiative at the White House, alongside Transportation Secretary Sean Duffy, left, and Veterans Affairs Secretary Doug Collins, on July 30, 2026. (Peter D'Abrosca/Fox News Digital)

Under the initiative, qualified veterans with heavy-vehicle experience gained during military service can apply to waive the CDL road-skills test, allowing them to avoid duplicating training they received in the military. Certain veterans in participating states may also qualify for a waiver of the written knowledge test. Veterans without military truck-driving experience will be eligible for expedited training that administration officials said could be completed in several weeks.

Trump said 34 states have joined or are working to implement the Even Exchange Program, including Indiana, Wyoming, Louisiana, Arkansas, Alabama, Florida and Maryland, and called on the remaining states to participate.

The president paired the promotion with his administration's ongoing crackdown on commercial drivers who do not meet federal English-language requirements or who were issued licenses while in the country illegally.
OUT OF CONTROL, UNQUALIFIED ILLEGAL ALIEN TRUCKERS ENDANGERING KIDS ON US ROADS, INSIDER WARNS: ‘JUST MADNESS’

Veterans, trucking industry representatives and administration officials attend a White House event announcing the Trump administration's Freedom Haulers Initiative. (Peter D'Abrosca/Fox News Digital)

Trump said the administration has removed more than 24,000 non-English-speaking commercial drivers from behind the wheel and worked with states to cancel more than 28,000 commercial driver's licenses he said were unlawfully issued to illegal immigrants. He also pointed to several fatal crashes allegedly involving illegal immigrants while arguing for the policy change.
Duffy said the initiative eliminates unnecessary barriers for veterans transitioning into civilian careers while prioritizing highway safety.
"These are great-paying jobs. They're anywhere from $80,000 to $100,000-plus a year," Duffy said. "…illegals are out. American patriots are in."
ILLEGAL TRUCKER CASES FUEL GOP PUSH TO CRACK DOWN ON CDL MILLS AS DEMS LARGELY SILENT
President Donald Trump delivers remarks during a White House event announcing the Freedom Haulers Initiative alongside Transportation Secretary Sean Duffy. (Peter D'Abrosca/Fox News Digital)

Collins said the Department of Veterans Affairs will also expand access to CDL training by allowing eligible veterans to use GI Bill benefits and by accelerating enrollment in existing training programs.
"Let's put veterans in the seats, making jobs safer and better for all Americans," Collins said, noting that roughly one in 10 truck drivers nationwide already are veterans.

Werner Enterprises President Nathan Meisgeier announced his company will hire 1,400 veterans over the next year as part of the Freedom Haulers Initiative, calling military veterans a natural fit for the trucking industry.
"This administration's Freedom Haulers campaign will have a direct and powerful impact on our ability to bring even more veterans into our workforce," Meisgeier said.

Transportation Secretary Sean Duffy speaks as President Donald Trump listens during a White House event announcing the Freedom Haulers Initiative, which aims to expand trucking opportunities for military veterans. (Peter D'Abrosca/Fox News Digital)
CLICK HERE TO DOWNLOAD THE FOX NEWS APP

Army veteran Ricky Washington, who transitioned into commercial trucking after serving for three decades in the Army and Army National Guard, said the profession offers former service members another opportunity to serve the country.

"The trucking industry is more than just a sector of our economy — it's the backbone of our commerce," Washington said. "It is a place where service members, veterans [and] military spouses can find a purpose, a community and a way to continue keeping our great nation moving forward."
Peter D'Abrosca is a politics reporter at Fox News Digital.

title: House panel demands classified briefings on noncitizen voting, alleged Chinese election interference
summary: Rep. Bryan Steil demands classified DHS briefings on noncitizen voting and cyber vulnerabilities in voting systems ahead of November midterms.
story: A "Fox News Sunday" panel examines the controversy surrounding non-citizens found on New Jersey's voter rolls, with over 400 reported to have cast ballots.
The House committee charged with overseeing American elections is demanding more information on allegations of noncitizens voting in federal races.

The Committee on House Administration is requesting classified briefings on foreign interference in U.S. elections after President Donald Trump raised such concerns during a speech earlier this month.
"Reports of noncitizens casting illegal ballots continue to emerge, undermining election integrity and public confidence in American elections," wrote Committee Chairman Bryan Steil, R-Wis.

"To inform potential legislative reforms, the Committee therefore requests a Member-level, classified briefing from DHS on the number of non-citizens registered to vote across the country and cyber vulnerabilities present in current voting systems. Please contact the Committee by August 13, 2026, to set up a briefing to be held in the month of September. The Committee also requests that any relevant documents be provided alongside the briefing."
HOUSE REPUBLICANS CONFRONT NJ GOVERNOR OVER 6,600 NON-CITIZENS REGISTERED TO VOTE IN ALLEGED SOFTWARE FAILURE
Inside the Fairfax Government Center in Fairfax, Va., a voter is seen at a polling station during a referendum on redistricting. (Julia Demaree Nikhinson/AP Photo)
The classified briefing requests were sent to Department of Homeland Security (DHS) Secretary Markwayne Mullin, FBI Director Kash Patel and acting Director of National Intelligence (DNI) Bill Pulte.

In the letters, Steil cited Trump's claim that DHS discovered roughly 278,000 noncitizens registered to vote as well as recent revelations that New Jersey mistakenly added 6,600 noncitizens to its voter rolls in 2023 and 2024.
TRUMP ACCUSED CHINA OF AN 'ELECTION SECURITY NIGHTMARE' BUT THEN UNDERCUT HIS OWN WARNING
Steil also pointed to Trump's comments in his speech on Chinese-led "cyberattacks on election infrastructure."
President Donald Trump during a primetime address to the nation in the East Room of the White House in Washington, D.C., on July 16, 2026. (Saul Loeb/AFP/Bloomberg via Getty Images)
The committee's release said there were "serious concerns about the security of American elections."

The briefing requests come less than 100 days before the November midterm elections, which will decide which party controls both houses of Congress for the latter half of Trump's final term in the Oval Office.
Republicans have long raised concerns about the security of American elections, which Democrats have argued are attempts to undermine people's faith in those elections.
House Administration Committee Chairman Bryan Steil, R-Wis., holds a press conference in Washington, D.C., on Oct. 10, 2025. (Anna Rose Layden/Getty Images)
CLICK HERE TO DOWNLOAD THE FOX NEWS APP

It is already a federal crime to vote in elections as a noncitizen, but the GOP is pushing for further guardrails such as proof of citizenship in the voter registration process and a federal voter ID standard at the polls.
To date, no evidence has been found that noncitizens have swayed the outcome of any federal election.
Elizabeth Elkind is a politics reporter for Fox News Digital leading coverage of the House of Representatives. Previous digital bylines seen at Daily Mail and CBS News.
Follow on Twitter at @liz_elkind and send tips to elizabeth.elkind@fox.com

title: Dem senator swipes credit for bill he opposed amid heated re-election bid: 'Disturbing pattern'
summary: Jon Ossoff touted Georgia military construction wins at Fort Benning and Fort Stewart despite voting against the bill that funded those improvements.
story: Secretary of War Pete Hegseth testified before the Senate, defending the administration's $1.5 trillion budget request as a ‘generational investment’ crucial for military readiness and troop welfare.
Sen. Jon Ossoff, D-Ga., is touting his advocacy for federal investment in Georgia military infrastructure despite having ultimately voted against the bill that secured the improvements.

Most recently, Ossoff highlighted new construction for an elementary school at Fort Benning, improved conditions at Fort Stewart, pay raises for military personnel and improvements to Georgia’s foster care system — all a part of the annual military funding bill known as Military Construction and Veteran Affairs (MilCon-VA).
At the time of its initial passage, Ossoff quickly released a press statement.
FOX NEWS POLL: AN EARLY LOOK AT THE GEORGIA SENATE RACE
Sen. Jon Ossoff, D-Ga., speaks at a campaign event for President Joe Biden at Pullman Yards March 9, 2024, in Atlanta, Ga. (Megan Varner/Getty Images)
"U.S. Senate passes Sen. Ossoff’s Bipartisan Bill that provides most funding for Georgia military construction in 15 years," his website announced.
When reconsidering it for final passage, Ossoff opposed the package.

Notably, Ossoff, as the ranking member on the Senate Subcommittee on Military Construction and Veteran Affairs, voted in favor of the bill in committee and as a standalone bill but opposed its final passage later that year when it was bundled together with other government funding legislation.
When asked about the voting record, his office reaffirmed the federal support secured in Georgia.

"Let's be clear: Georgia's massive 2026 military construction budget, the highest in 15 years, is a direct and undeniable result of Senator Ossoff's work as the senior Democrat on the Military Construction subcommittee," an Ossoff campaign spokesperson told Fox News Digital in a statement.

"Senator Ossoff makes no apology for having tried to stop Mike Collins from doubling premiums for more than a million Georgians and throwing 300,000 off their health insurance," the spokesperson added.
The spokesperson was referring to Ossoff's Republican challenger, Rep. Mike Collins, R-Ga., and caps on federal health subsidies Republicans had championed at the time of MilCon-VA's passage.

Like many Democrats, Ossoff has struggled to oppose legislation championed by President Donald Trump while at the same time making his case for re-election in one of the country’s most competitive Senate seats. Ossoff won in 2021 with a 50.6% to 49.4% victory over incumbent Sen. David Perdue, R-Ga.
In the case of the elementary school, Ossoff said he had been calling for those investments for years.

"I have been working for years now for a replacement for Dexter Elementary. That’s really important for those families down there in Columbus," Ossoff said. "I’m just a bit concerned by the lack of attention in this year’s base budget, so we’ll work together on that."

Ossoff made similar remarks about improvements to Fort Stewart, citing concerns in press releases about lead exposure affecting newborns' health on the base, mold contamination and flooded living areas.
Ossoff released findings in a seven-page report about the base’s conditions.
SEN BLUMENTHAL, REP. TAKANO: CONGRESS CAN FUND VETERANS’ CARE WITHOUT TAKING BENEFITS FROM DISABLED HEROES
Sen. Jon Ossoff, D-Ga., speaks during an interview at Dobbins Air Reserve Base April 26, 2025, in Marietta, Ga. (AP)

"Our military service members and their families make huge sacrifices for the country, and it’s a travesty how they’re being treated by privatized housing contractors in Georgia and nationwide," Sen. Ossoff said.
"The stories in this report should shock our conscience, and I will continue exposing the mistreatment of military families in privatized housing and working to protect them and improve conditions."
Notably, the package Ossoff ultimately voted against contained $8 million for Fort Stewart and $127.4 million to replace the Dexter Elementary School.
A veteran lawmaker ripped Ossoff for highlighting wins he didn’t participate in.

"Last year, he tried to take credit for my veterans housing bill, legislation he had absolutely nothing to do with. A politician who tries to erase a veteran’s work for political gain has forfeited the trust of the people he seeks to represent," Rep. Derrick Van Orden, R-Wis., said in a statement, referring to a bill he introduced last year.

Ossoff highlighted the bill on his website, calling it a "bipartisan bill backed by U.S. Senator Jon Ossoff" and announcing that "Sen. Ossoff brings Republicans and Democrats together to protect veterans from foreclosure."
Ossoff was not a sponsor of the bill and, because it passed unanimously in a voice vote, did not cast a vote for it either.
DEM SENATOR ACCUSED OF BEING 'NOWHERE TO BE FOUND' ON CRUCIAL ISSUE IMPACTING KIDS IN SWING STATE
Sen. Jon Ossoff, D-Ga., during a news conference after the weekly Senate Democrat policy luncheon at the U.S. Capitol in Washington, D.C., Dec. 9, 2025. (Aaron Schwartz/Bloomberg/Getty Images)
CLICK HERE TO DOWNLOAD THE FOX NEWS APP
"Ossoff’s disturbing pattern of taking credit for work he didn’t do and claiming victories he didn’t support demonstrates both gross incompetence and a complete lack of integrity," Van Orden said.
Leo Briceno is a politics reporter for the congressional team at Fox News Digital. He was previously a reporter with World Magazine.

title: Trump pushes F-35 sale to Turkey, but his own State Department says Erdoğan hasn't met legal requirements
summary: A State Department letter to Congress confirms Turkey has not met legal conditions for the F-35, despite Trump's promise to lift sanctions on Ankara.
story: Amidst the NATO summit, President Donald Trump asserts the U.S. relationship with Turkey is 'better than it's ever been' despite F-35 concerns. However, Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu warns Turkey supports Hamas. Wall Street Journal's Olivia Beavers details Republican discomfort with Trump's stance, noting backchannel pushback against potentially shifting the Middle East's balance of power.

President Donald Trump has opened the door to selling Turkey the U.S.' prized F-35 fighter jet, praising Turkish President Recep Tayyip Erdoğan and promising to remove sanctions imposed over Ankara’s purchase of a Russian missile defense system.
But a State Department letter to Congress makes clear that Turkey has not taken the steps legally required to receive the advanced fighter.
"Turkey has not yet met these conditions," the department said in the July 22 letter, first obtained by the Greek newspaper Kathimerini.
TRUMP COULD HAND PRIZED STEALTH JETS TO NATO ALLY ONCE SEEN AS ALLIANCE HEADACHE

Turkish President Recep Tayyip Erdogan welcomes US President Donald Trump at Ankara Airport, who is paying an official visit to Turkey ahead of the 36th NATO Heads of State and Government Summit in Ankara, Turkey, on July 07, 2026. (Dogukan Keskinkilic/Pool via REUTERS)

The letter said U.S. law prohibits the transfer of F-35 aircraft to Turkey until Ankara no longer possesses the Russian-made S-400 system or associated equipment, promises not to acquire it again and satisfies the remaining certification requirements established by Congress.
The finding came weeks after Trump stood alongside Erdoğan at the NATO summit in Ankara and said his administration would lift sanctions on Turkey and consider selling it the aircraft.
Asked about Turkey’s continued possession of the S-400, Trump said, "I have no concerns about anything having to do with Turkey."

Trump described relations with Ankara as "better probably than it’s ever been," said Turkey had been "much more loyal" than some other countries and called a potential F-35 sale "certainly something we will consider."
Erdoğan said Turkey previously has been promised five aircraft and expressed confidence in Trump.
"I know that Mr. Trump always keeps his promises," Erdoğan said, according to Reuters.
The dispute matters far beyond a single weapons sale.

Turkey is a pivotal NATO ally controlling access between Europe and the Middle East, but its ties to Russia and Hamas have fueled doubts in Washington about whether Ankara can be trusted with America’s most sensitive military technology. The outcome will test whether Trump’s personal relationship with Erdoğan can bring Turkey back into the Western defense fold — or whether Congress and national security concerns will block the deal.
WHO IS TURKEY'S RECEP TAYYIP ERDOĞAN? HOW NATO'S MOST UNPREDICTABLE LEADER KEEPS REINVENTING HIMSELF
A U.S. airmen watches an Air Force F-35 Lightning II joint strike fighter aircraft approach for the first time on July 14, 2011 at Eglin Air Force Base in Florida. (Samuel King Jr./U.S. Air Force)

A State Department spokesperson told Fox News Digital on background that Trump "recognizes the strategic importance of Türkiye" and that his administration is encouraging Ankara "to resolve pending issues."
"Türkiye is a valued NATO ally, and we continue to engage on all aspects of our important and multi-faceted relationship," the spokesperson said.

James Jeffrey, a former U.S. ambassador to Turkey and former special representative for Syria engagement, said Trump’s position reflects both his trust in Erdoğan and their cooperation on regional security issues.

"Trump is very much for this as he works well with Erdoğan and trusts him and has succeeded together on a host of security issues from Libya to Syria to Caucasus to Ukraine and PKK ceasefire with Ankara," Jeffrey, now a distinguished fellow at The Washington Institute, told Fox News Digital.
"He knows how important this is to Erdoğan and all Turks and doesn’t want Ankara to turn to Russia or China for weapons," he said.

Turkey was removed from the F-35 development program in 2019 after purchasing the S-400 from Russia. The United States imposed sanctions the following year under the Countering America’s Adversaries Through Sanctions Act.
U.S. officials have argued that operating the Russian system alongside the F-35 could allow Moscow to collect sensitive information about the stealth aircraft.
Jeffrey said Turkey would have to genuinely relinquish the S-400 but noted that the law does not specify exactly how.
"Certainly transferring to another country would meet the legal and technical requirement," he said.

Sinan Ciddi, director of the Turkey Program at the Foundation for Defense of Democracies, agreed that a third-country transfer could begin the process of restoring Turkey to the program. But he said Ankara would also have to provide guarantees that it would not again seek major Russian military equipment or maintain ties that could compromise the aircraft.
TRUMP BETS ON FORMER NATO TROUBLEMAKER AS TURKEY'S STRATEGIC VALUE SURGES

- Russia's President Vladimir Putin meets with Turkey's President Recep Tayyip Erdogan on the sidelines of the BRICS summit in Kazan on October 23, 2024. (ALEXANDER ZEMLIANICHENKO/POOL/AFP via Getty Images)
Reports have suggested the United Arab Emirates as a possible destination for the S-400. Ciddi said, however, that there is no confirmation Abu Dhabi would accept it.

The UAE would have to consider whether acquiring the Russian system could trigger U.S. penalties or jeopardize access to other American weapons, he said. Russia could also object to Turkey transferring the system without Moscow’s approval.

Jeffrey said Erdoğan is likely prepared to resist Russian pressure because the F-35 is both a prestige issue and an important military need for Turkey, whose air force relies heavily on F-16 aircraft.
Ciddi argued that resolving the S-400 dispute should not automatically clear the way for a sale.

"The S-400 issue that led to Turkey’s removal from the F-35 program is the floor, not the ceiling," Ciddi said, pointing to Ankara’s relationship with Hamas, continued ties with Russia, use of Chinese telecommunications technology and tensions with U.S. partners including Greece, Cyprus and Israel as additional obstacles.
The State Department letter reflected the administration’s competing views of Ankara.

While reiterating that Turkey remains legally ineligible for the F-35, the department credited it with supporting US diplomatic efforts involving Russia and Ukraine, Azerbaijan and Armenia, Gaza and counter-ISIS operations.
The letter said Turkey used its relationship with Hamas’ political leadership to help secure acceptance of Trump’s Gaza peace plan and advance the first phase of a ceasefire.
At the same time, it warned that Hamas continues to use financial channels operating from Turkish territory.

"Hamas’ use of informal financial networks and unlicensed exchange houses in Turkey to access funds remains a concern, and we are committed to disrupting these illicit financing streams," the State Department said.
Jeffrey said those Hamas ties could generate opposition in Congress but may carry less weight with Trump because his administration has relied on Ankara in Gaza diplomacy.
Ciddi interpreted the letter not as a rejection of Turkey’s return, but as a signal that the administration is prepared to move forward if Ankara meets the legal requirements.
"I think the letter is trying to convey to Congress, ‘Look, once Turkey makes good on the legal requirements of the NDAA, we can proceed with the sale,’" he said.

Congress could still be the most significant obstacle. Lawmakers have prohibited the transfer while Turkey possesses the S-400, and a bipartisan group of 18 House members recently urged congressional leaders to block any sale under current conditions, according to Axios.

The issue also has regional implications. Israel reportedly has pressed Trump not to provide Turkey with the aircraft, amid fears that a sale could weaken Israel’s qualitative military edge as tensions between Erdoğan and Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu deepen.
CLICK HERE TO DOWNLOAD THE FOX NEWS APP

F-35 fighter aircrafts fly over the White House during Polish President Karol Nawrocki's visit in Washington, DC on September 3, 2025. Trump and Nawrocki discussed the flyover in memory of a Polish pilot who recently died in training, calling him a "legend." (Oliver Contreras/AFP via Getty Images.))
For now, the State Department’s message is clear: Trump may favor the sale, but Erdoğan must first surrender the Russian system that caused Turkey’s expulsion from the program.
The State Department and Turkish Embassy in Washington did not respond to Fox News Digital’s requests for comment.

Efrat (Effie) Lachter is an investigative journalist, filmmaker and war correspondent. She has directed and produced over 200 documentary segments across more than 40 countries. Recipient of the 2022 Peres Center for Peace Award, Lachter is also a 2023-24 Knight-Wallace Journalism Fellow at the University of Michigan. She holds a bachelor's degree in communication and a master's degree in political science.

title: 'Worst of the Worst' judges are sabotaging Trump's immigration agenda, top DHS official says
summary: DHS General Counsel James Percival names federal judges he says are engaging in judicial activism to block Trump's immigration and deportation agenda.
story: DHS Chief Counsel James Percival said a group of federal district judges—not the judiciary as a whole—are repeatedly blocking deportations and Temporary Protected Status rollbacks despite SCOTUS rulings, calling it "naked political activism."

DHS General Counsel James Percival says Americans deserve to know which federal judges are repeatedly blocking the Trump administration's immigration agenda, accusing a small group of district judges of acting in "open defiance" of the Supreme Court and engaging in "naked political activism."

Percival has begun posting on X identifying federal district judges while accusing them of obstructing key portions of President Donald Trump's immigration agenda. Critics have argued the campaign improperly targets members of the judiciary.

"The American people hear about these terrible acts of judicial activism. I think what they don't often understand is this is not some epidemic that sort of crosses the entire judiciary," Percival said. "There are particular judges who are a problem in case after case after case."

Percival told Fox News Digital the effort is intended to educate the public — not intimidate judges — and highlights what he described as a handful of repeat offenders acting in "open defiance" of the Supreme Court or reaching outside their Article III authority.
DHS EVISCERATES MEDIA FOR ‘ABSOLUTE ABSURDITY’ OVER CONCERN ABOUT ‘WORST OF THE WORST’ ACTIVIST JUDGES LIST
Homeland Security General Counsel James Percival. (DHS official portrait)

Percival stressed that he does not believe the federal judiciary faces a systemic problem of defiance against the Supreme Court or the separation of powers, but said activist plaintiffs are adept at "forum shopping."
"They file in these locations, often with very sort of dubious arguments to [have their case heard] in that venue. And they do it to get the same judges over and over and again."
GOP SENATOR UNVEILS BOASBERG ACT TO STOP 'ROGUE' JUDGES FROM HANDPICKING TRUMP CASES

U.S. District Judge Brian Murphy has temporarily blocked key Trump administration decisions to terminate Temporary Protected Status (TPS) (United States Senate Committee on the Judiciary/ REUTERS/Nathan Howard)
He pointed to one such case in which Biden-appointed Judge Brian Murphy in Boston stopped a deportation flight until the Supreme Court intervened.
Murphy issued a 2025 order limiting the federal government's ability to deport illegal immigrants to receptive "third countries."
A flight bound for South Sudan was grounded in Djibouti, where the criminal illegal immigrants were taken to a U.S. military base.

"I think we had eight aliens on this flight to South Sudan. One of them had raped a child. One of them had raped a mentally-disabled person. These were very bad people that should not be in our country. And this Judge Brian Murphy was stopping us from doing this."
SUPREME COURT WEIGHS TRUMP EFFORT TO TERMINATE TEMPORARY PROTECTIONS FOR HAITIAN, SYRIAN MIGRANTS
This still from video from July 22, 2015 show Paula Xinis from US Senate Judiciary Committee (US Senate Judiciary Committee)
DHS petitioned the Supreme Court to intervene. Percival said the incident drew support from liberal Justice Elena Kagan, who sided with the Trump administration in the case.

"She said, ‘Even though I disagreed the first time, I do agree that Judge Murphy can't defy the U.S. Supreme Court’," Percival said. "And so when you see the same judge doing these acts of sabotage on TPS (Temporary Protected Status), we just think it's important for the American people to understand."

"And this is not an attempt by me to blast the entire judiciary. It's just the opposite. If I were a member of the judiciary, I would want people to know this is a handful of district judges who are causing the same problems over and over and over again and calling the credibility of the entire branch of government into question when many of these judges are following the law and doing their jobs."
Percival now frequently shares the "Worst of the Worst" judges series, separate from ICE's "Worst of the Worst" criminal illegal immigrants series.
"If you think about DHS' "Worst of the Worst" series, the main purpose of that is just to inform the American public about what's going on," he said.
SIGN UP TO GET THE POLITICS NEWSLETTER
US military aircraft as seen at US Military Base Camp Lemonnier in Djibouti. Camp Lemonnier is the only permanent United States military base in Africa. (Photo by Getty Images) (Getty Images)

"There's a lot of false narratives out there about immigration enforcement, but when we actually show people the types of people we're moving from our communities, we think that really makes a big difference to the public..."
Percival said both series are intended to educate the public about DHS operations and counter narratives that do not reflect the agency's day-to-day work.
Percival highlighted Clinton-appointed Illinois Judge Matthew Kennelly — who issued an order pausing termination of TPS for Burma nationals.

"He did so even though these decisions are not subject to judicial review, even though we have been vindicated by the Supreme Court on TPS four times, and even though the Seventh Circuit summarily reversed him on the same issue only days before," Percival said in a separate statement.
"This is judicial sabotage."
He also called out Obama-appointed Judge Paula Xinis in Greenbelt, Maryland.

Percival called Xinis the reason Kilmar Abrego Garcia — the illegal immigrant the press dubbed "Maryland Man" and whom Sen. Chris Van Hollen, D-Md., had boat drinks with in El Salvador — is still in the U.S.

"She entered an order preventing his removal and then ordered him released on the basis that we had no plans to remove him. If it sounds crazy, it’s because it is. Our efforts to reverse this decision remain pending," Percival tweeted.

He said Biden-appointed Judge Hernan Vera in Los Angeles has "micromanage[d]" DHS' use-of-force policy by describing violent anti-ICE agitators as "legal observers" while deeming the agency "violent."
"[T]here's a lot of times when the American public thinks that there's something DHS is not doing because we're choosing not to do it," he said in his Fox News Digital interview.
"We just think it's very helpful for people to understand what we're facing in the courts, how out of control they are."
He noted there has been public frustration at the appearance of DHS not doing certain things or not going in as hard on others as promised, pointing to the wind-down of TPS for foreign nationals.
"Of course, a lot of that is because of the judicial sabotage that we are facing in district courts and in other [places]."
Fox News Digital reached out to the judges' respective courts for comment.
The media has also criticized Percival for the lists, including a Chicago Sun-Times reporter who asked whether the catalog he posted on X risks increasing threats against the judiciary.

"Witness the absolute absurdity of the liberal media response... Legitimate fact-based critiques of judges and their rulings is fair-game in a free society. Also, the media has no issue with it if the judge is conservative," Percival wrote.
CLICK HERE TO DOWNLOAD THE FOX NEWS APP
He told Fox News Digital the issue is "classic separation-of-powers" in that the executive is allowed to tell another branch there’s disagreement.
Percival spoke with Fox News Digital from San Juan, where he was visiting personnel from Homeland Security Investigations.
He said HSI functions like an immigration-focused FBI, adding that it and other agencies reflect the "broad portfolio" he oversees as DHS's top lawyer.

"ICE is in the news the most, and so I think people are starting to associate me with ICE, but I love all my proverbial children equally. And I'm very dedicated to helping every single operator that my people are providing legal advice to be successful," he said, noting there are 50 DHS attorneys in Puerto Rico alone and that he felt it important to meet with them.
Critics' concerns about Percival's list come after other officials have also faced criticism for their rhetoric targeting certain judges.

Sen. Charles Schumer, D-N.Y., was criticized for claiming that Justices Brett Kavanaugh and Neil Gorsuch "released the whirlwind" by ruling against abortion protections in an incident that drew a rare public rebuke from Chief Justice John Roberts.
Kavanaugh, as well as Justice Amy Coney Barrett, have also been the target of threats from activist critics.
Born and raised in Allentown, Pennsylvania, worked in both the New York and Washington bureaus for Fox News since 2013.

title: Federal judge blocks DOJ access to NJ voter rolls amid statewide controversy
summary: District Judge Zahid Quraishi blocked the Justice Department from accessing New Jersey's unredacted voter registration list, citing privacy concerns.
story: State Sen. Declan O'Scanlon says New Jersey should halt its current automatic voter registration system, launch an independent investigation and consider federal oversight.
A federal judge in New Jersey blocked the Justice Department from gaining access to the state's unredacted voter rolls on Wednesday.

District Judge Zahid Quraishi, a Biden appointee, ruled that handing over the rolls could give rise to privacy concerns for voters. The ruling is the latest defeat for President Donald Trump's administration after the DOJ sued Utah, Oklahoma, Kentucky, West Virginia and New Jersey for access to their voter rolls earlier this year.
The administration argued that Title III of the Civil Rights Act granted federal authorities access to the lists, but Quraishi disagreed.
TRUMP-APPOINTED FEDERAL JUDGE TOSSES DOJ LAWSUIT SEEKING ARIZONA VOTER DATA
Voting booths are set up during a primary election. (iStock)

"The plain text of Title III applies only to records ‘which come into’ election officers’ ‘possession’ and thus does not extend to New Jersey’s computerized VRL [voter registration list] – a document the State itself created," Quraishi wrote.
Quraishi's ruling also comes amid a statewide controversy related to noncitizen voting in New Jersey.

New Jersey Gov. Mikie Sherrill admitted last week that a "serious software error" led to the mistaken registration of roughly 6,600 noncitizens through the state's Motor Vehicle System, while the company that provides the identity-related security services denied any wrongdoing.
DEMOCRATS CONCEDE NJ VOTER-ROLL FAILURE WAS ‘HORRIBLE’ — BUT REJECT BROADER FRAUD FEARS

"In New Jersey, we absolutely need to have accountability for what happened," Sen. Andy Kim, D-N.J., said of the incident. "It was just horrible. There was a big problem with that computer problem that they had. We need to try to address that going forward."
New Jersey Gov. Mikie Sherrill addresses a crowd in Middlesex County. (Michael Nagle/Getty Images)

Sherrill said she immediately ordered an investigation after the error was discovered and that the state's Division of Elections is removing ineligible voters from the rolls. She said fewer than 400 of those improperly registered cast ballots.
A noncitizen on the New Jersey voter rolls used this removal form to request to be unregistered. (Obtained by the RNC and NJGOP)
CLICK HERE TO DOWNLOAD THE FOX NEWS APP

Reports also surfaced this week that roughly 75,000 noncitizens had been summoned for jury duty through state databases, according to multiple reports, broadening the controversy beyond the Motor Vehicle Commission and prompting additional Republican calls for a wider investigation.
Fox News' Charles Creitz contributed to this report.
Anders Hagstrom is a reporter with Fox News Digital covering national politics and major breaking news events.

title: War powers resolution fails as Senate Republicans stand by Trump on Iran
summary: Senate Republicans blocked another war powers resolution as munitions dwindle and Sen. Bill Cassidy draws a hard line on ground troops in Iran.
story: Sen. Jim Banks, R-Ind., a member of the Senate Armed Services Committee, discusses the Pentagon's urgent request for $80 billion from Congress for potential conflict with Iran.
Despite reports of waning munitions, spiking gas prices and concerns of no clear objectives moving forward, Senate Republicans are still giving President Donald Trump wiggle room in the war in Iran.

Republicans again blocked another war powers resolution to force an immediate withdrawal of America’s military might from Iran on Thursday. Senate Democrats have tried and failed to convince enough of their Republican colleagues to consistently buck the war over a dozen times as it stretches into its fifth month.
The latest effort from Sen. Kirsten Gillibrand, D-N.Y., failed along similar lines as last week’s effort, where only a small cohort of Senate Republicans crossed the aisle to end the war.
REPUBLICANS FALL IN LINE WITH TRUMP ON IRAN WAR DESPITE RISING COSTS AND US DEATH TOLL
President Donald Trump during an announcement in the Oval Office of the White House in Washington, D.C., on July 29, 2026. (Aaron Schwartz/CNP/Bloomberg via Getty Images)
One Republican who did join Democrats, but has since reversed course, is Sen. Bill Cassidy, R-La., who got into a shouting match with Trump and demanded a briefing on the situation in Iran.

He got that briefing and has since flipped his vote, which he acknowledged was used as "leverage to get some information." Still, he doesn’t totally support what’s going on, but used "All the King's Men" as an example to show that the situation and the politics of it are not black and white.
"It is a gradation," Cassidy said. "What we're doing here is a gradation, a murkiness, a vagueness, but we're trying to see our way through it. And I'm trying to see my way through it."
WATCH: SCHUMER'S ANTI-CORRUPTION SPEECH DERAILED AFTER HECKLER BRANDS HIM 'GENOCIDAL MANIAC'
But he drew a hard line on ground troops entering Iran.
"If there are ground troops, by definition, there needs to be a declaration of war from Congress on this, period," Cassidy said.
The latest votes come as reports of munitions continuing to dwindle have reverberated through Congress, and as the Pentagon and War Secretary Pete Hegseth plead for more defense funding.
HEGSETH DISMISSES ‘FOOLISH’ US STOCKPILE CONCERNS AS IRAN CONFLICT TESTS MUNITIONS
The THAAD missile defense system is shown here being tested in Kodiak, Alaska, in July 2017. (Leah Garton/Missile Defense Agency/Reuters)

Sen. Thom Tillis, R-N.C., who has been wary of the war but has so far not broken with Trump to back Democrats’ resolutions, said, "Obviously, it’s concerning" that the nation’s munitions stockpile is dropping, but countered that a closed-door debriefing on the matter could sate concerns.
"And of course, if they are chronically low and affecting war strategy, then we should make it a priority," Tillis said.
When asked whether he had been adequately briefed, Tillis said, "No."
Munitions have been a concern throughout the war in Iran, and with renewed strikes starting last week, they are again back at the forefront of the conversation about the strategy in the region.

A report released Monday from the Center for Strategic and International Studies found, for example, that renewed fighting in the Middle East found that Patriot and THAAD interceptor missiles, which are used to thwart incoming projectiles and drones, had dwindled from prewar inventories of 2,330 and 452, respectively, to 759 and 234 missiles.

title: Kamala Harris' new $8M mansion is in a neighborhood with virtually no Black residents

story: Fox News contributor Marc Thiessen, a former speechwriter for George W. Bush, discusses big donors' skepticism toward Kamala Harris' 2028 presidential run. Despite a career-long commitment to combating racial disparities in housing and touting the importance of living among Black people, former Vice President Kamala Harris’ new California mansion is situated in a neighborhood with virtually no racial diversity.

Point Dume is situated entirely within Census tract 8004.08, which the Census Bureau’s American Community Survey estimated was just 0.2% Black and roughly 94% White as of 2019.

title: Capital culture war heats up as GOP lawmaker targets DC schools over Old Glory snub
summary: Sen. Ashley Moody's PLEDGE Act would require American flags and daily Pledge of Allegiance recitation in every Washington, D.C., school classroom.
story: Education Secretary Linda McMahon discusses the lack of patriotism and civic education in schools on ‘America 250: Celebrating Freedom.’

FIRST ON FOX: Florida Republican Sen. Ashley Moody introduced a bill targeting the Washington, D.C. public school system in a push to prioritize patriotism in the nation’s capital, Fox News Digital has learned.

The PLEDGE Act proposal would require teachers to feature the American Flag in their classrooms, and for administrators to provide students the opportunity to recite the Pledge of Allegiance every day.

"Currently, there are schools in Washington, D.C., the nation’s capital, that do not display our flag or set aside time for students to recite the Pledge of Allegiance, but they do teach them to be activists," claims the press release shared with Fox News Digital.
FAR-LEFT ACTIVIST CONFERENCE AT TEACHERS UNION HQ RAISES CLASSROOM CONCERNS
Activists burn a U.S. flag at Black Lives Matter Plaza near the White House on July 4, 2020, in Washington, D.C. (Alex Wong/Getty Images)

"Radicals want to teach kids to be ashamed of the United States of America and how to be activists instead. We should be teaching kids why America is worth loving, and most importantly, the principles and values that make America worth defending," said Moody in the release.
Over 40 states have varying Pledge requirements in their schools — but not in the nation’s capital.

"My PLEDGE Act helps restore pride in our nation by reminding students every day of the freedom, responsibilities, and blessings that come with being an American, and the sacrifices made for our flag and everything it represents," Moody said in a statement shared with Fox News Digital.
BERNIE SANDERS, DSA REVEAL DEMANDS FOR DEM PARTY AFTER SOCIALISTS SWEEP NEW YORK ELECTIONS

The DSA platform, which aims to appeal to younger voters, wants to replace free-market capitalism with social ownership. It also pushes for major constitutional changes, like abolishing the Electoral College and expanding voting rights for noncitizens.

Younger Americans are significantly less likely to express strong national pride than older generations, with just 41% of Generation Z saying they are extremely or very proud to be American, according to a June 2025 Gallup poll.
The same poll says 58% of U.S. adults say they are "extremely" or "very" proud to be American, the lowest level the pollsters have recorded since it began asking the question in 2001.
DEMS PUT ON BLAST OVER POLL THAT SHOWS RECORD-LOW PATRIOTISM IN US: 'TEAR OUR SOCIETY APART'

The DC Public School (DCPS) curriculum calls for students to learn more progressive politics, from studying Harvey Milk to learning how the LGBTQ+ community has shaped and defined the Washington, D.C., community.
