title: Trump admin's push to scrap DEI in federal government takes landmark step with new hiring rule
summary: OPM's new rule removes 1978 hiring guidelines tied to disparate impact, marking a deeper push to dismantle the legal framework behind federal DEI policies.
story: Office of Personnel Management Director Scott Kupor outlines how the Trump administration is transforming the federal government by prioritizing merit over DEI. He details the elimination of self-attestation, implementation of skills-based assessments and efforts to boost accountability for underperforming employees. These reforms aim to cut waste and restore performance across the 2.2 million-strong federal workforce.

FIRST ON FOX: The Trump administration on Wednesday took another step in its sweeping campaign to eliminate DEI policies from the federal government, removing decades-old hiring guidelines that officials say encouraged race-conscious employment decisions in favor of a renewed emphasis on merit-based hiring.

The U.S. Office of Personnel Management (OPM) issued a final interim rule on Thursday that removes references to the 1978 Uniform Guidelines on Employee Selection Procedures, which govern employee selection standards, citing a recent Justice Department legal opinion that found the guidelines unconstitutional in the way they encouraged race-conscious decision-making.

The move affects how federal agencies approach hiring by eliminating references to long-standing guidance centered on "disparate impact," the idea that hiring practices that could produce unequal outcomes among racial groups can be legally problematic even absent intentional discrimination.

Administration officials argue those guidelines pressured employers to focus on racial outcomes rather than qualifications, while supporters of the guidelines contend they help guard against subtle forms of discrimination.
DEI HIRING BOOST FOR ONE BLUE STATE'S MUSLIM COMMISSION INITIATIVE FLIES IN FACE OF TRUMP'S ANTI-WOKE PUSH
President Donald Trump takes questions from the media during a meeting in the Oval Office of the White House on July 21, 2026. (Kevin Dietsch/Getty Images)
"Federal hiring should be based on merit, qualifications, and the ability to perform the job," OPM Director Scott Kupor said in a statement to Fox News Digital.

"This rule ensures OPM's regulations reflect legal guidance while preserving the rigorous, job-related standards that help agencies recruit and hire the most qualified workforce in service to the American people."
The rule took effect immediately after it was published in the Federal Register on Thursday but will remain open for public comment for 60 days before OPM decides whether to make it permanent.
COAST GUARD ENDING RACE-BASED ADMISSIONS FOR OFFICER COMMISSIONING PROGRAM UNDER TRUMP DEI CRACKDOWN
Hundreds protest outside a rally held by President Donald Trump at Macomb County Community College in Warren, Mich., on April 29, 2025. (Getty Images/Dominic Gwinn)

OPM serves as the federal government's human resources agency, setting hiring, personnel and workforce policies for roughly 2 million civilian federal employees across executive branch agencies. It oversees the rules governing how federal agencies recruit, hire, promote and manage their workforces.

This move serves as the latest example of the administration moving beyond simply shutting down DEI offices or ending diversity training and now targeting the legal and regulatory framework that critics argue enabled DEI policies in the first place.
KEY TRUMP AGENCY PUTS TOP UNIVERSITIES IN CROSSHAIRS OVER ALLEGED RACE-BASED DORM PROGRAMS
The U.S. Office of Personnel Management building in Washington June 5, 2015. (Reuters/Gary Cameron)

Since the beginning of President Donald Trump's second term, the administration has highlighted hundreds of colleges that have rolled back DEI initiatives, along with policy changes involving transgender athletic participation, parental rights, race-conscious programs and merit-based admissions.

They also dismantled federal DEI programs, terminated DEI-related grants and contracts, cut ties with companies embracing DEI policies, required federal contractors to comply with the administration's requirements, and warned schools they could lose federal funding over certain DEI practices.
Andrew Mark Miller is a reporter at Fox News. Find him on Twitter @andymarkmiller and email tips to AndrewMark.Miller@Fox.com.

title: Trump threatens to yank his own AG nominee as GOP revolt grows
summary: Trump threatened to withdraw Todd Blanche's nomination until John Cornyn and Thom Tillis leave office, escalating a standoff over his tax settlement.
story: Acting Attorney General Todd Blanche faces renewed scrutiny during his Senate confirmation hearing on Capitol Hill.
President Donald Trump is taking a hardball tactic against Republican rebels demanding concessions for their vote to confirm Acting Attorney General Todd Blanche.

After Blanche’s confirmation hearing was postponed late Wednesday night, Trump took to Truth Social Thursday morning to excoriate the two key holdouts on the Senate Judiciary Committee standing in the way of his personal lawyer becoming the nation’s top prosecutor: Sens. John Cornyn, R-Texas, and Thom Tillis, R-N.C.
Trump threatened to withdraw Blanche’s nomination until both are out of office next year.
TRUMP AG PICK BLANCHE STALLED AS KEY REPUBLICANS REFUSE TO BUDGE
President Donald Trump addresses the nation from the East Room of the White House in Washington, D.C., on July 16, 2026. (Saul Loeb/AFP via Getty Images)

"Todd Blanche is a STAR, and everyone knows it! He has the potential to go down as one of the Greatest Attorney Generals of All Time," Trump said. "However, John Cornyn, of Texas, and Thom Tillis, of North Carolina, both of whom I refused to Endorse, and whose political careers have been ended by my action, are refusing to vote for this Great Nominee, who will remain, in any event, as Acting."

"Remember, both Cornyn and Tillis voted for Merrick Garland, and others, too numerous to mention," he continued. "I have no objection to temporarily withdrawing Todd’s name, if they do not do the right thing, and putting him back after Cornyn and Tillis are out of office."

While Trump did thwart Cornyn’s re-election bid by backing Texas Attorney General Ken Paxton as the Republican nominee, Tillis opted to retire on his own volition last year after raging over Trump's "big, beautiful bill."
DEMS REJECT TRUMP’S TOP SPY PICK AFTER DEMANDING REPLACEMENT, LEAVING COUNTER-TERROR TOOL IN AIR

Cornyn shrugged off the threat almost immediately. Both he and Tillis are in pursuit of explicit, written proposals to modify the settlement deal reached between the IRS and Trump and his family earlier this year.
"POTUS is mistaken if he believes concerns about the provisions in his tax lawsuit settlement are limited to me and Senator Tillis," Cornyn said on X.

Negotiations are still ongoing, but so far the duo have not gotten specifically what they want to permanently kill the now-defunct, nearly $2 billion anti-weaponization fund and a rewrite of Trump’s audit immunity baked into the settlement deal.
And there’s no guarantee that the Senate would be more accepting of Blanche next year, either, given that Republicans have more seats in danger than Senate Democrats.
Senate Majority Leader John Thune, R-S.D., said that waiting until 2027 is "a calculation they’ll have to make."

"The best answer to this is to figure out how to answer, to resolve, the questions that Tillis and Cornyn have," Thune said. "And I think there's a way to do that, and then let's get him confirmed. That would be my take. But, I mean, I'll defer to whatever the White House, the president decides what they’re gonna do."
DOZEN GOP REBELS FAIL TO PERMANENTLY KILL TRUMP'S CONTROVERSIAL $2B FUND
Trump says he will resubmit the acting attorney general's name after GOP Sens. John Cornyn, R-Texas, and Thom Tillis, R-N.C., leave office next year. (Getty Images)

Trump could leave Blanche as acting attorney general for some time, similar to how former President Joe Biden left former acting Labor Secretary Julie Su in the role from 2023 to the end of his presidency. But that also comes with its own time limit.

Under the Federal Vacancies Reform Act, a cabinet-level official can stay in an acting role for 210 days. That timer resets if there is a pending nomination in the Senate. If Trump were to formally withdraw his nominating paperwork, the clock would start over.
If Trump were to formally yank Blanche from consideration on Thursday, he would be allowed, under law, to stay as acting attorney general until late February.

Tillis and Cornyn's argument isn't necessarily against Blanche, either. The problem lies with the administration and resistance to their demands, specifically for him putting a permanent end to the anti-weaponization fund. Tillis feared that "there is somebody who wants to enable it," and that in doing so it would harm Republicans' chances in the midterm elections.
"Look, I've said I'm not a no [on Blanche]," Tillis said. "I'm still working on getting this done, and I'm still optimistic that we will."

Meanwhile, their resistance and demands are what caused Senate Judiciary Chair Chuck Grassley, R-Iowa, to postpone Blanche’s confirmation hearing scheduled for Thursday morning. Without their support, he wouldn’t be able to make it to the Senate floor.
Grassley said after Trump's threat that Blanche was "well qualified, and I want to get him approved."
"I think that right now I'm concentrating on the next few days to get this nomination through, and I'm not going to consider anything else," Grassley said.

title: Ex-Dem operative details 'new donor establishment' behind Mamdani-era progressives: 'Not from the grassroots'
summary: A former progressive fundraiser reveals how dark money super PACs and DSA candidates are reshaping the Democratic Party after its 2024 electoral loss.
story: Evan Barker, author of "Nothing Left: Confessions of a Democratic Operative," argues today's progressive movement is powered by a well-funded ecosystem of donors, consultants and advocacy groups.
Evan Barker, a former Democratic operative turned voter for President Donald Trump, detailed alleged dark money influence that she says has driven the party further left.

Barker, who raised money for Democratic candidates throughout her career, from Barack Obama to progressive lawmakers such as Rep. Alexandria Ocasio-Cortez, D-N.Y., before deciding to vote for Trump in 2024, explained in an interview with Fox News Digital that the party's major shift influenced her decision to defect.

"I first got activated in Democratic politics when Barack Obama was running in 2008. And if you look at him then and you compare him to the modern movement of the party today, it is just night and day. They have gone left on so many critical issues, like immigration and identity politics and defund the police and just all of these things that I did not sign up for," she told Fox News Digital.
HOW THE 'LONG MARCH' THROUGH THE INSTITUTIONS LED TO SOCIALIST TAKEOVER OF DEM PARTY: 'NEED TO WAKE UP'
Cover for "Nothing Left: Confessions of a Democratic Operative" by Evan Barker. (Simon and Schuster)
She argued that the party, in her eyes, abandoned the working class and ignored Americans like her family in Kansas.

"It was also seeing the way the people that I knew in progressive politics looked at people in the middle of the country. People like my family who had voted for Obama and then voted for Donald Trump, and they really just had a disdain for them. They truly did view them as deplorables. And then it got even worse when I saw them actually decide to write them off. To say that they would not even try to persuade them to vote for us anymore because there was no point," she told Fox News Digital.

"At that point, I knew the party was doomed, and I think I just experienced so much abuse working in the movement that at some point I got fed up and I was like, 'I'm gonna do this, like what other options have they given me?'" Barker added.
JAMES CARVILLE ARGUES ONE KEY MISTAKE FROM BIDEN HAS LEFT DEMOCRATS IN DISARRAY

In her new book, "Nothing Left: Confessions of a Democratic Operative," Barker writes about her trepidation and hesitance to vote for Kamala Harris after the party chose her to replace President Joe Biden as the Democrats' presidential candidate in 2024.

"I would say that Kamala Harris was me seeing in real time the manifestation of everything the Democrats had become. They were a party that was loud but said very little. They were a party without substance. They were empty. They were hollow," she told Fox News Digital.

"When I went to the DNC, I only saw Kamala talk about abortion and shouting out joy," Barker recalled. "She wasn't focused on the southern border, she wasn't focused on the economy. She wasn't connecting to the pain that people like my mom were experiencing in Missouri and it just became too much. And when they had Oprah Winfrey out to speak to tell us all that we should be feeling joy and to ignore everything that we were feeling, I had enough and I left. I left the convention before she even spoke."
MAMDANI CALLS OUT DEMOCRATIC PARTY AS 'WELL-PAID CONSULTANTS AND BIG MONEY INTERESTS'
Democratic presidential nominee and Vice President Kamala Harris takes the stage at the Democratic National Convention in Chicago, Aug. 22, 2024. (Reuters/Brendan Mcdermid)

Barker was on site for one of the first meetings between Sen. Bernie Sanders, I-Vt., and then-House candidate Ocasio-Cortez in 2018, when the pair flew to Kansas to stump for Brent Welder, a progressive House candidate who Barker was fundraising for at the time, she explains in her book.

While at the time Barker felt that Ocasio-Cortez could and should run for president, she now feels that the progressive congresswoman and other members of the "Squad" represent everything that's wrong with the party.
"I think AOC in 2018 and the 'Squad' members that came out of her rise have actually done the most damage to the Democratic Party," she told Fox News Digital.
Reps. Ilhan Omar, D-Minn., and Jamaal Bowman, D-N.Y., leave the U.S. Capitol after the last votes of the week on Sept. 14, 2023. (Tom Williams/CQ-Roll Call, Inc via Getty Images)

"I actually think that Bernie Sanders ran a very different campaign in 2015 and 2016 than how he is today. I think back then he was more moderate on issues like immigration. He was more moderate on guns, he wasn't anti-gun, you know, he didn't really talk about identity politics. And I think with the rise of AOC, she was identity-obsessed. And so was Ilhan Omar, and so was Jamaal Bowman," Barker continued.

As a fundraiser for the Progressive Change Campaign Committee (PCCC) and Left Rising, Barker said she raised money for progressive candidates. Barker argued the party's production of far-left stars like New York City Mayor Zohran Mamdani shows that Democrats are learning the wrong lessons from their 2024 losses.

"There was a brief period of time after the 2024 election when I really thought that maybe Democrats would learn lessons — losing multiple times to Donald Trump. I mean, come on. Like, what more do they need to wake them up? And instead, I just saw them go further to the left, with Zohran Mamdani, AOC, and all these DSA [Democratic Socialists of America] candidates that kind of have sprung up over the last cycle," she told Fox News Digital.
She attributed the DSA and other progressives' rise to the groups' alleged newfound willingness to deal in dark money.

"The biggest difference between then and now, and part of the reason we just saw somebody like Darializa Chevalier win in New York, is because the progressives, the DSA, they have learned how to utilize outside, independent expenditure, dark money super PACs to their benefit. They used to be afraid to go there because it contradicted with their principles, but after 10 years they've wised up and they've actually started playing the same games as the establishment and in many ways have created the new donor establishment in the Democratic Party, and I think that's what many people don't realize," Barker told Fox News Digital.
A spokesperson for Chevalier denied the charge that she takes corporate PAC money in a statement to Fox News Digital.

"Darializa does not take corporate PAC money, AIPAC money, ICE money, or money from people looking to harm or push people out of this community. She is accountable only to the people of this district. That’s a win for every tenant, every immigrant, and every working person in this district who deserves a representative who actually answers to working class people instead of corporate donors, CEOs, or lobbies. Our campaign was not only the first challenger candidate in NY-13 history to pass the $1 million raised mark, but Darializa also raised that staggering sum as a first-time, working class candidate from more than 10,000 individual donors and with an average donation of just $66," the statement read.

Mayor Zohran Mamdani joins hands with congressional candidates Claire Valdez, Brad Lander and Darializa Avila Chevalier during a Get Out the Vote rally at King's Theater on June 18, 2026, in New York City. (Michael M. Santiago/Getty Images)
Dark money and donors, Barker claimed, play a much larger role in progressive politics than most voters know.
"Most of the messaging is crafted by heads of organizations, consultants and especially donors," she told Fox News Digital.

Alexandria Ocasio-Cortez speaks in support of Brent Welder during a rally at The Reardon Convention Center on July 20, 2018, in Kansas City, Kan. Evan Barker was working for Welder as a fundraiser at the time. (Dan Videtich/ For The Washington Post via Getty Images)

"You know, I talk about one donor in my book, Leah Hunt-Hendrix, an oil heiress from Texas, and she ran a big donor network and at the same time was interfacing on campaigns and working with candidates. And they have a lot of influence over what candidates talk about, you know. It's hard to say no to someone who knows so many wealthy people and can connect to so many different people when they're giving you advice on what policies to adopt and how to speak about policy," she continued.

"I would say the majority of the ideas in the Democratic Party are not from the grassroots. But ironically, and this is kind of interesting, I think a lot of the base now at this point has been radicalized, so they are not necessarily disagreeing with what the Democratic elites are pushing," Barker added.
She explained the anatomy of a progressive pet policy and how the preferred party lines work their way from donors down to voters.
CLICK HERE TO DOWNLOAD THE FOX NEWS APP

"It's a combination of donors and consultants and the heads of organizations that push candidates into adopting their policy positions. When I was working with the far-left, around the year of 2020, something that I saw that was extremely worrisome to me actually was that any organization — it didn't matter if they were a veterans organization, just focused on veterans issues, or if they were a healthcare organization, just trying to focus on healthcare — donors demanded the concept of intersectionality to bring to all messaging related to these issues," she told Fox News Digital

"So that meant that if you were talking about veterans issues, you also had to be talking about racial justice or environmental justice or criminal reform justice. So they kind of pushed all of these other very unpopular, far-left social issues and moved them into the economic issues as well in a way that completely eroded their trust with the public and pushed people like me further away from them," Barker concluded.
Fox News Digital contacted the Democratic Socialists of America, Ocasio-Cortez, Mamdani, Chevalier, Sanders, Omar, Bowman and Hunt-Hendrix, via her Way to Win organization, for further comment.

title: US Navy plans major torpedo stockpile overhaul as military shifts to two-war strategy
summary: The Navy's torpedo overhaul targets MK-48 and MK-54 production as lawmakers push a two-war strategy amid depleted missile stockpiles from the Iran war.
story: Brent Sadler, a former Pentagon official, addresses a report on the U.S.'s declining munitions stockpiles, a critical issue for potential major combat operations against Iran. He highlights that this ongoing problem, known since 2012. Sadler stresses
The U.S. Navy is poised to overhaul its torpedo inventory under the newly-approved congressional budget as the military shifts toward a "two-war" strategy.
Lawmakers made it clear that the U.S. needs to build quantities of undersea weapons sufficient to maintain two major regional conflicts simultaneously, according to Naval News.

Manufacturers are now focused on building up supplies of the U.S. MK-48 Advanced Capability (ADCAP) heavyweight torpedoes and MK-54 lightweight torpedoes to meet the minimum base requirements set by the new budget.
US DRAINS CRITICAL MISSILE STOCKPILES IN IRAN WAR AS YEARSLONG REBUILD LOOMS

Sailors assigned to the Virginia-class fast-attack submarine USS Minnesota (SSN 783) guide a Mark 48 ADCAP (Advanced Capability) torpedo during a weapons offload at Naval Base Guam, Feb. 3, 2025. (U.S. Navy photo by Mass Communication Specialist 1st Class Nikita Custer)
The Navy has not clarified the exact number of undersea weapons that would entail, but it is based on internal estimates about potential conflicts with a near-peer forces.
The Navy is also required to build up a plan to massively increase torpedo production should it become necessary during war or peacetime.
The overhaul comes as the U.S. military is already scrambling to refill stockpiles of missiles and other weapons depleted in the war against Iran.
HEGSETH DISMISSES ‘FOOLISH’ US STOCKPILE CONCERNS AS IRAN CONFLICT TESTS MUNITIONS
A U.S. Navy warship. (U.S. Central Command (CENTCOM))

Defending Israel and the Al Udeid Air Base in Qatar from Iranian counterstrikes during the recent 12-day exchange of strikes cost the U.S. and Israel between $1.48 billion to $1.58 billion, according to an analysis by the Jewish Institute for National Security of America (JINSA).
The monthslong conflict has burned through a significant number of America's offensive and defensive missile systems.

The U.S. had roughly 632 Terminal High Altitude Area Defense (THAAD) interceptors before June 13, the day Israel began its offensive in Iran. About 540 interceptors remain in its arsenal based on JINSA’s calculations of interceptor deliveries and use, according to the report.
THE TWO MOST IMPORTANT AMERICAN WEAPONS SYSTEMS NATO IS EAGER TO HAVE

The U.S. has used up 14% of its global stockpile of prized THAAD missile interceptors. America’s THAAD system accounted for nearly half of all interceptions due to the "insufficient" capacity of Israel’s Arrow interception system.

U.S. Soldiers and civilians observe an MIM-104 Patriot surface-to-air missile (SAM) system during a static-display demonstration Aug. 15, 2019, at Katterbach Army Airfield in Ansbach, Germany. (U.S. Army photo by Charles Rosemond)
It would take three to eight years to replenish the THAAD interceptors used in the 12-day war at current production rates.
CLICK HERE TO DOWNLOAD THE FOX NEWS APP

Patriot interceptor production is more robust than THAAD, according to the report, but the U.S. is providing a number of Patriot interceptors to Ukraine. So, it’s unclear how many remain in the stockpile.
Fox News' Morgan Phillips contributed to this report.
Anders Hagstrom is a reporter with Fox News Digital covering national politics and major breaking news events.

title: Senator targets alleged China-linked Singham network in fiery floor speech
summary: Sen. Jim Banks says Neville Roy Singham's $278 million nonprofit network advances CCP interests from Shanghai while funding anti-ICE and pro-Iran groups.
story: The Indiana senator pointed to U.S. tech tycoon and Shanghai resident Neville Roy Singham as being part of the Chinese Communist Party's 'political warfare' against the U.S. (Credit: U.S. Senate)

Sen. Jim Banks, R-Ind., took to the Senate floor Wednesday to call out Neville Roy Singham, saying the communist tech tycoon's vast nonprofit network is helping China wage "political warfare" against the U.S.

Singham, a 72-year-old American who sold his tech company for $785 million in 2017 and now lives in Shanghai, has funneled $278 million into the broad network of nonprofits since 2017, according to a Fox News Digital investigation. These groups regularly organize and participate in anti-ICE, anti-Israel and pro-Iran demonstrations.

"From his Shanghai office, which he shares with a CCP propaganda outlet whose avowed mission is to ‘tell China’s story well,’ Singham began funding a complex network of left-wing NGOs and nonprofits that advance the interests of the Chinese Communist Party," Banks said.
SEE IT: GOP SENATOR FLIPS SCRIPT ON AGITATORS TIED TO PRO-CCP, SINGHAM NETWORK
Jodie Evans and Neville Roy Singham are pictured together. (Getty Images)

"Code Pink, that radical organization that chases me and other senators throughout the halls of Congress, used to, on occasion, condemn CCP human rights abuses," he added. "After Singham started lavishly funding the group—and married its co-founder—Code Pink stopped criticizing the Chinese government and started defending it."

Code Pink, which was co-founded by Singham’s wife, Jodie Evans, regularly confronts lawmakers on Capitol Hill, and publicly states that "China is Not Our Enemy." Evans and Singham have not responded to Fox News Digital’s repeated requests for comment.

Fox News Digital obtained footage of Sen. Rick Scott, R-Fla., being targeted by Code Pink on Wednesday over the conflict in Iran. Scott pushed back, questioning whether the group was bothered by the Oct. 7, 2023, Hamas attack on Israel.
TRUMP WELCOMES NETANYAHU TO WHITE HOUSE AS RAGING IRAN WAR THREATENS TO SOUR US-ISRAEL RELATIONSHIP
The Code Pink agitators did not respond to Scott’s question.
Banks’ floor speech also addressed Secretary of State Marco Rubio’s call to combat the far-left political terrorism that has taken root across the globe and in the U.S.

Rubio spoke to more than 60 countries at a summit in Washington, D.C., earlier this month, saying that networks are coordinating across multiple countries, providing training instructions and using encrypted communication to foment unrest. He said that international cooperation is critical to disrupting the financing of dangerous organizations, and that some are working with hostile foreign states.
JIM BANKS, GOP LAWMAKERS RALLY BEHIND DOJ PROBE INTO ALLEGED CCP-LINKED FUNDING NETWORK

"For far too long, however, our counterterrorism doctrine has had a blind spot – a blind spot when it comes to extremist violence from the political left," Rubio said. "Even today, the very idea that far-left terrorism could be a serious threat is treated as a right-wing fever dream, or worse, as a dangerous fascist conspiracy."

Singham currently faces a grand jury investigation in the Southern District of New York, a probe which was authorized by acting Attorney General Todd Blanche. The grand jury investigation focuses on Singham’s finances, and seeks to uncover any financial crimes that have taken place as he funds his pro-CCP network of nonprofits. Singham has not been charged to date.

Earlier this year, Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent held a meeting in New York with Goldman Sachs Chairman and CEO David Solomon, where he urged the firm to cooperate with the Justice Department's investigation into Singham's financial network, according to sources familiar with the discussion.
Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent. (Mark Schiefelbein/AP)
CLICK HERE TO DOWNLOAD THE FOX NEWS APP

One source familiar with the meeting told Fox News Digital the exchange was amicable rather than adversarial, adding that Solomon signaled Goldman Sachs was prepared to cooperate with the Justice Department's probe.

"All distributions from Mr. Singham's donor-advised fund were made to legally recognized nonprofit organizations, as determined by the IRS," a Goldman Sachs spokesperson told Fox News Digital. "No distributions have been made from the account since August 2023, and it was closed in early 2024."
Preston Mizell is a writer with Fox News Digital covering breaking news.

title: Embattled Seattle police chief relieved of his duties by democratic socialist mayor, Black protest planned
summary: Seattle Police Chief Shon Barnes was reportedly asked to resign after abruptly leaving a vigil for victims of the Bite of Seattle mass shooting.
story: Fox News Flash top headlines are here. Check out what's clicking on FoxNews.com.

Seattle Mayor Katie Wilson reportedly relieved embattled Police Chief Shon Barnes of his duties Wednesday night following mounting criticism over his absence from the city and the department’s delayed public response to a mass shooting, a run-in with a reporter and questions over his frequently being out of the city.

Barnes was asked to resign during a meeting with the democratic socialist Wilson after he abruptly left a silent vigil for the victims of Sunday’s Bite of Seattle shooting, five sources told FOX 13 Seattle.
It is unclear if Barnes accepted Wilson's call for resignation or was ultimately fired.

Barnes had canceled a series of scheduled interviews earlier Wednesday and later began texting people about his dismissal, according to the report. The mayor’s office and Seattle Police Department had not publicly confirmed the change or announced who would lead the department next.
SEATTLE POLICE CHIEF SNAPS OVER CHICAGO HOME QUESTIONS, ABSENCE FROM CITY AFTER MASS SHOOTING

Seattle Police Chief Shon Barnes, right, snapped at a reporter who questioned how often he is in the city, whose family lives in Chicago, seen at right. (Fox 13 Seattle and Aytac Unal/Anadolu via Getty Images)
Barnes was feeling the heat from the media for his alleged frequent weekend absences, reportedly due to the fact he is originally from Chicago, where his family still resides.
"Those reports are wrong, do you understand?" Barnes told a reporter during a tense exchange earlier in the week.
A staffer stepped between Barnes and the reporter as the chief defended his commitment to the city.

The confrontation followed criticism of Barnes’ absence when gunfire erupted Sunday evening outside the Seattle Center Armory during the Bite of Seattle festival. Seven people were struck, including three who died and four who were hospitalized.
THIRD SUSPECT EMERGES IN DEADLY SEATTLE MASS SHOOTING, ONE ALLEGED GUNMAN FOUND DEAD

Seattle Police Chief Shon Barnes, criticized for not attending a mass shooting news conference Sunday, speaks during a vigil a day after the Bite of Seattle food festival shooting at Seattle Center. (David Ryder)

Barnes was in Dallas attending the National Organization of Black Law Enforcement Executives’ annual conference when the shooting occurred. Assistant Chief Tyrone Davis eventually led the department’s first public briefing several hours after the gunfire, a delay that drew criticism from residents and local officials seeking information about the attack.
Barnes appeared alongside Wilson at another news conference Monday and defended being out of town during the crisis.
"I wish that I had a crystal ball, and we could schedule gun violence, but we can’t," Barnes said.

Notably, amid the reports of Barnes' ouster by Wilson, there is an 11 a.m. ET (8 a.m. local) protest planned at Seattle City Hall by Black community leaders, including the Seattle NAACP, Urban League of Metropolitan Seattle and the MLK Coalition, according to posts on X.
SOCIALIST MAYOR KATIE WILSON SILENT AMID PROTESTS OVER ‘HUMAN DUMPING GROUND’ AHEAD OF US WORLD CUP MATCH

Embattled Seattle Police Chief Shon Barnes reportedly did not make it through a Wednesday night meeting with Seattle Democrat Mayor Katie Wilson after a week of controversy after the weekend mass shooting. (Scott Olson/David Ryder)

Barnes had been expected to address questions about his travel and residency during one-on-one interviews with local media Wednesday. Those interviews were abruptly canceled, and the department released portions of his calendar instead. Hours later, Barnes attended the 9:30 p.m. ET (6:30 p.m. local) vigil at Seattle Center before leaving for his meeting with Wilson.

The reported removal represents a sharp reversal for Wilson, who had previously announced that she would retain Barnes and work with him to emphasize professionalism, accountability, compassion and community partnership within the department.
Barnes was appointed and sworn in just a year ago by Wilson's predecessor after a nationwide search, bringing on the police leader from the Midwest to the Great Northwest.
Barnes previously led the police department in Madison, Wisconsin, and held law enforcement leadership positions in Chicago, as well as Greensboro and Salisbury, North Carolina.
CLICK HERE TO DOWNLOAD THE FOX NEWS APP

After arriving in Seattle, Barnes promoted a data-driven strategy he called "Seattle-Centric Policing," which identified precinct-level crime priorities and emphasized cooperation among officers, businesses, schools, government agencies and community organizations.

Barnes’ departure leaves the department facing another leadership transition as detectives investigate one of the city’s deadliest recent acts of gun violence. A 15-year-old has been arrested and charged in connection with the shooting, while police continue seeking evidence and other people believed to have been involved.
Fox News' Adam Sabes contributed to this report.

Eric Mack is a breaking news reporter and writer Sunday through Thursday, 6 a.m. ET to 2 p.m. ET, with a particular interest in stories that lead the news cycle on politics, elections, foreign affairs and government.

title: Sen Chuck Schumer unveils anti-corruption agency aimed at Trump and future presidents
summary: Chuck Schumer's Anti-Corruption Bureau would have subpoena power and replace the Office of Government Ethics and Federal Election Commission.
story: Sen. Chuck Schumer, D-N.Y. gave a speech on Thursday morning excoriating President Donald Trump's alleged corruption and said his new bill would create a new agency to investigate abuses.

Senate Minority Leader Chuck Schumer, D-N.Y., announced Thursday morning that he is introducing legislation to create a new federal agency tasked with investigating alleged corruption involving President Donald Trump and future presidential administrations.

During Public Citizen's "Combating Corruption" event, Schumer unveiled the new bill, calling it the "biggest, boldest and broadest proposal ever put forward to revitalize our anti-corruption institutions."
It would establish the Anti-Corruption Bureau, a new agency that would have subpoena power and could investigate the Trump administration even once Trump leaves office.
The bill would also allow citizens and state attorneys general to file lawsuits "to recover money stolen from the public through government corruption."

Senate Minority Leader Chuck Schumer, D-N.Y., departs after a weekly Senate Democratic Policy luncheon at the US Capitol in Washington, D.C., on July 29, 2026. (Alex Wroblewski / AFP via Getty Images)
WATCH: SCHUMER'S ANTI-CORRUPTION SPEECH DERAILED AFTER HECKLER BRANDS HIM 'GENOCIDAL MANIAC'

"The idea is simple. If Donald Trump or one of his lackeys, sons or cronies uses government influence to steal from you, you deserve your day in court. Our bill has provisions that give priority to state attorneys general and to larger, more severe cases of corruption to ensure that frivolous suits don't get in the way of justice," Schumer said.

The Anti-Corruption Bureau would be led by seven board members who would be appointed by the president and confirmed by the Senate. To address possible bias, the board would be capped at three members from each party, with the seventh being nonpartisan.

The bill, if passed, would also represent a huge shake-up to the federal bureaucracy, since the Anti-Corruption Bureau would replace the Office of Government Ethics, the Federal Election Commission and the Office of Special Counsel, The Washington Post reported ahead of Schumer's speech.

More broadly, the bill would ban presidents and vice presidents — as well as their spouses and adult children — and many other senior administration officials from seeking or accepting gifts worth more than $50,000, the Post also reported.
President Donald Trump during an announcement in the Oval Office of the White House in Washington, D.C., on July 29, 2026. (Aaron Schwartz/CNP/Bloomberg via Getty Images)
REPUBLICANS TARGET TRUMP'S CRYPTO EMPIRE WITH NEW PLAN, DEMS SAY IT FALLS SHORT

The bill would empower the Anti-Corruption Bureau to investigate violations dating back to Jan. 20, 2025 — the first day of Trump’s second term — and would establish a 10-year statute of limitations, according to the Post.
Schumer said the bureau would be given "a self-sustaining funding source to guarantee its independence, much like the Federal Reserve."

Trump has repeatedly targeted Federal Reserve officials, including by considering whether to remove former Chair Jerome Powell before his term expired and attempting to fire Fed Governor Lisa Cook. None of those attempts were successful.

"What if Trump tries to commandeer [the Anti-Corruption Bureau] to go after his political opponents?" Schumer said. "This would come at a steep price. Our bill explicitly prohibits weaponizing the bureau."
Eric Trump, Donald Trump Jr. and Bettina Trump look on as U.S. President Donald Trump speaks to the press before he boards Air Force One on July 1, 2026. (Saul Loeb / AFP via Getty Images)
CLICK HERE TO DOWNLOAD THE FOX NEWS APP

Schumer rattled off a number of supposed conflicts of interest Trump has been accused of having, including his solicitation of private donations for the White House ballroom project and his family's various crypto ventures.

"Trump has raked in at least $2.2 billion since taking office 18 months ago. Together, the Trump family has made at least $4 billion in that time," Schumer said. "How does a president and his family secure billions in profits just after a year and a half in office? How? By exploiting the information, access and influence that only the president of the United States can have."
Throughout Schumer's remarks, he emphasized that while Trump was the genesis of the legislation, it would not solely apply to him.
Construction of the new helipad on the south lawn and the ballroom that will replace the East Wing of the White House on July 24, 2026. (Kent Nishimura / AFP via Getty Images)
TRUMP FAMILY PROFITS FROM BLOCKBUSTER DEAL IN CENTRAL ASIA DESPITE BACKLASH DUE TO 'PROOF PROBLEM': EXPERT

"Trump has created obnoxious new ways to undo government ethics that no one ever imagined the president would attempt. But picture if our next president is an even more devious or competent crook. The bill isn't just about this moment. It's about restoring American's trust in government long term," Schumer said.
He also suggested that Republicans are privately frustrated by Trump's alleged abuses of office and that they would "welcome this type of legislation."
The bill’s first cosponsors include Sens. Andy Kim, D-N.J.; Alex Padilla, D-Calif.; and Jeff Merkley, D-Ore., Schumer said.
James Cirrone is a writer on the Breaking/Trending News team at Fox News Digital. Story tips can be sent to james.cirrone@fox.com.

title: WATCH: Schumer's anti-corruption speech derailed after heckler brands him 'genocidal maniac'
summary: A protester accused Chuck Schumer of backing genocide in Gaza, moments before his major anti-corruption announcement at the National Press Club.
story: Senate Minority Leader Chuck Schumer, D-N.Y., was interrupted by an audience member during a speech meant to go after President Donald Trump for corruption. Instead, Schumer was slammed for his "diabolical record."

Senate Minority Leader Chuck Schumer, D-N.Y., wanted to talk about alleged corruption committed by President Donald Trump and his family, but instead was interrupted by a protester calling out his "diabolical record."

Schumer was just getting started with his speech at the National Press Club in Washington, D.C., to make a "major anti-corruption announcement," when an audience member seated in the front row tore into the Senate’s top Democrat.

"You talk about corruption, how can you talk about corruption when you back genocide? What can be more corrupt than genocide? This is part of the same con of you and Trump playing off of each other," the protester said.
REPUBLICANS TARGET TRUMP'S CRYPTO EMPIRE WITH NEW PLAN, DEMS SAY IT FALLS SHORT

Senate Minority Leader Chuck Schumer, D-N.Y., departs after a weekly Senate Democratic Policy luncheon at the U.S. Capitol in Washington, D.C., on July 29, 2026. (Alex Wroblewski/AFP via Getty Images)
The disruptor then noted that Schumer and other congressional Democrats were "put on notice" by the Center for Constitutional Rights in 2023 for "aiding and abetting" Israel in its war against Hamas.

Critics of that conflict have long pointed to the Jewish State for going above and beyond in their quest to snuff out the terrorist organization by leveling cities in Gaza, withholding food, aid and electricity and targeting civilians.
Schumer tried to regain control of the moment and told the audience member, "Thank you for your diatribe. Now let's continue. Let's continue."
But he wasn’t successful.
"You should be questioned about your diabolical record," the audience member said. "It's amazing that you can show your genocidal face in public."
REPUBLICANS FALL IN LINE WITH TRUMP ON IRAN WAR DESPITE RISING COSTS AND US DEATH TOLL
"Mr. Senator. Mr. Senator. Shame on Public Citizen for not allowing questions to this genocidal maniac," he said as he was escorted out.

Schumer has been a vocal supporter of Israel, voting to send aid and weaponry to the country during the conflict. But over the last several months, Senate Democrats have broken from him on a handful of occasions, and in growing numbers.
Earlier this year, Senate Democrats showed their slow creep away from Israel following the release of photos of starving children in Gaza.
GOP BLOCKS SCHUMER'S EFFORT TO GROUND TAXPAYER FUNDING FOR TRUMP'S QATARI AIR FORCE ONE

President Donald Trump takes questions from the media during a bilateral meeting with President of Lebanon Joseph Aoun in the Oval Office of the White House on July 21, 2026, in Washington, D.C. (Kevin Dietsch/Getty Images)
Forty Senate Democrats voted to halt arms sales and military bulldozers to Israel as an act of protest against Trump’s war in Iran in April.

The two resolutions from Sen. Bernie Sanders, I-Vt., combined would have blocked nearly $500 million in arms and equipment sales to Israel. One resolution would have halted the sale of roughly $295 million in Caterpillar bulldozers, while the other would have stopped the sale of nearly $152 million worth of 1,000-pound bombs.
CLICK HERE TO DOWNLOAD THE FOX NEWS APP
Meanwhile, despite the disruption, Schumer did get his point across: to announce the push for legislation to create a new anti-corruption agency.
"This bill is the biggest, boldest and broadest proposal ever put forward to revitalize our anti-corruption institutions," Schumer said.
Alex Miller is a writer for Fox News Digital covering the U.S. Senate.

title: Capitol sex scandals spark push to ban House lawmakers from sleeping with staffers
summary: Rep. Nancy Mace's legislation would ban House lawmakers from having sex with staffers or living with them amid scandals involving multiple members of Congress.
story: Nancy Mace, R-S.C., exposes taxpayer-funded 'slush fund' she claims is used to silence harassment claims in Congress and comments on Eric Swalwell's alleged inappropriate messages.
FIRST ON FOX: New legislation being dropped on Thursday is seeking to bar House lawmakers from having sex with staffers after a series of exposés rocked Capitol Hill.

Rep. Nancy Mace, R-S.C., is expected to introduce a pair of bills aimed at better defining the relationships lawmakers can have with employees of the House of Representatives, Fox News Digital is told.

One is a House resolution that would bar House lawmakers from having sex with any employee of the chamber. The other would block those lawmakers from living with House employees, except for married couples cohabitating.
CAPITOL HILL SEX SCANDALS TRIGGER NEW PUSH TO REDRAW THE LINE FOR LAWMAKERS
Sen. Ruben Gallego, D-Ariz., talks to reporters as he heads for a vote at the U.S. Capitol on June 1, 2026, in Washington, D.C. (Chip Somodevilla/Getty Images)
Mace told Fox News Digital, "If you're a member of Congress, your priorities should be serving your constituents and this country, not fooling around with staff."
And while the sex ban would apply to all members, regardless of gender, she made clear it was aimed at male lawmakers who she argued were abusing their power over female staff.
"Congress is not your personal dating pool. If you can't do your job without hitting on staff, find another job and leave the women you work with alone," Mace said.
REPUBLICAN LAWMAKER WELCOMES HOUSE ETHICS PROBE INTO SEXUAL MISCONDUCT ALLEGATIONS AGAINST HIM

On her second bill banning lawmakers from living with staff, she said, "No staffer should ever be coming home at night to the person who signs their paycheck. It's inappropriate, it's a conflict of interest, and it should have been banned decades ago."

Rep. Nancy Mace, R-S.C., spoke to reporters following a briefing by Trump administration officials on U.S. strikes on Iran at the U.S. Capitol on March 3, 2026, in Washington, D.C. (Nathan Posner/Anadolu via Getty Images)
Sen. Ruben Gallego, D-Ariz., is the latest member of Congress whose reported past trysts with Hill aides were made public.

Gallego previously had sexual relationships with two House staffers, the New York Post reported. Gallego's defenders have argued that he would not have run afoul of any rules because he was unmarried at the time and the staffers did not work for him.
GONZALES RESIGNS IN WAKE OF RENEWED EXPULSION THREAT AFTER SCANDAL

Before that, sexual misconduct and rape allegations against former Rep. Eric Swalwell, D-Calif., derailed his then-promising gubernatorial campaign and forced him to resign from Congress. Swalwell has denied those accusations but admitted to making unspecified personal mistakes in a public statement where he also apologized to his wife.
On the other side of the aisle, Rep. Tony Gonzales, R-Texas, was forced to resign his seat after scrutiny piled up over an affair with a staff member who later died by suicide.
And Rep. Chuck Edwards, R-N.C., is being probed by the House Ethics Committee over sexual harassment allegations himself, which Edwards has denied, Axios reported.
CLICK HERE TO DOWNLOAD THE FOX NEWS APP

Mace's bills are the latest response from Congress over the slew of scandals. Reps. Kat Cammack, R-Fla., Jeff Crank, R-Colo., Lisa McClain, R-Mich., and Speaker Mike Johnson, R-La., have all endorsed limits on what relationships House members can have with staff.
Cammack and Crank have also introduced legislation imposing limits on such conduct.
Elizabeth Elkind is a politics reporter for Fox News Digital leading coverage of the House of Representatives. Previous digital bylines seen at Daily Mail and CBS News.

title: Can Fauci hide behind the Fifth? Game-changing Biden pardon may not provide complete cover, experts say
summary: Sen. Rand Paul plans a contempt vote after Anthony Fauci invoked the Fifth Amendment more than 100 times, raising novel questions about presidential pardons.
story: Chief congressional correspondent Chad Pergram has the latest on Dr. Anthony Fauci invoking the Fifth Amendment 111 times during his Senate testimony, breaking down key moments from the contentious hearing and lawmakers' reactions on 'America Reports.'

Dr. Anthony Fauci's refusal to answer more than 100 questions during Wednesday's fiery Senate hearing has sparked a legal showdown over whether a witness granted a sweeping presidential pardon can still invoke the Fifth Amendment.

Sen. Rand Paul, R-Ky., who chairs the Senate Homeland Security and Governmental Affairs Committee, announced after the hearing that he plans to pursue contempt proceedings against Fauci following the repeated invocations of the Fifth Amendment and his refusal to answer lawmakers' questions.

"We're going to have a vote next week on contempt," Paul said. "I think there's another legal question that the courts may have to decide upon, and that is whether or not a presidential pardon offers you complete immunity."
RAND PAUL SEEKS CONTEMPT CHARGES AFTER FAUCI INVOKES FIFTH AMENDMENT MORE THAN 100 TIMES

Anthony Fauci declined to testify in a Senate committee hearing on his role in the U.S. response to COVID-19, invoking his 5th Amendment rights. (Alex WROBLEWSKI / AFP via Getty Images | Al Drago/Bloomberg via Getty Images)

Former President Joe Biden issued Fauci, who served as the chief architect for the government's COVID-19 guidelines, a full and unconditional pardon for all actions taken between Jan. 1, 2014, and Jan. 19, 2025. Biden's broad pardon protected Fauci from prosecution for the actions being investigated by the committee, leaving only the possibility of charges if he lied under oath.

Abhishek Kambli, a former Justice Department official who now represents former Trump advisor Peter Navarro in his contempt of Congress case, told Fox News Digital that the issue presents a novel legal question about whether Fauci can invoke the Fifth Amendment at all.
"Obviously, if he tells the truth, then he would be protected by that blanket pardon, since the past conduct that he reveals he's fully immunized from," Kambli told Fox News Digital.
Kambli questioned whether the Fifth Amendment privilege properly applies if truthful testimony could no longer expose Fauci to prosecution for the underlying conduct.
"His theory is that it's a witch hunt and that they're looking for perjury traps to charge him with, so that's why he needs to invoke the Fifth Amendment," Kambli said.
But Kambli said the argument becomes more difficult to sustain if lawmakers are asking straightforward factual questions.
"I think it gets a little problematic," Kambli said of Fauci invoking the Fifth Amendment for common knowledge questions like what day of the week it is.
FAUCI PLEADS FIFTH WITH 'ZERO LEGAL JUSTIFICATION' AS CRITICS ERUPT AND DEMAND CONTEMPT CHARGES

The attorney for former NIH Director Anthony Fauci (R), David Schertler (L), is removed from the hearing room at the direction of committee chairman Sen. Rand Paul (R-KY) during a hearing before the Senate Homeland Security and Governmental Affairs Committee on July 29, 2026, in Washington, D.C. Fauci declined to answer questions from the oommittee asserting his Fifth Amendment right during the hearing. (Kevin Dietsch/Getty Images)

"If it's just factual questions that he should know the answer on, it's hard to see how he would walk into a perjury trap if he's just telling the truth, because perjury also requires that you knowingly made a false statement," Kambli said. "If he had an incorrect recollection, that was an innocent mistake that typically wouldn't lead to a perjury charge."

Kambli said federal law distinguishes between witnesses who ignore a congressional subpoena and those who appear before Congress but refuse to answer questions. In the latter case, he said, prosecutors generally do not have to prove the witness intentionally violated the law. Instead, the central question is whether the witness had a valid legal basis for refusing to answer, such as a legitimate claim under the Fifth Amendment.

"The issue is [the witness] is already protected if he tells the truth, and it's only if he knowingly lies about something material that he can be charged," Kambli said. "So the issue becomes whether the Senate can make a referral to DOJ based on that."
George Washington University law professor Jonathan Turley said the legal issues surrounding Fauci's testimony are more complicated than either side suggests.

"The only risk that he faced would come from any false statements that he made in the hearing in dealing with these questions," Turley told Fox News Digital. "That would likely be viewed as sufficient, particularly since some questions could extend to statements and conduct from after the pardon grant."
Turley also pointed to Fauci's decision to deliver an opening statement before invoking the Fifth Amendment, suggesting it could raise additional legal questions.

"There are also questions about the questions limited to the period of his pardon as well as his decision to give an opening statement before invocation. Those are possible grounds for contempt. It would raise novel issues, though there is precedent from the Lois Lerner matter," Turley said.
TOP 5 MOMENTS FROM FAUCI'S HEARING: PAUL BOOTS LAWYER, MORENO ERUPTS AS CONTEMPT VOTE LOOMS

Former NIH Director Anthony Fauci testifies before the Senate Homeland Security and Governmental Affairs Committee in Washington, D.C., on July 29, 2026. Fauci was expected to be questioned about his diary entries during his handling of the COVID-19 pandemic. (Getty Images)

Turley was referring to former IRS official Lois Lerner, who declared her innocence in a voluntary opening statement before invoking the Fifth Amendment during a 2013 congressional hearing. House Republicans argued Lerner waived her right to invoke the Fifth Amendment when she made statements about the very subject under investigation. Although the House held Lerner in contempt, the Justice Department later declined to pursue criminal contempt charges.
But Hans von Spakovsky, a senior legal fellow at Advancing American Freedom, argued Paul's position is stronger than Fauci's.

"He can't be prosecuted by the federal government for any actions he took during the period the pardon covers," von Spakovsky said. "However, if he lies while under oath at his hearing today about any of those prior actions, he could be prosecuted for perjury."
SIGN UP TO GET THE POLITICS NEWSLETTER

While von Spakovsky acknowledged that Biden's pardon of Fauci covers only federal charges, it does not shield Fauci from facing state charges. But he noted no state has accused Fauci of violating state law, at least not yet. Florida Attorney General James Uthmeier on Wednesday announced a state investigation into Fauci, following his testimony on Capitol Hill.

"The possibility of a state prosecution is almost nonexistent because states generally cannot prosecute federal officials acting within the scope of their duties and Fauci would argue that everything he did over COVID was carried out in his official slot as head of NIAID," von Spakovsky told Fox News Digital.

"The only reason for him to take the Fifth is because he doesn't want to admit, based on his personal diaries, that he lied repeatedly to the public and Congress when he was head of the NIAID," von Spakovsky said.
CLICK HERE TO DOWNLOAD THE FOX NEWS APP
If Paul's contempt resolution clears the committee, it would move to the full Senate, but it will need to beat the 60-vote filibuster in order to pass.
Fox News Digital reached out to Fauci's attorney, David Schertler, for comment.
Elaine Mallon is a writer for Fox News Digital and Fox Business covering national politics.

title: Melania Trump helps reunite fifth group of Ukrainian, Russian children with families
summary: Five more Ukrainian children reunited with families as Melania Trump's program reaches roughly 30 kids returned from Russia amid the ongoing war.
story: First lady Melania Trump facilitates the fifth reunification of Ukrainian and Russian children with their families, separated by war. Peter Doocy reports that 35,000 Ukrainian children are believed to have been abducted by Russia.
First lady Melania Trump's office announced a fifth group of Ukrainian and Russian children that she helped reunite with their families, as five more children are now with their loved ones.

"While diplomacy and peace-building are important to this effort, they are surpassed by our collective ability to place children above international disputes," Melania Trump said in a statement. "Every reunion is a reminder that compassion, dignity, and family can transcend even the darkest of times: war. My representative and I continue working with the governments of Russia and Ukraine to safely return children to their families and communities."

The first lady's reunification program officially began in October 2025 after she had President Donald Trump hand-deliver her note to Russian President Vladimir Putin during their August 2025 summit in Alaska. Thus far, the White House reports around 30 Ukrainian children have been reunited with their families.
RUSSIA LAUNCHES BALLISTIC MISSILE ATTACK ON KYIV HOURS AFTER ZELENSKYY WARNS OF MAJOR STRIKE
First lady Melania Trump has made the reunification of Ukrainian children her top priority in the peace-making effort with Russia this past year. (Jacquelyn Martin)

Thousands of civilians, including children, have been killed since Russia invaded Ukraine in February 2022, with last year being the deadliest year since the war began, according to United Nations figures.
ZELENSKYY SAYS PUTIN 'LOST THE INITIATIVE' AS UKRAINE'S TECH INDUSTRY RESHAPES THE WAR
Vladimir Putin was handed a note from Melania Trump by President Donald Trump during their Aug. 15, 2025, summit in Alaska. (SERGEY BOBYLEV/POOL/AFP)

"The first lady’s leadership has bridged political divides in pursuit of a singular humanitarian mission: placing the well-being of children above conflict and helping restore families torn apart by war," the White House announced in a Thursday morning news release.
The returnees are the first since April.
MELANIA TRUMP, QUEEN CAMILLA TEAM UP AT WHITE HOUSE YOUTH EVENT SPOTLIGHTING US-UK BOND

"This is not an easy feat. I applaud leadership from both nations in working with my representative and me to bring love and safety back to each individual who has been displaced as a result of this horrible war," Melania Trump said in an April 23 speech. "I'm grateful for the opportunity to serve as first lady but understand that my persistence alone is not enough."

"Together we can change people's lives for the better."

title: Don't let fake election websites fool you before 2026 midterms
summary: Over 62,000 election-named domains were tracked since September 2025, with some active storefronts copying campaign branding to collect donations.
story: Fox News Flash top headlines are here. Check out what's clicking on FoxNews.com.

You spot a campaign shirt online that makes you laugh. The site carries the candidate's name. It also has polished product photos and a familiar checkout page. So, you assume the store supports the campaign.
A fake election website can copy enough campaign cues to make that assumption feel reasonable. Your money and personal information could then reach an operator with no verified campaign connection.

New research provided to CyberGuy by WhoisXML API, an internet intelligence company that analyzes domain, IP and DNS data, tracked 62,081 election-named domains created since September 2025. Researchers identified 13,645 addresses that read like campaign sites based on their names.

The research classifies only a portion of the domains as campaign-style addresses. Legitimate campaigns, supporters, merchants and domain investors may control many of them. However, researchers also found live storefronts that used candidates' names while selling merchandise and accepting donation-style payments. That smaller group creates the clearest risk for you.
FAKE PASSWORD-MANAGER ALERTS COULD PUT YOUR VAULT AT RISK
Voters should verify campaign websites, donation links and committee disclaimers before entering personal or payment information. (Getty Images)
CyberGuy Live: Missed "Sick of Spam?" Get the replay and checklist

Our free CyberGuy Live class, "Sick of Spam?," has ended, but you can still watch the full replay and download our spam-stopping checklist. Kurt "CyberGuy" Knutsson walks you step by step through simple ways to reduce robocalls, spam texts, junk email and unwanted messages. You’ll also learn how to curb political texts, clean up your inbox and spot messages that could put your personal information at risk.

Why fake election websites surge before the midterms

National elections create a rush for online real estate. Campaign teams want memorable web addresses before someone else claims them. Supporters may launch fan pages, while merchants see an opportunity to sell political products. Impersonators can follow the same naming formula.

According to WhoisXML API, nearly 46% of the curated campaign-style set used structures such as "[name]for[office]" or "for[state]." Domains referencing congressional races appeared most often. Senate-themed names came next. State names also appeared across about one-third of the curated set. Texas led with 537 registrations. Florida, Georgia, Ohio and Colorado followed.

Those names feel familiar because real campaigns use the same structure. As a result, a questionable domain can look credible before you open the page. Across the domains studied, researchers said 90% hid the registrant's identity. In addition, 88% carried a one-year registration term. Privacy protection and short registration terms can have legitimate uses. Still, those details deserve more attention when a new site also copies campaign branding or asks for money.
How fake election websites copy real campaign stores

A small change in a domain can hide in plain sight. WhoisXML API highlighted massiemoneybomb[.]us, which closely resembled the established massiemoneybomb[.]com fundraising address. The main difference appeared after the final dot.

That change may look obvious on a large computer screen. However, it becomes easier to miss on a phone, especially when a text or social media post opens the page directly. Researchers also examined kenpaxton[.]us. They said the domain was 58 days old when captured, while kenpaxton[.]com dated back to 2008.

The newer site reportedly sold supportive campaign products alongside merchandise criticizing the same candidate. That unusual mix offers a clue that the store may lack an official connection. Yet many shoppers will focus on the product photos or the price. A polished checkout can make the entire operation feel established. Alexandre François, the WhoisXML API domain scam researcher behind the study, told CyberGuy that AI can help operators build convincing websites quickly and at scale. That makes it even harder to judge a campaign page by its appearance alone.
How fake election donation pages collect personal data

Political merchandise may cost you more than the price on the screen. According to the research, some storefronts allowed visitors to add donation-style payments of up to $1,000 to a shopping cart. The sites then processed the payment through their own checkout flows.

One store reportedly continued accepting a donation-style payment after the candidate's official ActBlue page stopped taking contributions. The checkout requested a full name, street address, email address and phone number. It also collected payment card details.

A familiar payment processor can make that form feel safe. However, its presence only shows how the payment moves through the checkout. It cannot confirm that the candidate authorized the store or that the campaign receives the money.

François said the study found no direct evidence that donors lost money or had their data misused. "Only the payment platforms could see whether a donor lost money or had data misused, and their data was not part of this study," he told CyberGuy. The findings support caution rather than a claim that every highlighted site committed fraud.
What domain records reveal about fake election websites

Domain registration records can expose useful clues before or after a website launches. Researchers can review the creation date, registrar, paid registration period and privacy status. Sometimes, the records also identify the owner or registrant country. However, each clue has limits.

Many legitimate website owners use privacy services to keep home addresses and contact details out of public databases. Campaigns may also register several defensive domains so impersonators cannot claim them first. A one-year registration term also appears across ordinary websites. Price and convenience often drive that choice.
The risk grows when several details point in the same direction. A nearly copied domain may lead to a new storefront with an unofficial donation flow. A mismatched disclaimer adds another concern.

For federal political committees, public websites generally need a disclaimer that identifies who paid for the communication. The wording may also state whether a candidate authorized it. The FEC explains that disclaimer requirements cover political committee websites and online fundraising communications. A disclaimer cannot guarantee honesty. Still, a missing or mismatched statement gives you a strong reason to leave the page and verify the site elsewhere.

Campaigns also face limits when trying to secure every possible variation of a candidate's name. François said they should consistently promote one official domain and one donation link. He added that "the realistic option is monitoring" because registering every possible look-alike domain would be impractical. Monitoring new registrations can help campaigns find look-alike sites during their first days online. Campaigns can then report suspicious pages to the registrar, hosting company or payment provider.
SAME-NAME CANDIDATE DISQUALIFIED FROM KEY SENATE RACE OVER ALLEGED DEM SCHEME TO CONFUSE VOTERS
Fake election websites, like the one pictured, can copy campaign branding, storefront designs and donation pages to collect money and personal information. (WhoisXML API)
Ways to stay safe from fake election websites
Before you buy campaign merchandise or make a political contribution online, use these checks to confirm that the site connects to the candidate or committee you intend to support.

Avoid starting with a link from an unexpected text, email, online ad or social media comment. Instead, search for the candidate independently. Then compare the result with links from the candidate's verified social media account or established public profile. "No single sign is enough, so it's best to check a few together and to reach the page from the campaign's own channel," François told CyberGuy.

You can also use a personal data removal service to reduce the personal information available through data brokers and people-search sites. This may limit the details scammers can use to make unexpected messages, targeted ads or social media comments feel more convincing. Check out my top picks for data removal services and get a free scan to find out if your personal information is already out on the web by visiting CyberGuy.com.

For federal races, use the FEC's campaign finance database at fec.gov/data/ to look up candidates and registered committees. The database shows federal candidate and committee filings. For state or local races, check the appropriate state or local election authority. Many campaigns process contributions through ActBlue or WinRed. In those cases, the payment address should show secure.actblue.com or secure.winred.com. Some campaigns use other processors, so an unfamiliar payment provider alone does not prove the page is deceptive.
Tap or click the address bar before entering payment information. Check the spelling and domain ending. Then look for added words or letters that imitate the campaign's real address.

A scammer may replace ".com" with ".us." Another operator may add words such as "official," "store," "donate," or "support" to make the address feel authentic. François said the difference may also involve one word, a hyphen or an ending such as ".vote" or ".store."

Scroll to the bottom of the site and review the area around the donation form. A federal political committee website should identify who paid for the communication. Depending on the committee, the disclaimer may also explain whether the candidate authorized it.

Compare that committee name with the FEC database. Leave the page when the names conflict or the disclosure looks vague. Keep in mind that a deceptive page can copy a real committee's name. Treat the disclosure as one clue rather than proof that the page belongs to the campaign.
Open the candidate's established website in a separate tab. Look for a direct link to the merchandise store or donation page. If the official site sends you somewhere else, use the link it provides.

Also review the store's contact details and return policy. Be cautious if it sells products supporting a candidate alongside merchandise attacking that candidate. That unusual mix may signal the store has no official campaign connection. A page that keeps collecting contributions after a candidate withdraws also deserves closer scrutiny. The same applies when a store continues selling campaign merchandise after the official donation page closes.
The padlock in your browser means the site uses an encrypted connection. It offers no proof about the person or business behind the page.

CISA warns that phishing attacks may use malicious websites that impersonate trusted organizations to collect personal information. A professional design and secure connection still require you to verify the operator.
Pressure can push you past obvious warning signs. Be cautious when a site claims a donation match will disappear within minutes. A countdown clock that keeps resetting should also raise concern.
The FTC's broader donation-safety guidance recommends researching an organization and resisting pressure to give immediately.
WHAT A SCAMMER SEES THE MOMENT THEY GOOGLE YOUR NAME
Researchers found campaign-style websites selling political merchandise and accepting donation-style payments under candidates’ names. (yasindmrblk/Getty Images)

A credit card generally offers stronger dispute protections than a debit card. It also keeps the payment away from funds in your checking account. The FTC says legal protections for credit cards exceed those for debit cards in billing disputes.

Save your receipt and take screenshots of the product page and checkout. Make sure the full domain appears in at least one image. After you pay, check your statement to confirm the amount and make sure the site did not enroll you in recurring contributions.

A fake campaign website may try to push a malicious download or send you to another harmful page. Strong antivirus software can help detect suspicious files and block some dangerous websites. However, you still need to verify the campaign connection before you pay. Get my picks for the best 2026 antivirus protection winners for your Windows, Mac, Android and iOS devices at CyberGuy.com.

If a store asks you to create an account, use a unique password. A password manager can generate and save a strong password for you, so you do not have to remember it. Reusing a password could put your other accounts at risk if the login information gets exposed. Turn on two-factor authentication (2FA) when the site offers it.
What to do after paying through a fake election website

Contact your card issuer or bank as soon as you suspect a problem.Explain what happened and ask whether it can reverse the transaction. The FTC advises consumers who paid a suspected scammer by credit or debit card to contact the issuer and request a reversal.Next, report suspected fraud through the FTC's ReportFraud system. If the site may have violated federal campaign finance law, you can also review the FEC complaint process.The FEC accepts complaints about possible violations involving federal election financing. Its authority covers elections for the U.S. House, Senate and president.Watch your statements for unfamiliar charges. Also change any password that you reused on the store.If the website collected information that later appears in identity fraud, IdentityTheft.gov can create a recovery plan and guide you through the next steps.
Contact your card issuer or bank as soon as you suspect a problem.
Explain what happened and ask whether it can reverse the transaction. The FTC advises consumers who paid a suspected scammer by credit or debit card to contact the issuer and request a reversal.
Next, report suspected fraud through the FTC's ReportFraud system. If the site may have violated federal campaign finance law, you can also review the FEC complaint process.
The FEC accepts complaints about possible violations involving federal election financing. Its authority covers elections for the U.S. House, Senate and president.
Watch your statements for unfamiliar charges. Also change any password that you reused on the store.
If the website collected information that later appears in identity fraud, IdentityTheft.gov can create a recovery plan and guide you through the next steps.
Kurt's key takeaways on fake election websites

Election season gives questionable websites a powerful disguise. A candidate's name can create trust before you verify who operates the page. The scale of this research should make every online donor slow down. Researchers found more than 62,000 election-named domains, though many may serve legitimate purposes. The clearest concern comes from active storefronts that copy campaign-style branding and collect money outside a verified campaign path. Take an extra minute before buying a shirt or making a contribution. Find the official campaign site through a trusted source. Then confirm the web address and committee disclosure before you enter personal or payment information.
