Barr. She also served as Communications Director for Alliance Defending Freedom, and clerked for Court of Appeals of Virginia Judge William G. Petty.

title: Virginia university report finds officials did not disclose student’s terror conviction
summary: An ODU report says federal officials never alerted the university that a returning student had been convicted of supporting ISIS before the deadly ROTC classroom shooting.
story: ROTC cadets at Old Dominion University described stabbing and wrestling the attacker who killed Lt. Col. Brandon Shah during a March 12 shooting in Norfolk, Virginia. (Army ROTC)

An independent investigation into the deadly March terror attack at Old Dominion University (ODU) found that federal officials never warned the school that the returning student behind the shooting had previously been convicted of trying to support ISIS.

On March 12, Mohamed Bailor Jalloh reportedly yelled "Allahu Akbar" before opening fire inside an ROTC classroom a ODU, killing an Army veteran instructor and injuring two students before ROTC members fatally subdued him.
Jalloh was convicted in 2016 of attempting to provide material support to the Islamic State terror group in a plot to target U.S. military personnel.
Neither his federal probation officer, the FBI, nor any state or federal agency notified ODU of his conviction, the university-commissioned report concluded.
VIRGINIA MAN CHARGED WITH SELLING WEAPON USED BY OLD DOMINION UNIVERSITY GUNMAN
Mohamed Bailor Jalloh served in the Army National Guard before carrying out the March 12, 2026, shooting at Old Dominion University. (The Intercept)

"Had ODU known about Jalloh’s criminal history, it is highly likely that ODU would have sought his removal from campus due to the risk he posed, particularly to military-affiliated individuals," the independent report said.
The FBI told Fox News Digital Thursday it is not the agency responsible for notifying colleges.

"The FBI does not serve as a notification authority for colleges or universities regarding an individual’s criminal historyhat is a shared responsibility across state, local, federal and community partners," the FBI said.

Additionally, the bureau noted that Jalloh's terrorism-related convictions were widely publicized by the Department of Justice in 2016 and 2017, with at least three press releases detailing his case still available on the agency's website.

"Furthermore, the U.S. Attorney’s Office for the Eastern District of Virginia issued several press releases and publicly available information, including a press release when Jalloh was sentenced in 2017 for attempting to provide material support to a designated foreign terrorist organization," the agency said.
"The release remains on the Department of Justice website and can be found through an internet search with multiple links available."
OLD DOMINION UNIVERSITY SHOOTER IDENTIFIED AS MOHAMED JALLOH, FORMER NATIONAL GUARD MEMBER, ISIS SUPPORTER
ODU said that, under Virginia law enacted in 2022, public universities are prohibited from asking applicants about their criminal history during the admissions process.

In compliance with the law, ODU said it removed criminal history questions from its applications, leaving the university dependent on voluntary student disclosures or outside law enforcement notifications.
Under Jalloh’s federal supervised release, his probation officer reportedly had the authority to require him to disclose his criminal record to third parties.
However, no such notification was provided to any university office or campus police, according to the report.

"Given that Virginia law requires universities to rely on student self-disclosure, it is even more important that other law enforcement agencies ensure that information that universities need to know to safeguard their students is shared with universities. This critical failure led to tragic consequences here," the ODU report said.
Jalloh also never voluntarily disclosed his 2016 federal terrorism conviction to ODU, according to the report.
Mohamed Bailor Jalloh was identified as the shooter at Old Dominion University March 12, 2026. (AP Photo)

While Virginia law allows public universities to inquire about criminal history after an applicant is admitted, ODU's policy at the time only sent post-admission background questionnaires to first-time students, excluding readmitted returning students such as Jalloh.

According to the campus report, Jalloh first enrolled at ODU as an undergraduate student in 2007. After being academically suspended in 2010, he was readmitted in 2011 after serving in the Army National Guard.
He briefly took classes through spring 2012 before stopping for unknown reasons and was later convicted on federal terrorism charges in 2016.
He then served eight years in prison before being released in December 2024. Afterward, Jalloh applied for readmission as a returning student and was re-enrolled at ODU in 2025.

After Jalloh’s case exposed a gap in the university's post-admission screening policies, ODU said it officially expanded its post-admission criminal history questionnaire to include readmitted students alongside first-time students.
Lt. Col. Brandon Shah was killed in the deadly shooting at Old Dominion University March 12.  (Old Dominion University)
CLICK HERE TO DOWNLOAD THE FOX NEWS APP
Additionally, the report said nothing else on Jalloh’s readmission application raised any concerns.

Jalloh’s application reportedly listed a private residential address in Sterling, Virginia, rather than a federal prison address. Two professors who taught him in the months before the attack also reported no behavioral concerns.
The United States Probation and Pretrial Services Eastern District of Virginia did not immediately respond to a request for comment from Fox News Digital.

title: Jimmy Hoffa's family marks 51 years since iconic disappearance
summary: The FBI says the Jimmy Hoffa disappearance case remains active 51 years later as his family pushes for accountability in the unsolved cold case.
story: 'Riddle: The Search for James R. Hoffa' is available to stream on Fox Nation. Hosted by Eric Shawn, the show explores the 1975 disappearance of the legendary Teamsters union president.
Jimmy Hoffa disappeared 51 years ago today, and his family has not given up hope that the answers to their painful loss will finally come.

"We want the case solved," Hoffa's son, James P. Hoffa, the former five-term president of the International Brotherhood of Teamsters, told Fox News. "The family wants to have accountability for this horrible crime. We want the case solved so that the family can have closure."
Despite the passage of time, the FBI says the case remains ongoing and active. The bureau’s Detroit office is in charge of the case.

"The FBI has worked for five decades to investigate Jimmy Hoffa's disappearance, following every lead and carefully examining all evidence related to this investigation," the bureau said in a statement to Fox News.
TIPSTER CHARGED WITH MURDER AFTER POLICE SAY ANONYMOUS CALL HELPED SOLVE 30-YEAR DISAPPEARANCE
Fifty-one years after Teamsters leader Jimmy Hoffa disappeared, his family says it still hopes investigators will uncover the truth behind one of America's most enduring mysteries. (Getty Images)
"If the public has any new, credible information regarding the disappearance of Jimmy Hoffa, the FBI will investigate," the FBI said.

Hoffa vanished on this day in 1975 as he was on his way to what he thought was a meeting to help his bid to regain the Teamsters union presidency. He was last seen in the parking lot of the Bloomfield Hills, Michigan, restaurant, the Machus Red Fox, at about 2:30 p.m. getting into a car that whisked him away. It is believed that the Detroit Mafia kidnapped and killed him to stop his efforts to take back the union.
SAMMY 'THE BULL' REVEALS WHY HIS LOVE FOR JOHN GOTTI TURNED INTO PRISON HATE

The eight-part documentary series, "Riddle, The Search for James R. Hoffa," streaming on Fox Nation, focuses on a dominant theory. It says that Hoffa was picked up at the restaurant by Detroit mob capo Vito "Billy Jack" Giacalone, who, along with mobster Anthony "Tony Pal" Palazzolo, drove Hoffa to a nearby home owned by mobster Carlo Licata and murdered him. His remains were then possibly disposed of in a mob-run sanitation facility in Hamtramck.
Hoffa believes that his father was picked up at the restaurant by Giacalone, but beyond that, he will not speculate about who killed his father.

Fox Nation's "Riddle" series reported that an informant told the FBI that he was present when Hoffa was murdered and said that Giacalone killed him. Such information would have been documented in the FBI records, called 302s, but so far the information has not been made public.

Detroit journalist and mob historian Scott Burnstein, who runs the website "Gangster Report," has confirmed that the 302 exists and reported that "confidential informants" told the FBI "that ‘Tony Pal’ was the ‘doer’" in the Hoffa homicide conspiracy, and that Giacalone "headed the Hoffa hit team and was present at the time Palazzolo kidnapped and clipped Hoffa."
COVERT DNA SAMPLE FROM COLORADO MAN'S TRASH REVIVES 44-YEAR-OLD TEXAS MURDER CASE: REPORT

Hoffa said that he has been aware of the information that Giacalone murdered his father but cannot confirm that. He does say that his dad was lured to the meeting by Giacalone and his brother Anthony "Tony Jack" Giacalone, who was considered the Detroit mob's street boss. Both men have since died.

In a letter to FBI Director Kash Patel obtained by Fox News, Hoffa wrote last month, "It is important to us and the country that the truth about my father's disappearance (be) told and those involved in his disappearance, even if they are deceased, be exposed."
Through the years there have been a variety of claims about Hoffa's fate.

Fox Nation's series investigated the claims of Frank Sheeran, "The Irishman," which proved to be unfounded. It's also been said that Hoffa's remains were buried in a mob-owned garbage dump in the New Jersey Meadowlands, but the FBI dug at the site in 2022 and came up empty. Stories have circulated that he was cremated or entombed in the downtown Detroit Renaissance Center office building complex.
New claims continue to crop up.
Independent investigator Roscoe Clark told Fox News that he is certain that Hoffa is buried in an undisclosed location in Michigan, and that it would take less than five minutes.

"Forensics will help solve the Jimmy Hoffa cold case," Clark said. "A team of experts is ready to move forward because of a lack of action by law enforcement. A location has been identified within three feet," and he said the necessary locating equipment is ready to be deployed.

The FBI said it has "received countless tips and information from the public, which have been a tremendous help to the FBI. We are grateful to the public, and most importantly, for the Hoffa's family assistance and support over the years."
UNIVERSITY OF PITTSBURGH STUDENTS SAY SUDIKSHA KONANKI'S 'CRAZY' DISAPPEARANCE COULD 'HAPPEN TO ANYBODY'

Observers note that the legacy of Jimmy Hoffa is not what happened to him, but what he accomplished. His hard-fought victories at the bargaining table and on the picket lines enabled generations to enjoy the American Dream, with healthcare and benefits, good pay and retirement. Millions of sons and daughters and their families still benefit from the feisty labor leader's achievements. In some ways, that is how Jimmy Hoffa is still with us, even as he is still deeply missed and mourned by his family.
James Hoffa, his sister Barbara, their adult children and grandchildren somberly mark this day with each passing year.
CLICK HERE TO DOWNLOAD THE FOX NEWS APP

Every July 30 "is a hard day," said James Hoffa. "We always spend time with it. It is special time, a time to remember. The good thing is, that I had a great father and he did a great job in raising our family. He was a great man and we miss him."
The in-depth series "Riddle, The Search for James R. Hoffa," is streaming on Fox Nation.

Shawn is also the host of Riddle: The Search for James R. Hoffa on FOX Nation, FNC's on-demand subscription-based streaming service, which is based upon his extensive reporting into the appearance of notorious Teamsters boss Jimmy Hoffa.

title: 10-year-old boy's body pulled from New Jersey river as rescuers search for his sister
summary: A 10-year-old boy's body was recovered from the Passaic River as search and rescue teams race to find his missing sister amid high storm waters.
story: Rescuers in New Jersey search for a 10-year-old girl in the Passaic River. The body of the girl's 10-year-old brother was already found. (Credit: WNYW)
Rescuers in New Jersey are still searching for a 10-year-old girl after finding her 10-year-old brother's body in the Passaic River late Wednesday night, Passaic Mayor Hector Lora told reporters.

"Right now, all of our efforts are in trying to recover the body but hoping that perhaps, maybe hope against all things, that we could find the little girl still alive," Lora told FOX 5 New York in an interview.
Lora hoped aloud that the little girl was still alive, hypothesizing that her deceased brother helped push her to safety.
‘HERO' MOM DIES AFTER USING LAST STRENGTH TO SAVE 4-YEAR-OLD SON FROM FLORIDA RIVER

"The 10-year-old boy, as he was going down, maybe an angel, maybe God used him to push his little sister, and now she made her way out so she's home. But the mother has lost her little boy," Lora said.
Lora also told reporters that calls for help came in around 6:20 p.m. Wednesday after bystanders saw three children in the water, according to FOX 5.
A good Samaritan unsuccessfully tried to help the children out of the water, the outlet reported.

PARK VISITORS FACE FLOOD DANGER OUT WEST WHILE SEVERE STORMS RIP THROUGH NY, NJ
Search and rescue operations were ongoing into Thursday morning. The efforts were hampered in part by high water levels due to recent storms.
The search and rescue operations included members of the Passaic Police Department, the Passaic County Sheriff's Office and the New Jersey State Police.

title: Football player stomped, jabbed in alleged hazing incident with broomstick by teammates as coaches hid it: DA
summary: Video captured juvenile players allegedly holding down a Cheltenham High School teammate while others used a broomstick in a locker room hazing attack.
story: Polk County Sheriff Grady Judd arrested a Washington, D.C.-based basketball coach and five teen players after they allegedly shoplifted from a Florida 7-Eleven in the middle of the night. The coach, Malik Harvey, also faces charges for lying to deputies about the players' identities. A mother of one of the players cooperated with authorities.
Ten members of a Pennsylvania high school football team, including several coaches, face charges after a player was allegedly stomped with cleats, and jabbed in the buttocks with a broomstick.
According to the Montgomery County District Attorney's Office, a 15-year-old player was allegedly assaulted on two separate occasions in 2025 by teammates from Cheltenham High School.

title: Bryan Kohberger appointed new lawyer after Idaho murders case costs taxpayers over $8 million

story: A judge approved Bryan Kohberger's request for a new lawyer in his attempt to secure a new trial, despite his previous guilty plea for murdering four University of Idaho students in 2022. Legal analyst Mehek Cooke discusses the high bar for overturning a guilty plea, while the victim's family expresses the pain of reliving the tragedy.

Bryan Kohberger, whose murder case has reportedly cost taxpayers more than $8 million, has been appointed a new taxpayer-funded attorney as he seeks to withdraw his guilty plea in the stabbing deaths of four University of Idaho students.

Ada County District Judge Steven Hippler on Wednesday granted Kohberger's request for court-appointed counsel, directing the Idaho State Public Defender to appoint an attorney to represent him in all post-conviction proceedings.

The order comes just days after Kohberger filed a handwritten petition for post-conviction relief seeking to withdraw the guilty plea he entered last year in exchange for prosecutors dropping the death penalty.
KAYLEE GONCALVES' MOTHER SAYS FAMILY READY FOR TRIAL AFTER BRYAN KOHBERGER SEEKS TO WITHDRAW GUILTY PLEA

In the petition, Kohberger claimed he was "convinced to falsely confess" and alleged his defense attorneys – Anne Taylor, Elisa Massoth and Bicka Barlow – failed to disclose what he described as "exculpatory discovery," referring to evidence discussed in the recent book "Broken Plea" that was never examined in court.

Bryan Kohberger, left, looks toward his attorney, public defender Anne Taylor, right, during a hearing in Latah County District Court, Thursday, Jan. 5, 2023, in Moscow, Idaho. (AP Photo/Ted S. Warren, Pool)

Kohberger previously said he was entering the plea knowingly, intelligently and voluntarily and that no one had coerced him or promised him anything beyond the terms of the agreement. His new petition directly contradicts those statements.

As Fox News Digital previously reported, the filing outraged the family of victim Kaylee Goncalves, whose mother, Kristi Goncalves, said the family is prepared to return to court if Kohberger succeeds in reopening the case.

Hippler's order states Kohberger's motion for appointed counsel was granted under Idaho's post-conviction relief statute and directs the Idaho State Public Defender to appoint an attorney to represent him throughout the proceedings.

The judge also noted that Kohberger had filed a motion seeking to proceed on partial payment of court fees, but said filing fees do not apply to petitions for post-conviction relief.

title: California lifeguard speaks out on heartstopping ocean rescue: 'I love what I do'
summary: Ryder Williams described fighting volatile waves while holding the limp 10-year-old at Santa Cruz Beach, revealing details of the rescue seen worldwide.
story: Founder of Drown Zero Wyatt Werneth joins 'Fox & Friends' to discuss the dramatic video showing a 16-year-old lifeguard battling powerful 8-10 foot surf waves and rip currents to rescue a 10-year-old boy in Santa Cruz, Calif.
A 16-year-old lifeguard whose daring rescue of a 10-year-old on Saturday went viral finally spoke out about the harrowing save in a Wednesday statement.

Ryder Williams, the teen hero whose daring rescue of a young boy at Seabright Beach in Santa Cruz, California on Saturday captivated the nation, described the episode in a statement released by his employer, California State Parks.

"I was at the waterline 15 yards downcoast of Tower 2 making a safety contact when I looked up and saw a child about 20 (yards) up from the tower lose his footing in ankle-deep water," the statement opened.
OFF-DUTY ICE OFFICER RELIES ON 'SIXTH SENSE' TO SAVE DROWNING CHILD BEFORE DELIVERING MESSAGE TO CRITICS

Sixteen-year-old lifeguard Ryder Williams repeatedly disappeared beneath towering waves while refusing to let go of a child swept into dangerous California surf in Santa Cruz, California on July 25, 2026. (Scott Vander Dussen/Instagram @Santacruznow)

"I radioed it in, threw my radio and sunglasses at the base of my tower as I ran toward the kid. I put my fins on my wrist, popped my buoy and entered the water to get ahold of the child. Due to the volatility of the water, I was unable to tube up the victim. After the first wave I was unable to pull him out because he was limp and the waves were pushing so hard. There were two to three more waves before lifeguard Aaron Bohnen entered the water to help me. There were bystanders who jumped in to try to help, and I yelled at them all to get back to shore," Williams' statement continued.

"Once Bohnen and I got the kid to shore I was instructed to get the med bag from Bohnen’s unit and we assessed the child. Shortly after, I got back into my tower where I returned to provide lifeguard services for the rest of my shift," he continued.
‘HERO' MOM DIES AFTER USING LAST STRENGTH TO SAVE 4-YEAR-OLD SON FROM FLORIDA RIVER

"I’m grateful to have had the opportunity to return the child to his family safely. This is my job and I love what I do. I’m thankful to my fellow lifeguards who perform rescues just like this every day," Williams' statement concluded.

Witnesses say the dramatic rescue lasted far longer than the viral video shows, with the teen lifeguard refusing to release the child despite punishing surf. (Scott Vander Dussen/Instagram @Santacruznow)
Williams' heroics earned him national attention, praise and even an invitation to the White House.
MISSING GRAND CANYON HIKER, 83, RESCUED AFTER GETTING SEPARATED FROM COMPANION

"We’re going to bring this heroic young man, and his family, into the White House with, perhaps, the boy he saved, to give him a High Civilian Honor. Very brave, he deserves it!" the White House wrote in an X post attributed to President Donald Trump.
Williams' rescue was one of 34 rescues in the Santa Cruz district over the weekend, California State Parks said in a statement obtained by FOX 2 KTVU.

"All California State Park lifeguard towers were staffed, there were 6 units on, a two-person rescue water craft team, three permanent lifeguard units, and a lifeguard supervisor working in Pajaro Coast," California State Parks also said of the weekend.
Witnesses say the dramatic rescue lasted far longer than the viral video shows, with Ryder Williams refusing to release the child despite punishing surf. (Scott Vander Dussen/Instagram @Santacruznow)
The 10-year-old boy Williams rescued was identified by KTVU as being named Nathaniel. His father, Sumit Rai, praised Williams' efforts in an interview with KTVU.
"It was a remarkable effort to bring him back to shore. I mean Ryder fought the sea," he told the outlet.

"It's really hard to fight that, and my son was unconscious. He weighs about 100 pounds, and he was limp, so that's basically dead weight that he had to carry and hold onto to pull back to shore," he continued.

"It's so easy to let go, and he knew that if he lets go then he's gonna basically just float away, and he's gone. That's the end of it, and he would have died," Rai concluded.

title: Captured 'America's Most Wanted' fugitive Ronald Fischer abandons alias after 20 years on the run

story: After decades on the run as "Dr. Richard Graydon," Ronald Fischer appeared before a Rhode Island judge following his arrest last week. (WPRI)

After more than 20 years on the run, an "America's Most Wanted" fugitive who disappeared in the middle of his sexual assault trial stood before a Rhode Island judge this week under his real name for the first time since fleeing justice.

Ronald Fischer, 70, identified himself by his real name during a hearing in Newport Superior Court, where a judge canceled an outstanding warrant tied to his alleged failure to appear for trial in April 2005, arraigned him on a bail-jumping charge and set bail at $20,000 surety.
Fischer was arrested earlier this month aboard the 56-foot sailboat "Silver Lining" off the coast of New Jersey after investigators received a credible tip about his whereabouts.
'AMERICA'S MOST WANTED' FUGITIVE CAPTURED ON SAILBOAT OFF NJ COAST AFTER 20 YEARS ON THE RUN
During Monday's hearing, Fischer appeared without an attorney as the court discussed appointing counsel.
Ronald Fischer stands before a judge in Newport Superior Court after authorities arrested him last week aboard a sailboat off the New Jersey coast. (Pool)

Authorities said Fischer had been living under the alias "Dr. Richard Graydon" while eluding capture for more than 20 years.
'AMERICA'S MOST WANTED' EX-COP FUGITIVE RETURNED AFTER 20 YEARS ON THE RUN TO FACE MURDER, CHILD SEX CHARGES

Fischer disappeared during his 2005 sexual assault trial in Rhode Island, where he was accused of sexually assaulting a woman aboard his boat at a Portsmouth marina in 2003. title: Salman Rushdie attacker convicted of federal terrorism charges, motivated by Iranian fatwa
summary: Hadi Matar faces life in prison after a federal jury convicted him of terrorism charges related to his knife attack on Salman Rushdie in 2022.
story: The FBI confirms Michigan synagogue attack suspect Ayman Mohamad Ghazali was inspired by Hezbollah, with U.S. Attorney Jerome Gorgon clarifying the 'lone wolf' label is misleading. FMR Counterterrorism Analyst Jonathan Schanzer details Ghazali's family connection, including a brother killed as a Hezbollah commander. Schanzer stresses the heightened terror threat and the need for federal agencies to vigilantly monitor potential sleeper cells in the US.

The man who stabbed Salman Rushdie more than a dozen times on stage at an event in western New York was found guilty Wednesday of attempting to carry out a fatwa issued by Iran’s government against the award-winning British author more than 30 years earlier.

Hadi Matar, 28, is already serving a 25-year sentence after he was convicted last year in state court of attempted murder for the 2022 knife attack that left Rushdie blind in one eye and with nerve damage.

On Wednesday, a federal jury in Buffalo took less than two hours to convict Matar of all three charges — attempting to provide material support to the Iran-backed Hezbollah terrorist group, committing an act of terrorism that transcended national boundaries, and providing material support to terrorists, Reuters reported.
He now faces a maximum of life in prison and is set to be sentenced on November 3.
A HEZBOLLAH VETERAN IS HUNTING JEWS IN US COURTS — WE JUST NAMED HIM TO THE DOJ
Hadi Matar, the man convicted of stabbing author Salman Rushdie, arrives for his sentencing hearing at the Chautauqua County Courthouse in Chautauqua, New York, on May 16, 2025. (Geoff Robins / AFP)
Federal prosecutors argued that Matar had been enraged by Rushdie's 1988 novel "The Satanic Verses," which portrayed a fictionalized version of Muhammad that many Muslims saw as blasphemous.

A year later, Ayatollah Ruhollah Khomeini issued a fatwa, or a religious edict, urging Muslims across the world to kill Rushdie. Iran's government later backed away from the fatwa, only for Khomeini's successor, Ali Khamenei, to reaffirm it in 2017, Reuters reported, citing the U.S. Attorney's Office.

Prosecutors said Matar, who was born in the U.S. but has Lebanese citizenship, spent more than a year studying the fatwa before attempting to fulfill it. He had also turned to Islam after a visit to the Middle East years before the eventual attack.

On August 12, 2022, Rushdie was speaking at the Chautauqua Institution in Mayville, New York, when Matar rushed onstage and repeatedly stabbed the Indian-born author in the head, neck, torso and left hand.

Salman Rushdie with his Liberatum Cultural Honour award at Liberatum's 25th anniversary celebration, at Town Hall in King's Cross, north London, on July 8, 2026, (Jonathan Brady/PA Images via Getty Images)
MOJTABA KHAMENEI USING ‘BIN LADEN TEMPLATE’ TO SURVIVE, LEARNED FROM ABBOTTABAD: ANALYST
Matar's federal trial weighed whether he had committed an act of terrorism by attacking Rushdie.

Although prosecutors acknowledged that Matar never contacted anyone in Hezbollah, they argued that without the fatwa, he never would have been motivated to try to kill Rushdie, The New York Times reported.
Prosecutors presented Matar's notes to the jury, which referenced "Jihad" and the "need to kill him ASAP," according to the Times.
Matar's defense attorney, Nathaniel L. Barone II, argued that his client acted independently and was not being controlled by Hezbollah.
The Chautauqua Institution where Rushdie was attacked on August 12, 2022. (ANGELA WEISS/AFP via Getty Images)
AMERICAN ‘JIHAD’ FUELED BY 'RISKY SOURCE' INSIDE US BORDERS, WARNS NATIONAL SECURITY EXPERT

Prosecutors countered by showing evidence of Matar's devotion to Hezbollah, which included a photo of him wearing a Hezbollah shirt while making a salute, an essay he wrote that praised the terrorist group and a video he created using remarks from a former leader of Hezbollah, the Times reported.
Timothy Lynch, a federal prosecutor, said in his closing statement that Matar "wanted to be forever revered as a Hezbollah martyr," according to the Times.

People listen as writers gather to read selected works by British author Salman Rushdie, one week after he was stabbed while on stage, during a rally to show solidarity for free expression on Aug. 19, 2022. (TIMOTHY A. CLARY/AFP via Getty Images)
CLICK HERE TO DOWNLOAD THE FOX NEWS APP
Rushdie, who testified at the trial, has previously described the attack as something that took him back to the "distant past," when he spent a decade in hiding after the fatwa was issued.

"I saw the man in black running towards me, down the right-hand side of the seating area: black clothes, black face mask – he was coming in hard and low, a squat missile," Rushdie told "60 Minutes" host Anderson Cooper in April 2024. "I confess, I had sometimes imagined my assassin rising up in some public forum or other and coming for me in this way."

title: New audio released following Nolan Wells disappearance doesn't show 'anything nefarious': retired FBI agent
summary: A Sea Tow audio recording captures the frantic call from teens on a sinking boat at Horn Island the night Nolan Wells went missing on July 4.
story: A caller aboard the boat that brought Nolan Wells to Horn Island tells a Sea Tow dispatcher the vessel is sinking with seven people onboard on July 4. (Credit: MDMR)
A retired FBI agent says that new audio released following Nolan Wells' disappearance and death doesn't show "anything nefarious."

Wells, 18, went missing July 4 after a boat trip with friends to Horn Island, a barrier island off Mississippi's Gulf Coast. Crews searched the area for two days before a National Parks Service ranger found his remains on the island's northwestern tip on July 6.

Wells' friends returned to the mainland that afternoon without him. Jackson County Sheriff John Ledbetter has said investigators believe Wells chose to remain on the island, and it wasn't until later that night that his mother learned from one of his friends he was missing, prompting her to report it to authorities.

Fox News Digital obtained a recording of a call made to Sea Tow on the evening of July 4 by someone aboard the boat, who said the vessel was taking on water as it prepared to return to the mainland. The individual said there were seven people on board.
SEARCH CALLED OFF AFTER BODY MATCHING MISSING TEEN NOLAN WELLS FOUND OFF MISSISSIPPI COAST
Nolan Xavier Wells disappeared on the Fourth of July while boating with friends, according to authorities. (Jackson County Sheriff's Department via Facebook)
"Hey, we’re at the west tip of Horn, and our bilge pump stopped working. We’re sinking. Can y’all please come?" an individual can be heard saying to the Sea Tow dispatcher.
When the dispatcher asked how far the water is coming inside the boat, the individual replied, "It’s coming up... we’re just sinking. I don’t know. We’re going down though."
"And is everyone on board and in good health otherwise?" the dispatcher asked.
"Yeah, everyone is on board," the individual on the boat responded.
The man heard talking to the Sea Tow dispatcher requested someone to come help un-sink the boat and get it towed back to the Fort Bayou launch in Ocean Springs, Mississippi.
NOLAN WELLS INDEPENDENT AUTOPSY DOESN'T POINT TO FOUL PLAY, FORMER MEDICAL EXAMINER SAYS
Nolan Wells smiles on the field while playing wide receiver for Southwest Mississippi Community College. (Christine Wonsley/Facebook)

The dispatcher then spoke with a captain, who said he was already on the phone with a man who owned the boat, a relative of the teen who called, and said those on the boat were in a "panic" because the boat wouldn't crank.
SIGN UP TO GET THE LATEST TRUE CRIME NEWS

"It sounds like a bunch of kids on board on Horn Island," the dispatcher told the captain. "He’s saying the boat is sinking and he’s on Horn Island. It’s just unfortunate, he’s just a kid. It’s a lot going on.
LIKE WHAT YOU'RE READING? CLICK HERE FOR MORE
"He wants you guys to go out there and un-pump the boat and then tow it in," the dispatcher said.
The captain said the boat's owner told him the teens didn't "need any help right now, but if something changes, he'll call me back."
FOLLOW THE FOX TRUE CRIME TEAM ON X
Sea Tow didn't end up towing the boat.
Former FBI agent Jonathan Gilliam told Fox News Digital he doesn't believe the Sea Tow audio points to any signs of foul play, as some people on social media have claimed.
WATCH: Retired FBI agent says nothing 'nefarious' in newly released Nolan Wells boat audio
GOT A TIP?

"I don't hear anything nefarious... it just sounded like there was a lot of stuff going on, that they were taking on water — not panic as much as this young person was trying to resolve a situation in a party atmosphere."
Gilliam also pointed out that the call itself undercuts the idea of a cover-up.
LISTEN TO THE NEW 'CRIME & JUSTICE WITH DONNA ROTUNNO' PODCAST

"By the way, they're taking on water. They're going to be calling for assistance, which could lead to authorities. If they had done something, that'd be a very bad time for a person who'd done something nefarious to call out people and for them to get away with something. So I don't think it added anything to the conspiracies of something having occurred knowingly in a nefarious manner."

Several of Wells' friends told authorities he "chose to remain at the island" with an unidentified female rather than return to the mainland with the group he arrived with, according to a Mississippi Department of Marine Resources police report obtained by Fox News Digital.
GET BREAKING NEWS BY EMAIL

According to the police report, authorities "did not have reason to believe there were any water related exigencies or emergencies and he believed the most likely scenario was Nolan rode in on another vessel but did not have his phone in his possession to make contact with family."
CLICK HERE TO DOWNLOAD THE FOX NEWS APP

During a July 22 news conference, attorney Ben Crump revealed that an area of "red discoloration" was found on Wells' head, but said Dr. Roger Mitchell, who performed an independent autopsy, couldn't come to a conclusion on a cause or manner of death "pending further investigation." An official autopsy into Wells' death hasn't been completed.
Wells was a wide receiver at Southwest Mississippi Community College and had hopes to play at the Division 1 level, according to Crump, an attorney for his family.

title: Nancy Guthrie case: Unclaimed $1.2M reward suggests 'very small circle' of suspects, retired FBI agent says
summary: A retired FBI negotiator says the unclaimed $1.2 million reward in Nancy Guthrie's suspected abduction is a clue in and of itself six months after her kidnapping.
story: The Nancy Guthrie kidnapping group is likely small and not very professional, retired FBI supervisory agent Jason Pack told Fox News Digital, based on his understanding of the evidence.

EXCLUSIVE: TUCSON, Ariz. — The fact that a seven-figure reward remains unclaimed nearly six months after the suspected abduction of Nancy Guthrie from her home in Tucson's Catalina Foothills neighborhood tells one veteran investigator that if the masked intruder on her porch had help, it came from a small, tight-knit group.

"That tells me the circle who knows is very small, and whoever is in it is bound by something stronger than money: blood, fear, shared exposure," said Jason Pack, a retired FBI negotiator and supervisory agent who has been closely following the case. "Those bonds hold. Until they don't."

The more people who know about a crime, the more likely someone would come forward and claim the reward money, he said. The combined sum of rewards in the case is over $1.2 million — and none of it has been claimed 179 days after Guthrie's suspected abduction.
NANY GUTHRIE SHERIFF CHRIS NANOS SAYS HE'S 'STILL POSITIVE' CASE WILL BE RESOLVED DESPITE LONG WAIT

This image released by the FBI shows an armed individual appearing to have tampered with the camera at Nancy Guthrie's front door the morning of her disappearance in Tucson, Arizona, Sunday, February 1, 2026. (L) An undated photo of Nancy Guthrie was provided by NBC in response to the disappearance of the 84-year-old mother of Today Show host Savannah Guthrie. (Provided by FBI; Courtesy of NBC)
"Money like that usually pulls somebody loose from almost any group," Pack told Fox News Digital. "It hasn't."
Rather than a dead end, Pack sees the untouched reward as another clue.

"In my experience, a meaningful share of cases like this break sideways," he said. "Somebody gets arrested for something unrelated and starts talking. A relationship ends badly. Somebody's conscience finally outruns their fear. Six months is a long time to hold something this heavy, and the people around whoever did this have had six months to notice the change in them."
NANCY GUTHRIE CASE POINTS TO CRIMINAL UNDERWORLD 'WRENCH ATTACK' THEORY, RETIRED DETECTIVE SAYS
Savannah Guthrie poses alongside her mother Nancy Guthrie during a production break whilst hosting NBC's "Today Show" live from Australia. (Photo by Don Arnold/WireImage)

Pack said it looks like the abductor or abductors tried to plan the crime — and did it poorly. At least one suspect is believed to have cased out the house. He wore a ski mask, long sleeves and gloves, and covered the lens of her Nest doorbell camera — which was missing when police arrived the next day.

"When it went wrong, and I believe it went wrong fast, they had no plan for that either," he said. "Everything since reads to me like improvising around a failure, not professionals executing a plan."
Guthrie, the 84-year-old mother of "Today" co-host Savannah Guthrie, is dependent on heart medication and has a pacemaker. She has limited mobility — and a close-knit family.
Photos released on Feb. 10, 2026, show a "subject" on Nancy Guthrie's property. (Provided by FBI)
SAVANNAH GUTHRIE'S EMOTIONAL PLEA TO MOM'S KIDNAPPER MAY SIGNAL 'NEW LINE OF COMMUNICATION': REPORT

"She had dinner with her family on a Saturday night, went home, and never made it to church the next morning," Pack said. "That's who we're talking about. Not a case number. A mother who was supposed to be at church."
FOLLOW THE FOX TRUE CRIME TEAM ON X
While the suspects made critical mistakes, he said, that doesn't mean the investigation has stalled.
The Pima County Sheriff's Department marked six months into the investigation in a post shared Thursday, saying the probe remains active with DNA and digital evidence analysis still underway.
SIGN UP TO GET THE LATEST TRUE CRIME NEWS

Pima County Sheriff’s deputies speak outside of Nancy Guthrie's home in the Catalina Foothills after the disappearance of Guthrie, the 84-year-old mother of U.S. journalist and television host Savannah Guthrie, who went missing from her home in Tucson, Arizona, U.S. February 12, 2026. (Rebecca Noble/Reuters)
Pack also shared a direct message for Guthrie's neighbors and residents of the surrounding communities:
SEND US A TIP

"Go back and check your own cameras from that time period. Doorbell, security, dashcam," he said. "A lot of systems archive further back than people realize. If you drove through the area that night, pull your dashcam files."

Exterior view of the home of Nancy Guthrie in Tucson, Az., Wednesday, July 29, 2026. The mother of Today Show host, Savannah Guthrie was last seen alive in late January, and is believed to have been abducted. (Kat Ramirez for Fox News Digital)
If you saw something but don't have video, it's still worth speaking out, he said.

"And think about the people in your own life. Somebody who left town. Somebody whose behavior turned in February and never turned back," he said. "You don't have to be sure. That's not your job. Sorting it out is [the investigators' job]."

Investigators search the edges of Nancy Guthrie's street in the Catalina Foothills after the disappearance of Guthrie, the 84-year-old mother of U.S. journalist and television host Savannah Guthrie, who went missing from her home in Tucson, Arizona, U.S. on Feb. 11, 2026. (Rebecca Noble/Reuters)
In May, a source with knowledge of the case told Fox News Digital that the FBI was bringing new technology into the investigation.
LISTEN TO THE NEW 'CRIME & JUSTICE WITH DONNA ROTUNNO' PODCAST
Pima County Sheriff Chris Nanos, whose department is the lead agency, said in an interview this week that he still believes the case will be resolved.
"We have so much DNA to sort through," he said in an interview aired on "Today." "We have so much, in terms of video evidence, to look at."
Law enforcement agents check vegetation areas around Nancy Guthrie’s home in Tucson, Ariz., Wednesday, Feb. 11, 2026. (AP Photo/Ty ONeil)
And they've spent months learning things from the DNA and the video and other forensics that the public hasn't seen, Pack noted.

"I've watched cases break in month eight, month 14, month 30," said Pack, whose FBI career lasted 21 years, 11 of them as a negotiator. "Most every one of those families had stopped believing it was ever coming."
Anyone with information on the case is asked to dial 1-800-CALL-FBI. An anonymous reward can also be obtained by calling 520-88-CRIME with information that leads to an arrest in the case.

title: Man sentenced to 6 months in jail for ramming car into Jewish group's world headquarters in New York
summary: A man was sentenced to six months and a week behind bars for ramming his car into the Chabad Lubavitch World Headquarters earlier this year.
story: The New York Police Department and Department of Justice are investigating a possible hate crime after a car repeatedly rammed the door of Chabad-Lubavitch World Headquarters in Brooklyn Wednesday. (Daniel David Yeroshalmi via Storyful)
A man was sentenced on Wednesday to six months and a week behind bars for ramming his car into the Chabad Lubavitch World Headquarters in January, damaging some of the side-entrance door.

Dan Sohail, 36, of New Jersey, was sentenced in Brooklyn federal court, where he was also ordered to pay $20,000 in restitution. The sentence will allow Sohail, who has already spent six months in custody, to be released in about a week.
Sohail was charged with intentionally damaging religious property, and he pleaded guilty in May.

Prosecutors recommended a 14-month sentence, which would have kept Sohail behind bars for roughly another eight months, but the judge declined the request. Prosecutors sought the longer sentence as a deterrent to future attacks on Jewish institutions amid a rise in antisemitic hate crimes.
DRIVER RAMS CAR REPEATEDLY INTO DOORS OF NYC JEWISH SITE, SUSPECT DETAINED
Dan Sohail was sentenced to six months and a week behind bars for ramming his car into the Chabad Lubavitch World Headquarters. (AP Photo/Yuki Iwamura)

On Jan. 28, Sohail repeatedly rammed his vehicle into the Chabad Lubavitch World Headquarters. He moved protective barriers, gestured to congregants to get out of the way and drove his car into the building’s side entrance five times, knocking the door off its hinges and destroying his car's front bumper.
While the doors were damaged, no injuries were reported.

Judge Eric N. Vitaliano said he was "somewhat saddened" that the Justice Department wanted him to be influenced at sentencing by the public’s mistaken initial impression that the attack was a hate crime.
Prosecutors said ahead of sentencing that 80 of 146 hate crime incidents across New York City since the start of the year were based on crimes targeting Jewish people and institutions.
NY ASSEMBLYMAN CALLS FOR DOJ TO INVESTIGATE MAMDANI, PROTECT JEWISH NEW YORKERS AFTER STABBING ATTACKS

Judge Eric N. Vitaliano said he was "somewhat saddened" to see that the DOJ attempted to influence him because of a mistaken initial belief among the public that the attack was a hate crime. (Spencer Platt/Getty Images)

But Vitaliano said the government's push for a stricter sentence as a deterrent to future attacks was in part based on the incident initially being labeled as an "I-hate-the-Jews crime, or, worse, an act-of-terrorism crime."
The judge cited a psychiatric report and said Sohail's mental health challenges "played an important role" in his sentencing.
"This is a sad tale," Vitaliano said.
Sohail's lawyer, Mia Eisner-Grynberg, said he had been trying to win acceptance at the Jewish institution as he struggled with psychological issues.
Dan Sohail was charged with intentionally damaging religious property, pleading guilty in May. (Spencer Platt/Getty Images)
CLICK HERE TO DOWNLOAD THE FOX NEWS APP

Eisner-Grynberg told the judge in court papers before sentencing that Sohail was battling depression and post-traumatic stress disorder after a traumatic childhood when he carried out the attack, even as he "desperately sought belonging and understanding through his exploration of Judaism."
She said Sohail attended the Chabad he later attacked, finding rabbinical students there "warm and welcoming."

Sohail "danced with them" and followed their recommendation to visit Israel, but he became erratic and extremely anxious after returning to the U.S., "begging" members of Chabad to help him, Eisner-Grynberg said.
Ramming the car into the building was "an irrational cry for help," she said.
The Associated Press contributed to this report.

title: Lindsay Clancy prosecutors ‘squeeze’ timeline from ex-husband as jury weighs ‘murder versus madness’: expert
summary: Patrick Clancy's testimony reveals the timeline of texts, calls, and errands just before his three children were strangled in their Duxbury home.
story: Attorney Shari Karney discusses how Patrick Clancy’s testimony could shape the prosecution’s case and Lindsay Clancy’s murder defense.
If you or someone you know is having thoughts of suicide, please contact the National Suicide Prevention Lifeline at 1-800-273-TALK (8255).

Patrick Clancy’s painstaking account of the night his three children died may have given prosecutors their clearest framework yet for arguing that Lindsay Clancy was lucid, deliberate and criminally responsible at the time of the killings, a legal expert says.

Testifying Wednesday in Plymouth Superior Court, Patrick walked jurors minute by minute through the errands that took him away from the family’s Duxbury, Massachusetts, home on Jan. 24, 2023: a trip to CVS for a child’s stool softener, followed by a stop to pick up dinner.
HEATED LINDSAY CLANCY COURTROOM EXCHANGE OVER 911 CALL, CRIME SCENE PHOTOS SETS STAGE FOR MOM’S MURDER TRIAL

He said Lindsay called him back while he was inside CVS, understood why he was there and calmly approved a generic substitute. When he returned home, he found an eerily quiet house, blood inside the couple’s locked bedroom and Lindsay injured beneath an open second-story window.
Lindsay Clancy attends her murder trial at Plymouth Superior Court in Plymouth on July 29, 2026. (David L. Ryan/Pool)
When Patrick found Lindsay Clancy lying on her back beneath their bedroom window, he said she had deep cuts on her wrists and a red line across her neck.
LINDSAY CLANCY’S EX-HUSBAND DETAILS ‘BIG SPIRAL’ AS EXPERT SAYS ONE PART ‘SCARED ME’ IN MOM’S MURDER TRIAL
"What happened?" he recalled asking her.
"I tried to kill myself," she responded, according to Patrick.
He then asked, "Where are the kids?"
Lindsay and Patrick Clancy with two of their three children in this undated photo (Lindsay Marie Clancy/ Facebook)
LINDSAY CLANCY’S EX-HUSBAND DETAILS PILL USE AS EXPERT SAYS EVIDENCE COULD SHAPE MURDER TRIAL
"They’re in the basement," Lindsay told him.
Patrick testified that she did not say the children were injured, in danger or needed help.
The defense is expected to argue Clancy lacks criminal responsibility because she suffered from postpartum psychosis and was overmedicated. (Greg Derr/The Patriot Ledger via Pool)

Attorney Shari Karney said those seemingly mundane details, the text messages, phone call, dinner order and timing of Patrick’s drive, may become critical as prosecutors try to prove Lindsay understood her actions when the children were strangled with exercise bands.
"I call this case murder versus madness," Karney told Fox News Digital.
Exterior view of the home of Patrick and Lindsay Clancy in Duxbury, MA on Wednesday, Feb. 15, 2023. (David McGlynn for Fox News Digital)

Karney said Patrick’s testimony largely helped the prosecution because it portrayed Lindsay as responsive and organized shortly before the killings. The state, she said, is attempting to "squeeze that timeline" as tightly as possible around the precise moment the children were killed.
WATCH: Patrick Clancy recounts finding wife after she said she tried to kill herself
FOLLOW THE FOX TRUE CRIME TEAM ON X
"That’s fairly lucid," Karney said of Lindsay’s ability to discuss the CVS purchase and coordinate the takeout order.

But the defense is expected to argue that competence during routine tasks does not establish criminal responsibility during the killings. Lindsay’s attorneys contend she suffered from severe mental illness, including postpartum psychosis, and was impaired by a shifting regimen of psychiatric medications.
Patrick Clancy on the stand. The Lindsay Clancy murder trial is held at Plymouth Superior Court in Plymouth on July 29, 2026. (David L. Ryan/Pool)
LIKE WHAT YOU'RE READING? CLICK HERE FOR MORE

Patrick testified that Lindsay later told him she heard a man’s voice telling her that if she did not act then, she would "lose her chance." He also said she had never previously told him she was hearing voices or experiencing psychosis.
Karney said the case will likely turn on whether jurors view the killings as a calculated act or "a catastrophic collapse" caused by severe psychological illness.
WATCH: Lindsay Clancy breaks down as jury hears husband's frantic 911 call
SEND US A TIP

The emotional stakes were on display when prosecutors played Patrick’s 911 call for the jury. The recording was barred from broadcast or reproduction under a court order, and the pool camera remained trained on Lindsay.
She sobbed and buried her face in her hands as the call played.
GOT A TIP?
Karney said that reaction could help both sides.

For the defense, she said, it humanized Lindsay as a "shattered, broken" mother confronting the consequences of the worst night of her life. For prosecutors, the same reaction captured the horror of the killings.
LISTEN TO THE NEW 'CRIME & JUSTICE WITH DONNA ROTUNNO' PODCAST
Before the recording was played, Judge William Sullivan warned jurors not to allow sympathy, anger, passion or pity to influence their verdict.

"You must not be influenced in any way by the unpleasant nature of some of the evidence," Sullivan said, reminding jurors that their verdict must not be based on "sympathy, anger, passion or prejudice or pity."
GET BREAKING NEWS BY EMAIL

Assistant Plymouth County District Attorney Jennifer Sprague entering a bag of prescription pills that were prescribed to Lindsay Clancy into evidence during the first day of her trial. (Greg Derr/Pool/The Patriot Ledger)

Clancy, a former labor and delivery nurse at Massachusetts General Hospital, has pleaded not guilty to three counts each of murder and strangulation.

title: Army conducts first overseas test of 'Hammer of the Gods' weapon-disrupting system
summary: The Army says its "Hammer of the Gods" electronic warfare system completed its first overseas maritime test, disrupting navigation signals used by enemy precision weapons.
story: French Adm. Pierre Vandier said Ukraine has exposed an arsenal that cannot be produced at the scale now required, warning there is "no way to produce 50,000 Patriots a year."

The U.S. Army on Sunday revealed it has tested a new warfare system overseas designed to covertly scramble the navigation signals used by enemy precision weapons, making it harder for adversaries to accurately strike targets from long distances while avoiding detection.
The electronic system, dubbed "Hammer of the Gods," was tested at sea off the U.S. West Coast for the first time in mid-July as part of the Project Convergence Capstone 6 (PC-C6) experiment.
While land-based versions have been demonstrated over the past two years, the exercise marked the official debut of the maritime variant, the Army said.
The portable signal disruptor can reportedly blind enemy to several precision-guided weapons such as long-range artillery, guided missiles and cruise missiles.
UKRAINE’S BATTLEFIELD IS TRANSFORMING THE FUTURE OF NATO
The Hammer of the Gods was tested overseas for the first time in mid-July. (U.S. Army)
The radio signals specifically jam positioning, navigation and timing (PNT) signals, including GPS data, that precision weapons rely on to navigate accurately.
Without reliable PNT data, weapon accuracy drops sharply, increasing the likelihood of delayed missions and missed targets.
The system also creates a resilient communications network that allows friendly forces to stay connected despite heavy electronic jamming.
REPORT WARNS RUSSIA USING SHADOW FLEET TO PROBE NATO DRONE DEFENSES
U.S. Army soldiers march during a military parade on Armed Forces Day in Vilnius, Lithuania, Nov. 25, 2023.  (Yauhen Yerchak/SOPA Images/LightRocket via Getty Images)
It links military devices together, so troops can continue to "shoot, move and communicate" even while operating in degraded environments.
Army officials said the experiment demonstrated the counter-PNT system could be successfully launched, operated and recovered in real-world maritime environments.
CLICK HERE TO DOWNLOAD THE FOX NEWS APP
Multiple U.S. Army soldiers walk behind a U.S. flag. (istock)

The testing brought together the U.S. Army, Navy and Space Force, alongside U.S. Space Forces Pacific, Naval Base San Diego and the U.S. Army Space and Missile Defense Command, to integrate space, cyber and conventional capabilities during the exercise.
Bonny Chu is a Breaking and Trending News Writer for Fox News Digital

title: Grandmother's missed pickup leads to grim discovery in church parking lot
summary: Emmanuel Wesley allegedly shot his mother twice in the back as she sat in her car, then drove away. He now faces up to 50 years to life in prison.
story: Fox News Flash top headlines are here. Check out what's clicking on FoxNews.com.

A California grandmother vanished after failing to pick up her grandchild, sparking a desperate search that ended days later with the grim discovery of her body inside her car in a church parking lot and murder charges against her son.
Emmanuel Wesley, 23, of Santa Ana, is charged with murder in the death of his 61-year-old mother, Theresa Jones.

Prosecutors allege he shot her twice in the back while she sat behind the wheel of her vehicle outside the Fullerton Police Department on the Fourth of July before moving her body into the passenger seat and driving away.
Jones' disappearance first raised alarms on July 7 when she failed to pick up one of her grandchildren and stopped answering repeated calls from loved ones, according to prosecutors.
MISSOURI MOM OF 5 FATALLY SHOT WHILE BUYING SLUSHIES WITH CHILDREN; POLICE SEARCH FOR GUNMAN
Theresa Jones' family said the 61-year-old was known for her infectious personality and unwavering devotion to her children and grandchildren. (GoFundMe)

Four days later, on July 11, officers found Jones' body inside her vehicle, which had been abandoned in the parking lot of a church in Fullerton. Prosecutors allege she had been shot twice in the back.
Investigators say surveillance cameras captured the moments surrounding the killing.
TWO FOUND SHOT TO DEATH INSIDE CAR ON UNIVERSITY OF CHICAGO CAMPUS: REPORT
Exterior of the Fullerton Police Department, where investigators say Theresa Jones was fatally shot before her vehicle was driven away. (Photo by Kevork Djansezian/Getty Images)
Video allegedly shows Jones pulling up outside the Fullerton Police Department around 2:46 p.m. on July 4 with Wesley riding in the back seat.
Authorities say Jones suddenly slumped over in the driver's seat before Wesley climbed out of the back seat, pushed her body into the passenger seat, got behind the wheel and drove away.

"The death of any human being is a tragedy," Orange County District Attorney Todd Spitzer said. "For someone to kill their own mother is another level of depravity. We will do everything we can to pursue justice for Ms. Jones and everyone who loved her."
BELOVED TEACHER KILLED AS SHE SLEPT, DAUGHTER STABBED IN ATTACK AS MOTIVE REMAINS UNCLEAR: DA
Theresa Jones is pictured holding a baby in a family photo shared after her death. (GoFundMe)
Jones' family remembered the 61-year-old as a devoted Christian whose faith shaped every part of her life.

"She loved her family fiercely, always putting the needs of her children and grandchildren above her own," the family wrote in a GoFundMe created to help cover funeral expenses. "To know Theresa was to love her."
Loved ones described Jones as smart, funny and full of life, saying her vibrant personality earned her the nickname "Cardi B."
The fundraiser recalls the family's agonizing search after Jones unexpectedly failed to pick up her beloved grandchild, ending with the heartbreaking discovery of her body a week later.

"We want to honor the beautiful life Theresa lived and the immense love she poured into the world," the family wrote. "The shock of her loss has left a profound, empty space in the hearts of everyone who loved her."
CLICK HERE TO DOWNLOAD THE FOX NEWS APP
Wesley has pleaded not guilty and remains held without bail in the Orange County Jail.
If convicted of murder and the firearm enhancement, prosecutors say he faces up to 50 years to life in prison.
